summary: Blueprint of Arithmetic statistics, counting fields and Selmer distributions, stages ST.0–ST.5, following the accepted restructuring RS-07 (which narrows ST.0–ST.4) and built on Bhargava–Shankar (arXiv:1006.1002), Bhargava–Shankar–Tsimerman (arXiv:1005.0672), Bhargava's Higher Composition Laws, and the maintainer-added Burungale–Tian (arXiv:2506.03465). ST.0 owns arithmetic families with their equivalence relations, height orderings, local conditions and weights, the binary-quartic invariants I and J with the eligible pairs and the height normalisation 27·H_E = 4·H', and Burungale–Tian's squareclass-height family of quadratic twists with its finiteness and density comparison; the elliptic-curve minimal-pair height is imported from Tau Ceti EllipticCurves layer 8. ST.1 proves the orbit parametrizations: 2-Selmer elements as locally soluble binary quartics with stabilizers and the comparison to the cohomological Selmer group, the embedding into pairs of ternary quadratic forms, and the Delone–Faddeev and Bhargava parametrizations of cubic and quartic rings (quintic at statement level). ST.2 counts integral orbits in fundamental domains, cuts off the cusp, bounds reducible forms and proves the uniformity estimate that passes to infinitely many local conditions, importing Davenport's lemma from GeometryOfNumbersAndQuadraticArithmetic GN.4. ST.3 proves Davenport–Heilbronn (cubic fields and the average 3-torsion of quadratic class groups) by the Bhargava–Shankar–Tsimerman route, states the quartic and quintic counts, and states the Cohen–Lenstra and Malle predictions only as explicit hypotheses. ST.4 decomposes Bhargava–Shankar §3: local masses, the Tamagawa number of PGL2, the average size 3 of the 2-Selmer group (with the positivity of every local mass made explicit) and the average-rank bound 1.5. ST.5 states the higher Selmer averages, the Poonen–Rains and Cohen–Lenstra models, function-field results, and Burungale–Tian's two distribution inputs: Smith's 2^∞ theorem as a stated input owned by the Part II ArithmeticStatisticsPartIISmithMethod (no dependency on it), and the BKLOS 3^∞ corank deduction in full. Open: the proofs of the quartic/quintic counts and several higher-moment theorems, BKLOS §§3–8, the requests to GN.4, AN.5, AN.8, SelmerIwasawaCohomology, CM and the Tau Ceti elliptic-curve layers, and the items of the other accepted paper routes to this roadmap, which a later queue will add.

nodes.title: Arithmetic families: objects up to equivalence, ordered by a Northcott height, with weighted and unweighted counting functions
nodes.statement: An arithmetic family is a pair (ι, H) in which ι is a type of arithmetic objects already taken up to the family's equivalence relation — a quotient type Quotient s of a type of representatives by a setoid s (integral models up to change of variables, number fields up to ℚ-isomorphism) or an orbit type Γ\V = MulAction.orbitRel.Quotient Γ V of a group action (integral binary quartic forms up to GL₂(ℤ)) — and H : ι → ℝ is a height with Mathlib's Northcott property: {i : H(i) ≤ B} is finite for every real B. For a weight w : ι → M into an additive commutative monoid, the weighted counting function is N_H(w; X) := Σ_{H(i) ≤ X} w(i), a finite sum over heightLE X = {i : H(i) ≤ X}; the unweighted count of a subfamily S ⊆ ι is N_H(S; X) := #{i ∈ S : H(i) ≤ X} = N_H(1_S; X); the strict-cutoff count written by the sources is N_H^<(S; X) := #{i ∈ S : H(i) < X}. Constructions: ofQuotient, from a class-invariant height on representatives whose induced height is Northcott; comap along a map f : κ → ι with finite fibres (Northcott by Mathlib's Northcott.comp_of_finite_fibers), with the multiplicity formula N_{H∘f}(f⁻¹S; X) = N_H(#f⁻¹(·)·1_S; X), which is how an isomorphism multiplicity is made explicit; rescale by c > 0, with N_{cH}(S; X) = N_H(S; X/c); ofNat for a natural-valued Northcott height N, whose carrier heightLE is Tau Ceti's normLE N and whose weighted count is Tau Ceti's summatory N w; ofMulHeight, the elements of a number field ordered by Mathlib's multiplicative Weil height mulHeight₁ (Northcott by NumberField.finite_setOfPred_mulHeight₁_le). Proposed declaration: the structure ArithmeticFamily ι with fields height and northcott.
hypotheses: The equivalence relation is built into the type ι: counts are counts of classes, never of representatives, unless comap is used with its explicit fibre multiplicities.
Heights are real-valued. A natural-valued height enters through ofNat and then agrees with Tau Ceti's normLE/summatory carrier, so Tau Ceti's counting lemmas apply unchanged.
The cutoff is inclusive (H(i) ≤ X), as in Tau Ceti's normLE. The strict cutoff H(i) < X of the sources is countLT; relative densities do not depend on the choice (ST.0/relative-density).
proofSteps: heightLE X is the toFinset of the finite set {i : H(i) ≤ X} given by the northcott field; weightedCount is the finite sum over it and count is Set.ncard of {i ∈ S : H(i) ≤ X}.
count_eq_weightedCount_indicator, count_mono_set, count_mono, count_union_of_disjoint and count_eq_zero_of_lt are finite-set identities.
tendsto_count_atTop: an infinite S is not contained in any bounded-height set (those are finite), so its members have unbounded height and the monotone count tends to infinity.

comap is Northcott by mathlib:Northcott.comp_of_finite_fibers (the instance Filter.TendstoCofinite f is exactly finiteness of fibres); count_comap splits {k : f(k) ∈ S, H(f(k)) ≤ X} into the fibres over heightLE X.

rescale: {i : cH(i) ≤ B} = {i : H(i) ≤ B/c}. ofNat: {i : (N i : ℝ) ≤ B} ⊆ {i : N i ≤ ⌊B⌋₊}, finite by Northcott N; its heightLE has the members of tauceti:TauCeti.normLE (tauceti:TauCeti.coe_normLE), so weightedCount (ofNat N) w = tauceti:TauCeti.summatory N w.
ofMulHeight: the northcott field is mathlib:NumberField.finite_setOfPred_mulHeight₁_le.
acceptance: The integers ordered by |n| have exactly 7 members of height at most 3.

The rationals ordered by |x| are rejected: the absolute value of a representative is not Northcott. The same mistake in arithmetic form is ordering rational Weierstrass equations instead of ℚ-isomorphism classes (EllipticCurves Layer 8 records that bounded-height finiteness fails there).
For ofNat N, weightedCount agrees with TauCeti.summatory N w at every X, so eventually_summatory_indicator_sub_eq and the Abel-summation interface of Tau Ceti apply to every natural-valued family.

Representatives against classes: for the squareclass twist family of y² = x³ − x over ℚ the twist map has fibres {t, t + [−1]} (ST.0/isomorphism-multiplicity-of-the-twist-family), and count_comap records the factor 2 between counting squareclasses and counting isomorphism classes of twists.

nodes.title: Upper, lower and limiting relative densities of a subfamily in a height-ordered family
nodes.statement: Let (ι, H) be an arithmetic family and S, T ⊆ ι. The proportion of T lying in S at cutoff X is r_X(S | T) := N_H(S ∩ T; X)/N_H(T; X), read as 0 when N_H(T; X) = 0. The upper relative density is d̄(S | T) := limsup_{X→∞} r_X(S | T), the lower relative density (the lower limiting proportion) is d̲(S | T) := liminf_{X→∞} r_X(S | T), and S has relative density d in T, HasDensity S T d, when r_X(S | T) → d as the real cutoff X → ∞. The strict-cutoff proportion r^<_X(S | T) uses N_H^<. Properties: 0 ≤ r_X ≤ 1; HasDensity S T d if and only if d̲(S | T) = d̄(S | T) = d; if T is infinite then T has density 1 in itself; ∅ has density 0; for infinite T, the complement T ∖ S has density 1 − d and disjoint S, S′ have density d + d′; a finite set has density 0 in an infinite T, and changing S by a finite set does not change its density (the difference of the two counts is eventually constant, Tau Ceti's eventually_summatory_indicator_sub_eq); the inclusive and the strict cutoffs give the same density; H and cH (c > 0) give the same densities. Proposed declarations: ArithmeticFamily.ratio, upperDensity, lowerDensity, HasDensity, ratioLT.
hypotheses: The reference family T is always named: 'density one' is relative to a stated T. Burungale–Tian's 'density one subset of the positive square-free integers n ≡ 1, 2, 3 mod 8' is HasDensity A S 1 with S that family, not density one among all integers.
A lower bound for the lower density (Burungale–Tian's 'at least 50%' in Proposition 1.3) is not the existence of a limit.

The density depends on the height. For the same S and T, two heights give the same densities only when a comparison lemma applies (ST.0/constant-rescaling-of-a-height, ST.0/piecewise-rescaling-of-a-height).
proofSteps: Nonnegativity and ratio_le_one: N_H(S ∩ T; X) ≤ N_H(T; X).

hasDensity_iff_lowerDensity_eq_upperDensity: the proportion is bounded in [0, 1], so limsup and liminf exist in ℝ and coincide exactly when the limit exists (mathlib:Filter.limsup and its order dual).
hasDensity_self and hasDensity_empty: the proportion is eventually 1 (T infinite, so N_H(T; X) > 0 eventually), respectively identically 0.
diff and union: N_H((T ∖ S) ∩ T; X) = N_H(T; X) − N_H(S ∩ T; X) and additivity of counts on disjoint sets.

hasDensity_zero_of_finite and congr_finite: the numerator is eventually constant (tauceti:TauCeti.eventually_summatory_indicator_sub_eq for natural-valued heights; the same finite-set argument in general) while the denominator tends to ∞ (ST.0/arithmetic-family, tendsto_count_atTop).

hasDensity_iff_tendsto_ratioLT: since heightLE is finite, for each X there is ε > 0 with N^<(·; X) = N(·; X − ε) and N(·; X) = N^<(·; X + ε); so every strict proportion is an inclusive one at a nearby cutoff and conversely, and the limits agree.
hasDensity_rescale_iff: r_X(S | T) for cH is r_{X/c}(S | T) for H (count_rescale), and X/c → ∞ with X.
acceptance: The even natural numbers have density 1/2 in ℕ ordered by n; the union of the blocks [4^k, 2·4^k) has lower density 1/3 and upper density 2/3, hence no density.
Under the height n on even and n² on odd numbers the even numbers have density 1: the same set in the same ambient family has a different density for a different height.
Strict and inclusive cutoffs give the same limit, as the sources' Σ(X) = {H < X} and Burungale–Tian's S(X) = {n ≤ X} require.

nodes.title: Relative densities multiply along a tower of subfamilies
nodes.statement: Let S ⊆ T ⊆ U be subfamilies of an arithmetic family. If S has relative density α in T and T has relative density β in U, then S has relative density αβ in U. Proposed declaration: ArithmeticFamily.HasDensity.trans.
hypotheses: No infinitude hypothesis is needed: the proportions are read with 0/0 = 0.
proofSteps: For S ⊆ T ⊆ U and every X: if N(T; X) > 0 then N(S; X)/N(U; X) = (N(S; X)/N(T; X))·(N(T; X)/N(U; X)); if N(T; X) = 0 then N(S; X) = 0 and both sides vanish. So r_X(S | U) = r_X(S | T)·r_X(T | U) identically.
Take limits with mathlib:Filter.Tendsto.mul.
acceptance: With P the positive squarefree integers, S ⊆ P those ≡ 1, 2, 3 (mod 8) and A of density one in S, A has density 1/2 in P (ST.0/density-one-in-the-even-parity-classes-is-half-of-all-squarefree): the passage from Burungale–Tian's Theorem 1.2 to the '50% of the positive square-free integers' of their abstract.
With α = 1/3 and β = 1/2 (one residue class of S inside S, S inside P) the class n ≡ 1 (mod 8) has density 1/6 in P.

nodes.title: A density-one subset stays of density one in every subfamily of positive lower density
nodes.statement: Let A ⊆ ι and U ⊆ T be subfamilies of an arithmetic family. If A has relative density 1 in T and U has positive lower relative density in T, then A ∩ U has relative density 1 in U. Proposed declaration: ArithmeticFamily.HasDensity.inter_of_lowerDensity_pos.
hypotheses: Positivity of the lower density of U in T is necessary: a density-one set may miss a density-zero subfamily entirely.
proofSteps: For every X with N(U; X) > 0: r_X(U ∖ A | U) = N((U ∖ A); X)/N(U; X) ≤ N((T ∖ A); X)/N(U; X) = r_X(T ∖ A | T)/r_X(U | T).
By ST.0/relative-density (diff), r_X(T ∖ A | T) → 0, while r_X(U | T) ≥ d̲(U | T)/2 > 0 for all large X; hence r_X(U ∖ A | U) → 0 and r_X(A ∩ U | U) = 1 − r_X(U ∖ A | U) → 1.
acceptance: Each residue class n ≡ a (mod 8), a ∈ {1, 2, 3}, has relative density 1/3 in Burungale–Tian's family S (ST.0/even-parity-classes-have-half-density and ST.0/squarefree-integers-in-residue-classes); so a density-one subset of S is of density one in each of the three classes. This is the input to the comparison with Goldfeld's ordering by fundamental discriminants (ST.0/piecewise-rescaling-of-a-height, sourceIssue ArithmeticStatistics/E104).
Necessity of positivity: in ℕ ordered by n, A = ℕ ∖ {perfect squares} has density 1 but A ∩ U = ∅ for U the perfect squares.

sources.match: The family of Theorem 1.2 is a union of three residue classes of positive lower density; statements about the whole family restrict to each class by this lemma.

nodes.title: Rescaling a height by a constant preserves densities and multiplies an X^κ constant by c^(−κ)
nodes.statement: Let (ι, H) be an arithmetic family and c > 0, and let H′ = cH (ArithmeticFamily.rescale). Then N_{H′}(S; X) = N_H(S; X/c) for all S and X; relative densities (upper, lower, limiting) for H′ and for H coincide; and if N_H(S; X)/X^κ → C as X → ∞, then N_{H′}(S; X)/X^κ → C·c^(−κ). Applied to Bhargava–Shankar's two heights on elliptic curves, H′ = (27/4)H (ST.0/quartic-to-curve-height-normalisation): the curves with H′(E) ≤ X are those with H(E) ≤ 4X/27, the two heights order every set of curves identically, averages do not change, and an asymptotic constant C for the count by H becomes (4/27)^(5/6)·C for the count by H′ (κ = 5/6). Proposed declaration: ArithmeticFamily.tendsto_rescale_count_div_rpow.
hypotheses: c > 0 is a constant; a height comparable to H only up to bounded factors does not preserve densities (see ST.0/piecewise-rescaling-of-a-height for the piecewise-constant case).
proofSteps: count_rescale (ST.0/arithmetic-family): {i ∈ S : cH(i) ≤ X} = {i ∈ S : H(i) ≤ X/c}.
N_{H′}(S; X)/X^κ = (N_H(S; X/c)/(X/c)^κ)·c^(−κ), and X/c → ∞; take limits.
Densities: hasDensity_rescale_iff of ST.0/relative-density.
acceptance: Bhargava–Shankar: an X^(5/6) constant for the ordering by H becomes (4/27)^(5/6) times itself for the ordering by H′ (the decomposition review corrected the direction of this factor).
The average of #S₂(E) over a large family is the same for H and H′ (it is a ratio of two counts at the same cutoff).

sources.excerpt: Note that H and H′ only differ by a constant factor; namely, for every elliptic curve E over Q we have 27H(E) = 4H′(E).
sources.match: The comparison is a constant rescaling; this lemma is what makes 'the same ordering' precise for counts, densities and constants.

nodes.title: Changing a height by constant factors on finitely many pieces averages the piecewise densities
nodes.statement: Let H and H′ be two heights on the same objects ι (families F = (ι, H), G = (ι, H′)), let T₁, …, T_k ⊆ ι be pairwise disjoint and c_j > 0 with H′ = c_j·H on T_j. Suppose that for some κ > 0 and a_j > 0, N_H(T_j; X)/X^κ → a_j for every j, and that A ⊆ ι has relative density d_j in T_j for H. Then A has relative density (Σ_j c_j^(−κ) a_j d_j)/(Σ_j c_j^(−κ) a_j) in T = ⋃_j T_j for H′. In particular density one in every piece gives density one for H′. Proposed declaration: ArithmeticFamily.hasDensity_piecewise_rescale.
hypotheses: The pieces must each have an X^κ asymptotic with the same exponent κ and positive constant; without it the weights of the pieces are not defined.
The lemma compares two orderings of the same objects; it is the 'comparison' that the roadmap requires before a theorem for one height is used for another.
proofSteps: On T_j, N_{H′}(A ∩ T_j; X) = N_H(A ∩ T_j; X/c_j) (count_rescale restricted to T_j).
Sum over j: N_{H′}(A ∩ T; X) = (Σ_j c_j^(−κ)a_j d_j + o(1))X^κ and N_{H′}(T; X) = (Σ_j c_j^(−κ)a_j + o(1))X^κ; divide.
acceptance: Goldfeld's ordering against Burungale–Tian's for E : y² = x³ − x. The twist by a fundamental discriminant d is the twist by its squarefree part m = |d| or |d|/4 (the squareclass), and E^(−m) = E^(m) (ST.0/isomorphism-multiplicity-of-the-twist-family). Each positive squarefree m occurs for two fundamental discriminants (one of each sign) with |d| = c·m, c = 1 for d ≡ 1 (mod 4) and c = 4 otherwise: for m ≡ 1 (mod 4) the factors are 1 and 4, for m ≡ 3 (mod 4) they are 4 and 1, for m ≡ 2 (mod 4) both are 4. With κ = 1 and a_j = 1/π² for each of the six classes of m modulo 8 (ST.0/squarefree-integers-in-residue-classes), the classes 1, 2, 3 (mod 8) (root number +1) carry weight 5/4 + 1/2 + 5/4 = 3 of the total 6, so exactly half of the fundamental discriminants ordered by |d| have root number +1, and a subset of density one in each of those classes for the ordering by m has density one among them for the ordering by |d| (with ST.0/density-one-restricts-to-subfamilies-of-positive-lower-density). A numerical count to 2·10⁶ gives the proportion 0.49999.
With k = 1 this is ST.0/constant-rescaling-of-a-height.

nodes.title: Stabilizer weights 1/#Stab and the weighted orbit count of a family of orbits
nodes.statement: Let a group Γ act on a type V and let F be an arithmetic family on the orbit type Γ\V = MulAction.orbitRel.Quotient Γ V (for instance GL₂(ℤ) or PGL₂(ℤ) acting on integral binary quartic forms, with the class height H). The stabilizer weight of an orbit Γv is w(Γv) := 1/#Stab_Γ(v) (Nat.card, so an infinite stabilizer gets weight 0); it is well defined because Stab_Γ(γv) = γ·Stab_Γ(v)·γ⁻¹ (Mathlib's MulAction.stabilizer_smul_eq_stabilizer_map_conj). The stabilizer-weighted orbit count of S ⊆ Γ\V is N^w(S; X) := Σ_{Γv ∈ S, H(Γv) ≤ X} w(Γv) = weightedCount (1_S·w) X; the unweighted count is N(S; X) = count S X. Properties: w ≤ 1; w > 0 when the stabilizer is finite; w = 1 exactly when the stabilizer is trivial; the mass formula Σ_{orbits} w = #V/#Γ for finite Γ and V (Mathlib's class formula MulAction.card_eq_sum_card_group_div_card_stabilizer); if a finite subgroup Z ≤ Γ acts trivially, #Z·w(Γv) = 1/#(Stab_Γ(v)/Z) is the weight for the faithful action of Γ/Z. For GL₂(ℤ) on binary quartic forms −1 acts trivially (ST.0/binary-quartic-form), every GL₂(ℤ)-stabilizer has even order 2r, and Bhargava–Shankar's weight 1/r is 2w = 1/#Stab_{PGL₂(ℤ)}(f). Proposed declarations: stabilizerWeight, weightedOrbitCount.
hypotheses: The orbit family, with its Northcott property, is an input. For GL₂(ℤ)-classes of irreducible integral binary quartic forms of bounded height, finiteness comes from reduction theory (Bhargava–Shankar §§2.1–2.2; they quote Borel–Harish-Chandra [10, Thm 6.9]); forms of height 0 (all multiples of x⁴) must be excluded.
The normalisation by a trivially acting subgroup is an explicit factor #Z, never absorbed silently: Bhargava–Shankar's 1/r is twice the GL₂(ℤ)-stabilizer weight.
proofSteps: stabilizerWeight is Quotient.lift of v ↦ (Nat.card Stab_Γ(v))⁻¹; the lift condition is that conjugate subgroups have the same cardinality (mathlib:MulAction.stabilizer_smul_eq_stabilizer_map_conj and the conjugation equivalence).
stabilizerWeight_eq_one_iff, _pos, _le_one: Nat.card of a finite nontrivial group is ≥ 2; of the trivial group 1.
finsum_stabilizerWeight: divide mathlib:MulAction.card_eq_sum_card_group_div_card_stabilizer, #V = Σ_ω #Γ/#Stab(ω), by #Γ.
natCard_mul_stabilizerWeight: Z ≤ Stab_Γ(v) for every v, and #Stab_Γ(v) = #Z·#(Stab_Γ(v)/Z) (Lagrange).
acceptance: For {±1} = (ℤ/3)ˣ acting on ℤ/3 by multiplication, the orbits {0} and {1, 2} have weights 1/2 and 1, total 3/2 = #V/#Γ; weighting by reciprocal orbit length would give 2.
In the regular action of a group on itself every weight is 1 and the weighted count is the count.

Bhargava–Shankar p. 9: n_i·N(V^(i); X) is the number of integral points in the fundamental multiset, with orbits whose GL₂(ℤ)-stabilizer has order 2r counted with weight 1/r; that weight is natCard_mul_stabilizerWeight with Z = {±1}.

nodes.title: Weighted and unweighted orbit counts differ by at most the number of orbits with a nontrivial stabilizer
nodes.statement: In the setting of ST.0/stabilizer-weighted-orbit-count, if every stabilizer is finite then for every S and X: 0 ≤ N(S; X) − N^w(S; X) ≤ #{Γv ∈ S : H(Γv) ≤ X, Stab_Γ(v) ≠ 1}. Hence N and N^w have the same asymptotics as soon as the orbits with nontrivial stabilizer are negligible. For binary quartic forms apply it to the faithful action of PGL₂(ℤ) (whose orbits on V_ℤ are the GL₂(ℤ)-orbits, Bhargava–Shankar (32)); the negligibility input is Bhargava–Shankar's Lemma 2.4 (O(X^(3/4+ε)) orbits with stabilizer in PGL₂(ℚ) of size > 1), proved at ST.2. nodes.title: Families defined by local conditions, local densities and largeness
nodes.statement: Local conditions on a family ι over a set P of places consist of localisation maps loc_v : ι → X_v into local spaces and subsets cond_v ⊆ X_v; the family they define is F_Σ = {i ∈ ι : loc_v(i) ∈ cond_v for all v ∈ P}. It is defined by finitely many local conditions if cond_v = X_v for all but finitely many v. When the X_v carry topologies and measures μ_v, the conditions are regular if each cond_v is measurable with μ_v(∂cond_v) = 0, and the local density (local mass) at v is μ_v(cond_v). Given bad loci B_v ⊆ X_v, the family is large relative to B if, for all but finitely many v, the closure of loc_v(F_Σ) contains X_v ∖ B_v. Instances. (1) Bhargava–Shankar's families of elliptic curves defined by congruence conditions: X_p = ℤ_p², loc_p(E) = (I(E), J(E)), Haar probability measure, a sign condition at ∞, and B_p = {p² | Δ(I, J)}, for which 'large relative to B' is their largeness (ST.0/elliptic-families-defined-by-congruence-conditions). (2) Sets S ⊆ V_ℤ of integral binary quartic forms defined by congruence conditions, with μ_p(S) the p-adic density of the closure of S in V_{ℤ_p}, μ_p(V_{ℤ_p}) = 1 (Bhargava–Shankar §2.5). (3) BKLOS's squareclass families Σ = F×/F×² ∩ ∏_v Σ_v with X_v = F_v×/F_v×², the measure of the preimage in O_{F_v} at finite v and the discrete measure at infinite v. (4) Burungale–Tian's positive squarefree n ≡ 1, 2, 3 (mod 8), which is the squareclass family of ℚ with Σ_∞ = {+1} ⊂ ℝ×/ℝ×² and Σ_2 = the classes of 1, 3, 2, 10 in ℚ₂×/ℚ₂×² (ST.0/positive-squarefree-family-over-q). (5) Bhargava–Shankar–Tsimerman's local specifications Σ_p of isomorphism classes of orders in étale cubic ℚ_p-algebras (X_p discrete, masses 1/(Disc_p(R)·|Aut(R)|)). Proposed declarations: the structure LocalConditions with family, FinitelyMany, IsRegular, localDensity and IsLargeRel.
hypotheses: The local spaces and measures are part of the data: 'density of a local condition' is meaningless until μ_v is fixed (Haar probability on ℤ_p-points, BKLOS's preimage measure on F_v×/F_v×², counting masses weighted by 1/|Aut| for étale algebras).

Finitely many conditions and 'large' are different: the squarefree integers are cut out by a condition at every prime (not finitely many conditions) and still form a large family relative to B_p = {p² | n}.
Regularity (boundary of measure zero) is what the sieve of ST.2 needs; a condition with boundary of positive measure is excluded.
proofSteps: family, FinitelyMany, IsRegular, localDensity and IsLargeRel are direct definitions; mem_family unfolds family.
family_inf: imposing two collections with the same localisation maps intersects the families; family_eq_univ: trivial conditions cut out everything.
acceptance: The integers n with n ≢ 0 (mod p²) for every prime p are the squarefree integers, and this family is not defined by finitely many local conditions.

Bhargava–Shankar's semistable family is defined by conditions at every prime and is large; the family y² = x³ + Ax (B = 0) is defined by congruence conditions and is not large (ST.0/elliptic-families-defined-by-congruence-conditions).

nodes.title: Weights defined by congruence conditions and acceptable weights
nodes.statement: Following Bhargava–Shankar §2.7, let a family ι carry localisations loc_p : ι → X_p at the primes. A weight φ : ι → [0, 1] is defined by congruence conditions via local weights φ_p : X_p → [0, 1] if (1) for every i the Euler product ∏_p φ_p(loc_p(i)) converges to φ(i) (Mathlib's HasProd over the primes), and (2) each φ_p is locally constant outside a closed subset S_p ⊆ X_p of measure zero. Given bad loci B_p ⊆ X_p, φ is acceptable if for all sufficiently large p, φ_p = 1 off B_p. For integral binary quartic forms X_p = V_{ℤ_p}, loc_p the inclusion and B_p = {f : p² | Δ(f)}; the characteristic function of the forms of squarefree discriminant is acceptable. Through the localisation (I(E), J(E)) ∈ ℤ_p², the indicator of a large family of elliptic curves is acceptable relative to B_p = {p² | Δ(I, J)} (this is how ST.4 uses largeness). Proposed declarations: the structure CongruenceWeight with weight, ConvergesTo, IsLocallyConstantAE, IsAcceptable.
hypotheses: Weights take values in [0, 1].
Acceptability concerns all sufficiently large p; finitely many primes (2 and 3 among them) are unrestricted.
proofSteps: weight is the tprod of the local weights; weight_mem_Icc: a convergent product of numbers in [0, 1] lies in [0, 1].
IsAcceptable of an indicator 1_{X_p ∖ B_p} holds for every p by definition; the constant weight 1 is acceptable for every B.
acceptance: The constant weight 1/2 is not acceptable when the bad loci are proper subsets.
Bhargava–Shankar's example: the characteristic function of squarefree discriminant is acceptable (it equals 1 off {p² | Δ} at every p).

nodes.title: Binary quartic forms, the GL₂ action by linear substitution and the twisted PGL₂ action
nodes.statement: For a commutative ring R, a binary quartic form over R is f(x, y) = a x⁴ + b x³y + c x²y² + d xy³ + e y⁴, recorded by its coefficients (a, b, c, d, e) ∈ R⁵ (the structure BinaryQuartic R, in the style of Mathlib's WeierstrassCurve), with evaluation f(x, y), dehomogenisation f(X, 1) ∈ R[X] and the associated homogeneous polynomial of degree 4 in two variables. GL₂(R) acts on the left by linear substitution, γ·f(x, y) := f((x, y)·γ) with (x, y)·γ = (γ₀₀x + γ₁₀y, γ₀₁x + γ₁₁y) (Bhargava–Shankar (3)); for γ with rows (p, q) and (r, s) the new coefficients are a′ = f(p, q), e′ = f(r, s), b′ = 4a p³r + b p³s + 3b p²qr + 2c p²qs + 2c pq²r + 3d pq²s + d q³r + 4e q³s, c′ = 6a p²r² + 3b p²rs + 3b pqr² + c p²s² + 4c pqrs + c q²r² + 3d pqs² + 3d q²rs + 6e q²s², d′ = 4a pr³ + 3b pr²s + b qr³ + 2c prs² + 2c qr²s + d ps³ + 3d qrs² + 4e qs³. The twisted action is γ⋆f := (det γ)⁻²·f((x, y)·γ) (Bhargava–Shankar (21), (32)): scalars act trivially, so it is an action of PGL₂(R); for det γ = ±1 the two actions agree, so on V_ℤ the PGL₂(ℤ)-orbits are the GL₂(ℤ)-orbits; −1 acts trivially under both. Base change along ring homomorphisms is equivariant. V_ℤ ⊂ V_ℝ is the lattice of integral forms. Proposed declarations: BinaryQuartic R, subst, the MulAction instance, twistedSMul.
hypotheses: The action is by the row vector (x, y)·γ, a left action: (γ₁γ₂)·f = γ₁·(γ₂·f). Using γ·(x, y)ᵀ instead gives a right action and different orbits formulas; the unit tests separate the two.
Coefficients are arbitrary (Bhargava–Shankar allow all integer coefficients, not the even middle coefficients of classical conventions).
The twisted action needs det γ invertible, which holds for every γ ∈ GL₂(R).
proofSteps: subst is the explicit polynomial map above; one_smul and mul_smul are polynomial identities in the coefficients (ring normalisation).
twistedSMul multiplies the substituted coefficients by the unit (det γ)⁻²; twistedSMul_scalar: for γ = u·1, f((x, y)·u) = u⁴f and det = u².
neg_one_smul: f(−x, −y) = f(x, y) since f is homogeneous of even degree.
map_smul: ring homomorphisms commute with the polynomial formulas; eval_smul: substitute and expand.
acceptance: The swap matrix (0 1; 1 0) reverses the coefficients: (a, b, c, d, e) ↦ (e, d, c, b, a).
(x, y) ↦ (x + y, y) sends x³y to x³y + 3x²y² + 3xy³ + y⁴.
x⁴ is fixed by (1 1; 0 1) (row convention), whereas the column convention would give (x + y)⁴.

nodes.title: The invariants I and J and the discriminant Δ of a binary quartic form
nodes.statement: For f = (a, b, c, d, e) ∈ V_R put I(f) = 12ae − 3bd + c² and J(f) = 72ace + 9bcd − 27ad² − 27eb² − 2c³ (Bhargava–Shankar (4)), and let the discriminant be the integral polynomial Δ(f) = 256a³e³ − 192a²bde² − 128a²c²e² + 144a²cd²e − 27a²d⁴ + 144ab²ce² − 6ab²d²e − 80abc²de + 18abcd³ + 16ac⁴e − 4ac³d² − 27b⁴e² + 18b³cde − 4b³d³ − 4b²c³e + b²c²d², so that 27·Δ(f) = 4I(f)³ − J(f)² (Bhargava–Shankar write Δ(f) = (4I³ − J²)/27). Homogeneity: I(rf) = r²I(f) and J(rf) = r³J(f) for the coefficientwise scaling rf. Under the twisted action I, J (hence Δ) are invariant; under the untwisted action Δ(γ·f) = (det γ)¹²Δ(f). I and J commute with base change. For a pair (I, J) not assumed to come from a form, the conditions used downstream are stated with 4I³ − J² (= 27Δ), which carries the same p-adic information as Δ at p ≠ 3. Proposed declarations: BinaryQuartic.invI, invJ, disc.
hypotheses: Δ is the integral polynomial, not (4I³ − J²)/27: this makes it defined over every commutative ring (ℤ_p, ℤ/p^k, rings where 3 is not invertible) and makes 27Δ = 4I³ − J² a theorem.
I, J are relative invariants for the untwisted action with weights (det γ)⁴, (det γ)⁶ (ST.0/relative-invariance-of-i-and-j) and absolute invariants for the twisted one.
proofSteps: twentySeven_mul_disc, invI_scale, invJ_scale, map_invI, map_invJ: polynomial identities (ring normalisation); 27Δ = 4I³ − J² was also checked on 3000 random integral forms while writing this node.
invI_twistedSMul, invJ_twistedSMul: by ST.0/relative-invariance-of-i-and-j and homogeneity, the factor (det γ)⁻² contributes (det γ)⁻⁴ to I and (det γ)⁻⁶ to J.
disc_smul: from 27Δ = 4I³ − J² and the weights 4, 6 over ℤ[coefficients, entries], where 27 is a nonzerodivisor, then by specialisation.
acceptance: x³y − xy³: I = 3, J = 0, Δ = 4 (roots 0, ±1, ∞).
x⁴ − y⁴: I = −12, J = 0, Δ = −256, the polynomial discriminant of X⁴ − 1.
x⁴: I = J = Δ = 0 (the null cone contains forms with a fourfold root).

nodes.title: Δ(f) is Mathlib's polynomial discriminant of f(X, 1)
nodes.statement: Let f = (a, b, c, d, e) ∈ V_R with f(X, 1) = aX⁴ + bX³ + cX² + dX + e of degree 4. Then Δ(f) = discr(f(X, 1)), Mathlib's Polynomial.discr (the Sylvester determinant of the polynomial and its derivative, signed so that polynomials over ℝ with all roots real have nonnegative discriminant). Over a field containing the roots α₁, …, α₄ of f(X, 1), Δ(f) = a⁶∏_{i<j}(α_i − α_j)². Proposed declaration: BinaryQuartic.disc_eq_discr.
hypotheses: Degree exactly 4 (a is not a zero divisor suffices); for a = 0 the form has the root [1 : 0] and f(X, 1) has lower degree.
proofSteps: Reindex the 7 × 7 matrix sylvesterDeriv of a degree-4 polynomial to Fin 7 exactly as Mathlib does in degree 3 (mathlib:Polynomial.discr_of_degree_eq_three) and expand the determinant; compare with the sixteen-term polynomial Δ.

With 27Δ = 4I³ − J² (ST.0/binary-quartic-invariants) this recovers Bhargava–Shankar's Δ = (4I³ − J²)/27. The identity discr(f(X, 1)) = (4I³ − J²)/27 was checked exactly (Sylvester resultant over ℚ) on 300 random integral quartics while writing this node.
acceptance: Δ(x⁴ − y⁴) = −256 = discr(X⁴ − 1) (the discriminant of X⁴ + e is 256e³).
The sign of Δ separates the real types: Δ > 0 for four or zero real roots, Δ < 0 for two (Bhargava–Shankar §2.1).

nodes.title: The height H(I, J) = max{|I|³, J²/4} on pairs of invariants and on integral binary quartic forms
nodes.statement: For real I, J put H(I, J) := max{|I|³, J²/4}, and for an integral binary quartic form H(f) := H(I(f), J(f)) (Bhargava–Shankar (6)). Properties: H ≥ 0, with H(I, J) = 0 iff I = J = 0; H(t²I, t³J) = t⁶H(I, J), so H(rf) = r⁶H(f) (a 'degree 6' function of the coefficients) and H(2⁴I, 2⁶J) = 2¹²H(I, J) (the scaling in Theorem 3.5 and in the proof of Theorem 3.19); H(I, J) ≤ X implies |I| ≤ X^(1/3) and |J| ≤ 2X^(1/2); for integers 4H(I, J) = max{4|I|³, J²} ∈ ℕ, so the ℕ-valued carrier of ST.0/arithmetic-family applies to 4H; (I, J) ↦ H(I, J) is Northcott on ℤ²; H is invariant under GL₂(ℤ). Proposed declarations: BinaryQuartic.pairHeight, BinaryQuartic.height.
hypotheses: The factor 1/4 on J² is a normalisation; the constants 4/135, 32/135, 8/135 of Theorem 1.6 and 8/135, 32/135 of Proposition 2.10 depend on it.

H is a height on invariant pairs; on classes of forms it is well defined by GL₂(ℤ)-invariance. The null cone (height 0) contains the infinitely many classes of kx⁴, so orbit families exclude it (Bhargava–Shankar count irreducible forms only).
proofSteps: pairHeight_scale: |t²I|³ = t⁶|I|³ and (t³J)²/4 = t⁶J²/4.
abs_le_of_pairHeight_le: |I|³ ≤ X and J²/4 ≤ X.
northcott_pairHeight: {(I, J) ∈ ℤ² : H ≤ X} lies in the box |I| ≤ X^(1/3), |J| ≤ 2X^(1/2).

nodes.title: Eligible invariant pairs and the eligibility congruences modulo 27
nodes.statement: A pair (I, J) ∈ ℤ² is eligible if it occurs as (I(f), J(f)) for an integral binary quartic form f. The eligibility congruences are: (a) I ≡ 0 (mod 3) and J ≡ 0 (mod 27); (b) I ≡ 1 (mod 9) and J ≡ ±2 (mod 27); (c) I ≡ 4 (mod 9) and J ≡ ±16 (mod 27); (d) I ≡ 7 (mod 9) and J ≡ ±7 (mod 27). The invariant pair of every integral form is eligible by definition, and eligibility is preserved by (I, J) ↦ (r²I, r³J) for integers r (scale the form by r) — in particular by (I, J) ↦ (2⁴I, 2⁶J) (r = 4), the scaling of Theorem 3.5. Proposed declarations: BinaryQuartic.IsEligible, BinaryQuartic.EligibilityCongruence.
hypotheses: Eligibility is a property of integer pairs; the equivalence with the congruences is Theorem 1.7 (ST.0/eligibility-criterion-modulo-27).
proofSteps: IsEligible and EligibilityCongruence are direct definitions; invariants_isEligible is the witness f itself; isEligible_selmer_scaling uses invI_scale and invJ_scale of ST.0/binary-quartic-invariants with r = 4.

sources.excerpt: Theorem 1.7 A pair (I, J) ∈ Z × Z occurs as the invariants of an integral binary quartic form if and only if it satisfies one of the following congruence conditions: (a) I ≡ 0 (mod 3) and J ≡ 0 (mod 27), (b) I ≡ 1 (mod 9) and J ≡ ±2 (mod 27),
sources.match: Eligibility and the congruence conditions (cases (c), (d) continue on p. 5).

nodes.title: The invariants of an integral binary quartic form satisfy one of the congruences (a)–(d)
nodes.statement: For every integral binary quartic form f, the pair (I(f), J(f)) satisfies one of the eligibility congruences (a)–(d). Proposed declaration: BinaryQuartic.eligibilityCongruence_invariants.
hypotheses: Only the coefficient formulas for I and J are used; no resolvent.
proofSteps: Modulo 3, I ≡ c².
If 3 | c, write c = 3c′. Then 72ace = 216ac′e ≡ 0, 9bcd = 27bc′d ≡ 0, 2c³ = 54c′³ ≡ 0 and 27ad² ≡ 27eb² ≡ 0 modulo 27, so J ≡ 0 (mod 27) and I ≡ 0 (mod 3): case (a).
If 3 ∤ c, then modulo 9 and 27 respectively I ≡ c² + 3w and J ≡ −2c³ − 9cw, with w ≡ ae − bd (mod 3) (use 12 ≡ 3 mod 9, 72 ≡ 18 mod 27, and 2ae + bd ≡ −(ae − bd) mod 3).

For c = 1 + 3k: c² ≡ 1 + 6k (mod 9), c³ ≡ 1 + 9k (mod 27), so with m ≡ 2k + w (mod 3), I ≡ 1 + 3m (mod 9) and J ≡ −2 − 9m (mod 27). For c = −1 + 3k: with m ≡ w − 2k, I ≡ 1 + 3m and J ≡ 2 + 9m. As m runs over 0, 1, 2 this gives (I mod 9, J mod 27) = (1, ∓2), (4, ±16), (7, ±7): cases (b)–(d).

Bhargava–Shankar prove the same inclusion through the monic cubic resolvent (§2.8), which lives in ST.1 (pairs of ternary quadratic forms); the direct computation keeps ST.0 independent of ST.1. The inclusion was verified exhaustively over all coefficient vectors modulo 27 while writing this node.
acceptance: The residues (I mod 9, J mod 27) of all 27⁵ coefficient vectors modulo 27 are exactly the nine eligible residue pairs.

sources.excerpt: If I is not divisible by 3, then r equals 1 or −1 and we have I ≡ 1 (mod 3). Thus I must be congruent to 1, 4, or 7 (mod 9), which happens exactly when s is congruent to 0, 2, or 1 (mod 3), respectively. Because r2 = 1, we see that J ≡ r(9s − 2) (mod 27).

nodes.title: Every pair satisfying the congruences is the invariant pair of x³y + r x²y² + s xy³ + t y⁴
nodes.statement: If (I, J) ∈ ℤ² satisfies one of (a)–(d), then there are integers r, s, t with I(f) = I and J(f) = J for f = x³y + r x²y² + s xy³ + t y⁴ (a = 0, b = 1, c = r, d = s, e = t), for which I(f) = r² − 3s and J(f) = −2r³ + 9rs − 27t. Take r = 0 in case (a); in cases (b)–(d) take r = 1 when J ≡ −2, 16 or 7 (mod 27) and r = −1 when J ≡ 2, −16 or −7 (mod 27); then s = (r² − I)/3 and t = (−2r³ + 9rs − J)/27 are integers. Proposed declaration: BinaryQuartic.isEligible_of_eligibilityCongruence.
hypotheses: The witness has a = 0 (a rational root at [1 : 0]); eligibility says nothing about irreducibility.
proofSteps: With a = 0, b = 1: I = −3s + r² and J = 9rs − 27t − 2r³.
Cases (b)–(d): r = ±1, s = (1 − I)/3 ∈ ℤ since I ≡ 1 (mod 3); then J ≡ r(9s − 2) (mod 27) holds exactly for the sign chosen above (I ≡ 1, 4, 7 (mod 9) ⇔ s ≡ 0, 2, 1 (mod 3)), so t ∈ ℤ.
Checked by computer for all |I| ≤ 60, |J| ≤ 200 satisfying the congruences while writing this node.
acceptance: (1, 2): r = −1, s = 0, t = 0, i.e. x³y − x²y² has I = 1, J = 2.

nodes.title: Lemma 2.9: the eligible pairs are nine translates of 9ℤ × 27ℤ
nodes.statement: There is a set R ⊂ ℤ/9 × ℤ/27 of exactly nine residue pairs, R = {(0, 0), (3, 0), (6, 0), (1, 2), (1, −2), (4, 16), (4, −16), (7, 7), (7, −7)}, such that (I, J) ∈ ℤ² is eligible iff (I mod 9, J mod 27) ∈ R. So the eligible pairs are a union of 9 distinct translates of 9ℤ × 27ℤ and have density 9/243 = 1/27 in ℤ². Proposed declaration: BinaryQuartic.exists_eligible_residues.
hypotheses: Case (a) is a condition on I modulo 3, i.e. three residues modulo 9.
proofSteps: By ST.0/eligibility-criterion-modulo-27, eligibility depends only on (I mod 9, J mod 27); list the residues of (a)–(d): 3 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 9.

nodes.title: Elliptic curves over ℚ ordered by naive height, on EllipticCurves Layer 8's minimal-pair carrier, with the invariant map (I, J) = (−3A, −27B)
nodes.statement: Let Carrier be the set of integral short Weierstrass equations W : y² = x³ + Ax + B over ℤ that are minimal pairs in the sense of EllipticCurves Layer 8 (IsMinimalPairNF: short normal form, and no prime ℓ with ℓ⁴ | A and ℓ⁶ | B) and elliptic over ℚ (4A³ + 27B² ≠ 0). By Layer 8's exists_minimalPairModel and minimalPairModel_unique, W ↦ [W ⊗ ℚ] is a bijection from Carrier onto the ℚ-isomorphism classes of elliptic curves over ℚ (toIsoClass, into Mathlib's orbit type of the VariableChange action). The arithmetic family of elliptic curves over ℚ is (Carrier, H) with H(E_{A,B}) = max{4|A|³, 27B²} (Layer 8's shortEquationHeight, i.e. its naiveHeight of the curve), Northcott by Layer 8's bounded-height finiteness. Its invariant map is E ↦ (I(E), J(E)) := (−3A, −27B) (Bhargava–Shankar (48)); it is injective, takes values in 3ℤ × 27ℤ, hence in the eligible pairs (case (a) of Theorem 1.7), and satisfies 4I³ − J² = −27(4A³ + 27B²), so Δ(I(E), J(E)) = −(4A³ + 27B²) = Δ_E/16 with Mathlib's Δ_E = −16(4A³ + 27B²). The curve height of Bhargava–Shankar §3 is H′(E) := H(I(E), J(E)) = max{|I(E)|³, J(E)²/4} ((49)). The localisation at a prime p is (I(E), J(E)) ∈ ℤ_p² (ST.0/elliptic-families-defined-by-congruence-conditions). Proposed declarations: EllipticFamily.Carrier, EllipticFamily.family, EllipticFamily.invariants, EllipticFamily.heightPrime.

This construction imports Layer 8's predicate, height and finiteness; it adds only the invariant map, H′ and the family structure.

nodes.title: Families of elliptic curves defined by congruence conditions, Inv_p, and large families
nodes.statement: For each prime p let Σ_p be a subset of {(I, J) ∈ ℤ_p² : Δ(I, J) ≠ 0}, closed in it, with boundary of Haar measure 0, and let Σ_∞ be one of {Δ > 0}, {Δ < 0}, {Δ ≠ 0}. The family F_Σ consists of the E in the family of elliptic curves over ℚ with (I(E), J(E)) ∈ Σ_p for all p and (I(E), J(E)) ∈ Σ_∞ (Bhargava–Shankar §3; the printed condition 'Σ_p ⊆ ℤ_p² ∖ {Δ ≠ 0}' is a misprint, ArithmeticStatistics/E101). For S ⊆ Carrier, Inv(S) = {(I(E), J(E)) : E ∈ S}, Inv_p(S) = (closure of Inv(S) in ℤ_p²) ∖ {Δ = 0}, and Inv_∞(S) is the sign set. S is large if, for all but finitely many p, Inv_p(S) ⊇ {(I, J) ∈ ℤ_p² : p² ∤ Δ(I, J)}; for p ≠ 3 the condition p² ∤ Δ(I, J) is p² ∤ 4I³ − J². This is ST.0/family-defined-by-local-conditions for the family of elliptic curves with X_p = ℤ_p², loc_p = (I, J), the Haar probability measure, and B_p = {p² | Δ}. Largeness is monotone. The family of all curves is large (ST.0/all-elliptic-curves-form-a-large-family); every nonempty family defined by finitely many congruence conditions on (A, B) is large; the curves semistable at every prime ℓ ≥ 5 (for a minimal pair: ℓ ∤ gcd(A, B)) form a large family — the arithmetic content of Bhargava–Shankar's remark that the semistable family is large, since conditions at the finitely many primes 2, 3 (reduction types of EllipticCurves Layer 4) do not affect largeness. The curves with B = 0 (j = 1728) form a family defined by congruence conditions that is not large. Proposed declarations: EllipticFamily.invLocal, IsLarge, congruenceFamily.
hypotheses: Largeness allows infinitely many local conditions but forbids excluding, at infinitely many p, pairs with p² ∤ Δ; the semistable family excludes a set of positive measure at every p (additive reduction, where p² | Δ) and is still large.
Largeness is a property of the closure of the actual invariants of the family, not of the sets Σ_p alone.
proofSteps: invLocal, IsLarge and congruenceFamily are direct definitions over Mathlib's ℤ_p (mathlib:PadicInt).
IsLarge.mono: Inv_p is monotone in S.

isLarge_semistableAwayFromSix: for p ≥ 5 and (I, J) with p² ∤ Δ, (A₀, B₀) = (−I/3, −J/27) ∈ ℤ_p² is not ≡ (0, 0) mod p (else p² | Δ); approximate it p-adically by integral minimal pairs with ℓ ∤ gcd(A, B) for all ℓ ≥ 5, as in the proof of ST.0/all-elliptic-curves-form-a-large-family.
The j = 1728 non-example: Inv_p({B = 0}) ⊆ ℤ_p × {0} misses (0, 1), where p² ∤ Δ = −1/27 for p ≠ 3.
acceptance: The family of curves with A ≡ 1 (mod 5) is large; the family with B = 0 is not.
With Σ_p = ℤ_p² ∖ {Δ = 0} for all p and no sign condition, F_Σ is the whole family.

nodes.title: The family of all elliptic curves over ℚ is large
nodes.statement: The whole family of elliptic curves over ℚ (the carrier of minimal pairs) is large: for every prime p ≥ 5 and every (I, J) ∈ ℤ_p² with p² ∤ Δ(I, J), (I, J) is a p-adic limit of invariant pairs (−3A, −27B) of minimal pairs (A, B) with 4A³ + 27B² ≠ 0. Proposed declaration: EllipticFamily.isLarge_univ.
hypotheses: Only p ≥ 5 is needed (largeness ignores finitely many primes).
proofSteps: For p ≥ 5 put (A₀, B₀) = (−I/3, −J/27) ∈ ℤ_p²; p² ∤ Δ(I, J) = −(4A₀³ + 27B₀²) rules out p⁴ | A₀ and p⁶ | B₀.

Given k, choose integers (A, B) ≡ (A₀, B₀) (mod p^k) that form a minimal pair with 4A³ + 27B² ≠ 0: by the Chinese remainder theorem impose (A, B) mod p^k and, for every prime ℓ ≤ L, a residue class mod (ℓ⁴, ℓ⁶) outside {ℓ⁴ | A, ℓ⁶ | B}; in any box of such pairs the proportion with ℓ⁴ | A and ℓ⁶ | B for some ℓ > L is at most Σ_{ℓ>L} ℓ^(−10) + o(1) < 1, and the singular pairs are a curve, so a suitable (A, B) exists.
Then (−3A, −27B) ≡ (I, J) (mod p^k); let k → ∞.
acceptance: Consequently Theorem 3.1 contains Theorem 1.1 (the average of #S₂(E) over all curves is 3).

nodes.title: The eligible invariant pairs ordered by H(I, J), with the curve normalisation 27·H_E = 4·H′ (the binary-quartic invariant and height interface)
nodes.statement: This node packages ST.0's binary-quartic interface, consumed by ST.1–ST.4 and by AnalyticNumberTheory:AN.8: the invariants I, J with weights (det γ)⁴, (det γ)⁶ (ST.0/binary-quartic-invariants, ST.0/relative-invariance-of-i-and-j), the discriminant with 27Δ = 4I³ − J², equal to the polynomial discriminant (ST.0/quartic-discriminant-is-the-polynomial-discriminant), the height H(I, J) = max{|I|³, J²/4} (ST.0/binary-quartic-height), the eligible pairs characterised modulo 27 (ST.0/eligibility-criterion-modulo-27; nine translates of 9ℤ × 27ℤ, ST.0/eligible-pairs-are-nine-lattice-translates) and the normalisation to curves (ST.0/quartic-to-curve-height-normalisation). Definition: the arithmetic family eligibleFamily of eligible pairs (I, J) ∈ ℤ² ordered by H(I, J) (Northcott because H is Northcott on ℤ²), with the map ofCurve sending E_{A,B} (EllipticCurves Layer 8's minimal pair) to its eligible invariant pair (−3A, −27B), for which 27·H(E) = 4·H(ofCurve E). The sign of Δ(I, J) splits eligible pairs of nonzero discriminant into those counted by Proposition 2.10(a) (Δ > 0: forms with four or no real roots) and (b) (Δ < 0: two real roots). nodes.title: The squareclass height H(t) = ∏_{ord_v(t) odd} N v on F×/F×²
nodes.statement: Let F be a number field, O_F its ring of integers and t ∈ F×/F×² a squareclass (Tau Ceti's SquareClassGroup F). For a finite prime v (Mathlib's HeightOneSpectrum O_F) the parity of ord_v(u) for a representative u ∈ F× (Mathlib's valuationOfNeZero) depends only on t. The odd support of t is the finite set of v with ord_v(t) odd (finite by Tau Ceti's finite_setOfPred_valuation_ne_one), its support ideal is the squarefree integral ideal 𝔞(t) := ∏_{v odd} v, and the squareclass height is H(t) := ∏_{v : ord_v(t) odd} N v = N(𝔞(t)) ∈ ℕ (Ideal.absNorm). Properties: H(0) = 1 (trivial class); H(s + t)·g² = H(s)·H(t) with g = N(gcd(𝔞(s), 𝔞(t))) (the odd support of a product is the symmetric difference); H(t) = 1 iff every ord_v(t) is even, i.e. t lies in the Selmer group K(∅, 2) (Mathlib's selmerGroup with S = ∅, n = 2), which contains the classes of units and of generators of squares of ideals and is nontrivial in general; for F = ℚ the class of a squarefree integer n has H = |n|, so [1] and [−1] both have height 1 (BKLOS §2: 'the squareclasses of all squarefree integers of absolute value less than X'). H is not the norm of a representative and not the discriminant of F(√t). Proposed declarations: squareclassHeight, oddSupport, supportIdeal.
hypotheses: F is a number field; only finite primes enter H (infinite places are local conditions, not height factors).
The height is defined on squareclasses; representatives are used only through parities of valuations.
proofSteps: oddSupport is a subset of the finite set of v with ord_v(u) ≠ 0 (tauceti:IsDedekindDomain.HeightOneSpectrum.finite_setOfPred_valuation_ne_one).
Independence of the representative: u′ = u·w² changes every ord_v by an even number (valuationOfNeZero is a homomorphism; tauceti:TauCeti.squareClass_eq_iff_isSquare_mul).
squareclassHeight_add_mul_sq: the odd support of uu′ is the symmetric difference of the odd supports, and N is multiplicative on coprime products.
squareclassHeight_rat: for squarefree n the odd support is the set of primes dividing n, and N(pℤ) = p.
acceptance: ℚ: H([12]) = 3, H([−1]) = 1, H([3]) = 3 (the discriminant of ℚ(√3) is 12).
ℚ(i): K(∅, 2) = {[1], [i]} (−1 = i² is a square, the class number is 1) and [2] = [−i(1 + i)²] = [i] has height 1.

nodes.title: Bounded-height finiteness for squareclasses of a number field
nodes.statement: For every number field F the squareclass height is Northcott: {t ∈ F×/F×² : H(t) ≤ X} is finite for every X. Precisely, t ↦ 𝔞(t) maps onto the squarefree ideals whose class lies in Cl(F)², with fibres the cosets of K(∅, 2), so #{t : H(t) ≤ X} = #K(∅, 2)·#{squarefree 𝔞 : N𝔞 ≤ X, [𝔞] ∈ Cl(F)²} ≤ #K(∅, 2)·#{ideals of norm ≤ X}. Proposed declaration: northcott_squareclassHeight.
hypotheses: The finiteness is for squareclasses under their height, not for representatives: each class has infinitely many representatives in F×.
proofSteps: K(∅, 2) is finite: tauceti:IsDedekindDomain.finite_selmerGroup_of_numberField (class number theorem and Dirichlet's unit theorem, via the exact sequence 1 → O_F×/O_F×² → K(∅, 2) → Cl(F)[2] → 0).
The fibres of t ↦ 𝔞(t) are cosets of K(∅, 2) (ST.0/squareclass-height-fibres-are-selmer-cosets), hence finite.
The absolute norm is Northcott on nonzero ideals (tauceti:TauCeti.instNorthcottAbsNormNonZeroDivisors, from mathlib:Ring.HasFiniteQuotients.finite_absNorm_le).
H = N ∘ 𝔞 is Northcott by mathlib:Northcott.comp_of_finite_fibers.
Image: (u) = 𝔞(u)·𝔟² for a fractional ideal 𝔟, so [𝔞(u)] = [𝔟]⁻² ∈ Cl²; conversely if 𝔞𝔟² = (u) then 𝔞(u) = 𝔞 for squarefree 𝔞.
acceptance: F = ℚ: #{t : H(t) ≤ X} = 2·#{1 ≤ n ≤ X squarefree} ~ (12/π²)X.
F = ℚ(i): K(∅, 2) = {[1], [i]}, so every squarefree ideal of norm ≤ X is 𝔞(t) for exactly two classes.

nodes.title: The unweighted squareclass-height family of quadratic twists E^(t), t ∈ F×/F×²
nodes.statement: Let F be a number field and E : y² = x³ + Ax + B an elliptic curve over F in short form (Tau Ceti's shortCurve A B; every elliptic curve over F has one, Mathlib's exists_variableChange_isShortNF). For a squareclass t ∈ F×/F×² with representative u, the quadratic twist E^(t) is the class of the model u y² = x³ + Ax + B, equivalently E^(u) : y² = x³ + u²A x + u³B, modulo F-isomorphism (Mathlib's orbit type of the VariableChange action). It is well defined: replacing u by us² changes the model by the change of variables with u_C = s; the trivial class gives E; E^(u) is Tau Ceti's quadraticTwistOf 0 (−u) (the model y² = x³ + 16u²A x + 64u³B) after the change of variables with u_C = 1/2, and for u ∉ F×² it is F-isomorphic to Tau Ceti's quadraticTwist E F(√u) (exists_smul_quadraticTwist_eq with the generator √u, of trace 0 and norm −u); Δ(E^(u)) = u⁶Δ(E) and j(E^(u)) = j(E). The squareclass twist family of E is the arithmetic family (F×/F×², H) with H the squareclass height (ST.0/squareclass-height; Northcott by ST.0/finiteness-of-squareclasses-of-bounded-height), together with the twist map t ↦ [E^(t)]. It is unweighted: each squareclass is counted once, whatever the multiplicity of the twist map (ST.0/isomorphism-multiplicity-of-the-twist-family). Proportions of twists 'ordered by H(t)' (Burungale–Tian Proposition 1.3 and Theorem 3.5; BKLOS Theorems 2.1–2.7) are relative densities in this family, and its subfamilies defined by local conditions on F_v×/F_v×² are instances of ST.0/family-defined-by-local-conditions. Proposed declarations: twistModel, twistClass, twistFamily.
hypotheses: F has characteristic 0, so the short model exists and the twist is elliptic exactly when E is (Δ(E^(u)) = u⁶Δ(E)).
The trivial class is included.
The family counts squareclasses, not isomorphism classes of twists; the two differ exactly at j = 1728.
For F = ℚ the family is ordered by |n| for squarefree n of both signs; Burungale–Tian's congruent-number family is its positive part (ST.0/positive-squarefree-family-over-q).
proofSteps: twistModel is the short curve with coefficients u²A, u³B; exists_smul_twistModel_mul_sq: the change of variables with u_C = s sends (u²s⁴A, u³s⁶B) to (u²A, u³B) (mathlib:WeierstrassCurve.variableChange_a₄, variableChange_a₆).
twistClass is the lift of u ↦ [twistModel u] to F×/F×², well defined by the previous step.

nodes.title: Isomorphism multiplicity of the twist map: injective unless j = 1728, fibres {t, t + [−1]} at j = 1728
nodes.statement: Let F be a number field and E : y² = x³ + Ax + B with 4A³ + 27B² ≠ 0. (a) If B ≠ 0 (so j(E) ≠ 1728; j = 0 included), the twist map t ↦ [E^(t)] on F×/F×² is injective: E^(u) ≅_F E^(u′) iff u′/u ∈ F×². (b) If B = 0 (j = 1728), E^(−u) and E^(u) are the same model y² = x³ + u²A x, and E^(u) ≅_F E^(u′) iff u′/u ∈ ±F×²; so when −1 ∉ F×² every fibre of the twist map is {t, t + [−1]}, of size 2, and the unweighted squareclass count counts each isomorphism class of twists twice (count_comap of ST.0/arithmetic-family). In particular for y² = x³ − x over ℚ, E^(n) = E^(−n), which is why Burungale–Tian index their family by positive squarefree n. Proposed declaration: twistClass_injective_or_neg.
hypotheses: Characteristic 0 (a number field): short models and the shape of changes of variables between them use 2, 3 invertible.
proofSteps: A change of variables between two short models over F has s = r = t = 0: a₁′ = u_C⁻¹·2s, then a₂′ = u_C⁻²·3r and a₃′ = u_C⁻³·2t must vanish (mathlib:WeierstrassCurve.variableChange_a₁, variableChange_a₂, variableChange_a₃); then (a₄′, a₆′) = (u_C⁻⁴a₄, u_C⁻⁶a₆) (variableChange_a₄, variableChange_a₆).

So E^(u) ≅ E^(u′) iff there is w ∈ F× with u′²A = w⁴u²A and u′³B = w⁶u³B. Let q = u′/u. If A, B ≠ 0: q² = w⁴ and q³ = w⁶ give q = q³/q² = w² ∈ F×². If A = 0 (then B ≠ 0): q³ = w⁶ gives q = ζw² with ζ³ = 1, and ζ = (ζ²)² is a square. If B = 0 (then A ≠ 0): q² = w⁴ gives q = ±w².
Conversely q = w² (and, when B = 0, q = −w²) gives the isomorphism with u_C = w⁻¹.

Cross-check (not needed for the proof): Tau Ceti's tauceti:WeierstrassCurve.not_exists_smul_quadraticTwist_eq says that for j ∉ {0, 1728} a twist by a nontrivial quadratic extension is not F-isomorphic to E.
acceptance: y² = x³ − x over ℚ: E^(n) = E^(−n) = y² = x³ − n²x; over ℚ(i) (−1 a square) the twist map is injective.

nodes.title: The positive squarefree integers ordered by n, and Burungale–Tian's subfamily n ≡ 1, 2, 3 (mod 8)
nodes.statement: Over ℚ, squareclasses correspond to squarefree integers n ↦ [n], with H([n]) = |n| (ST.0/squareclass-height). Burungale–Tian's families are P, the positive squarefree integers ordered by n — the squareclasses of ℚ positive at the real place (local condition Σ_∞ = {+1} ⊂ ℝ×/ℝ×²) — and S ⊆ P, the positive squarefree n ≡ 1, 2, 3 (mod 8): the squareclasses with Σ_∞ = {+1} and Σ_2 = {[1], [3], [2], [10]} ⊂ ℚ₂×/ℚ₂×² (for squarefree n the class of n in ℚ₂×/ℚ₂×² determines n mod 8 when n is odd and n/2 mod 8 when n is even, and n ≡ 2 (mod 8) iff n/2 ≡ 1 or 5 (mod 8)). Both are ordered by n with the cutoff n ≤ X (Burungale–Tian's S(X) = {0 < n ≤ X}), realised as subsets of ℕ in the family natFamily = (ℕ, n); 'density one in this family' is HasDensity A S 1 (ST.0/relative-density). No positive squarefree n is ≡ 0 or 4 (mod 8). S is the family of positive squarefree n for which the twist E^(n) of y² = x³ − x has root number +1 (Burungale–Tian footnote 2, from Birch–Stephens; RankZeroOneBSD:BSD.0 owns that computation). Proposed declarations: SquarefreeFamily.natFamily, posSquarefree, evenParityClasses.
hypotheses: Positive n only: the class [−n] gives the same curve (ST.0/isomorphism-multiplicity-of-the-twist-family) and is excluded, not identified.
The ordering is by n, not by the fundamental discriminant (n or 4n); the comparison is ST.0/piecewise-rescaling-of-a-height.

nodes.title: Squarefree integers in a coprime residue class: (6/π²)·q⁻¹·∏_{p|q}(1 − p⁻²)⁻¹·X + O_q(√X)
nodes.statement: For integers q ≥ 1 and a with gcd(a, q) = 1 there is C_q such that for all X ≥ 1: |#{1 ≤ n ≤ X : n squarefree, n ≡ a (mod q)} − (6/π²)·q⁻¹·∏_{p | q}(1 − p⁻²)⁻¹·X| ≤ C_q·√X. Proposed declaration: SquarefreeFamily.squarefree_residue_count.
hypotheses: q is fixed (the constant depends on q; Hooley's bound O((X/q)^(1/2) + q^(1/2+ε)) is uniform but not needed here).
gcd(a, q) = 1; non-coprime classes reduce to coprime ones by factoring out the common part (for q = 8, a = 2: n = 2m with m ≡ 1 (mod 4)).
proofSteps: By ST.0/squarefree-indicator-as-a-moebius-sum the count is Σ_{d ≤ √X} μ(d)·#{n ≤ X : d² | n, n ≡ a (mod q)}.
If gcd(d, q) > 1 the inner set is empty (d² | n and gcd(n, q) = 1 force gcd(d, q) = 1); otherwise it is one residue class modulo qd² and has X/(qd²) + θ elements with |θ| ≤ 1.
Hence the count is (X/q)·Σ_{d ≤ √X, (d,q)=1} μ(d)d⁻² + O(√X), and the tail Σ_{d > √X} d⁻² ≤ 2/√X costs another O(√X).

Σ_{d ≥ 1, (d,q)=1} μ(d)d⁻² = L(χ₀μ, 2) = 1/L(χ₀, 2) for the trivial Dirichlet character χ₀ mod q (mathlib:DirichletCharacter.LSeries.mul_mu_eq_one and mathlib:DirichletCharacter.LFunction_eq_LSeries at s = 2), and L(χ₀, 2) = ∏_{p|q}(1 − p⁻²)·ζ(2) (mathlib:DirichletCharacter.LFunctionTrivChar_eq_mul_riemannZeta) with ζ(2) = π²/6 (mathlib:riemannZeta_two).

Numerically to 2·10⁶ the classes 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7 (mod 8) each contain (1.000 ± 0.001)·X/π² squarefree integers.

nodes.title: The classes n ≡ 1, 2, 3 (mod 8) have relative density 1/2 among positive squarefree integers
nodes.statement: Among the positive squarefree integers ordered by n, Burungale–Tian's family S of n ≡ 1, 2, 3 (mod 8) has relative density 1/2: #{n ≤ X : n ∈ S}/#{n ≤ X : n ∈ P} → 1/2. Proposed declaration: SquarefreeFamily.hasDensity_evenParityClasses.
hypotheses: The six squarefree classes modulo 8 (1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7) have equal density 1/6; the eight residue classes do not (0 and 4 contain no squarefree integer).
proofSteps: Classes 1 and 3 (mod 8): ST.0/squarefree-integers-in-residue-classes with q = 8 gives X/π² + O(√X) each.
Class 2 (mod 8): n = 2m with m squarefree and m ≡ 1 (mod 4); the count is #{m ≤ X/2 : m squarefree, m ≡ 1 (mod 4)} = (6/π²)(1/4)(4/3)(X/2) + O(√X) = X/π² + O(√X) (q = 4).
So #S(X) = 3X/π² + O(√X), while #P(X) = 6X/π² + O(√X) (q = 1); the ratio tends to 1/2 (ST.0/relative-density).
acceptance: Up to 20: 7 members of S among 13 positive squarefree integers; to 2·10⁶ the proportion is 0.49999.

nodes.title: Number fields ordered by |Disc|: embedded fields, isomorphism classes, degree and automorphism weights
nodes.statement: Fix a field A of characteristic 0 (an algebraic closure of ℚ for counting). The embedded number fields are the intermediate fields ℚ ⊆ K ⊆ A that are finite-dimensional over ℚ; ordered by |Disc(K)| they form an arithmetic family (embeddedFamily), Northcott by Hermite's theorem (Mathlib's NumberField.finite_of_discr_bdd; Tau Ceti's explicit bound NumberField.ncard_setOf_finiteDimensional_abs_discr_le_le). ℚ-isomorphism is an equivalence relation on embedded fields (isoSetoid); its classes ordered by |Disc| form the family of number fields up to isomorphism (isoFamily; Northcott because each class of bounded discriminant has a representative among the finitely many embedded fields of bounded discriminant). A class carries its degree n = [K : ℚ] (isoDegree) and its automorphism weight w(K) := n/#Aut(K/ℚ) (autWeight). This is the convention of Bhargava–Shankar–Tsimerman's Theorems 1 and 3 ('cubic fields K, up to isomorphism') and of the Davenport–Heilbronn count at ST.3. Proposed declarations: NumberFieldFamily.embeddedFamily, isoFamily, autWeight.
hypotheses: The counted objects are isomorphism classes; embedded subfields of ℚ̄ are counted with multiplicity n/#Aut(K) (ST.0/embedded-and-isomorphism-class-counts-of-number-fields).
The discriminant is Mathlib's NumberField.discr of the ring of integers, an isomorphism invariant.
Restricting further by the Galois group of the normal closure (as in N_n(G, X)) is not part of this node.
proofSteps: embeddedFamily: height K ↦ |discr K|, northcott from mathlib:NumberField.finite_of_discr_bdd (monotone in the bound).
isoSetoid: AlgEquiv is reflexive, symmetric and transitive; isoFamily's height is well defined since isomorphic fields have equal discriminants.
isoFamily is Northcott: every class of height ≤ X contains an embedded field of height ≤ X, and there are finitely many of those.
autWeight and isoDegree are well defined: isomorphic fields have the same degree and isomorphic automorphism groups.
acceptance: ℚ has height 1; a Galois field of degree n has weight 1; a cubic field with trivial automorphism group has weight 3.
Bhargava–Shankar–Tsimerman Theorem 1: N₃(0, X) counts totally real cubic fields up to isomorphism with 0 < Disc < X.

nodes.title: Binary cubic forms, their discriminant and the twisted GL2-action
nodes.statement: For a commutative ring R, a binary cubic form over R is f(x,y) = a x^3 + b x^2 y + c x y^2 + d y^3 with a, b, c, d in R, recorded by its four coefficients (V_3(R) = R^4). Its discriminant is disc(f) = b^2 c^2 - 4 a c^3 - 4 b^3 d - 27 a^2 d^2 + 18 a b c d, which is Mathlib's Cubic.discr of the coefficient vector (valid also when a = 0). The group GL2(R) acts on the left by the twisted action (gamma . f)(x,y) = (det gamma)^{-1} f((x,y) gamma), where (x,y) gamma = (g00 x + g10 y, g01 x + g11 y) for gamma = (g_ij). The action is faithful: the scalar u.1 acts as multiplication by u. It satisfies disc(gamma . f) = (det gamma)^2 disc(f), and it commutes with base change of coefficients along ring homomorphisms.
hypotheses: R is a commutative ring; no assumption on 2 or 3 is made.

Convention pinned: the substitution is by the row vector (x, y) times gamma, and the twist is (det gamma)^{-1}; with this convention the Delone-Faddeev correspondence is GL2(R)-equivariant for the change of basis of R(f)/R.
The discriminant is the discriminant of the binary form, not of the dehomogenized polynomial: for a = 0 it is b^2 (c^2 - 4 b d), not the discriminant of a quadratic.
proofSteps: Define the structure with four coefficients, the evaluation, the substitution by (x,y) gamma (expanded coefficientwise) and the scaling by (det gamma)^{-1}; the action axioms reduce to the substitution being an anti-homomorphism in gamma composed with the multiplicativity of det, a polynomial identity.

disc(gamma . f) = (det gamma)^2 disc(f): disc is homogeneous of degree 4 in the coefficients, disc(f o gamma) = (det gamma)^6 disc(f) for the untwisted substitution (an identity in Z[a,b,c,d,g_ij], checked by expansion), and the twist multiplies the coefficients by (det gamma)^{-1}, contributing (det gamma)^{-4}.
The scalar u.1 gives f(ux, uy) = u^3 f and det = u^2, so the twisted action is multiplication by u; hence the action is faithful.
acceptance: disc(x^2 y - x y^2) = 1 and disc(x^3) = 0.
The scalar 2 in GL2(Q) sends f to 2f (the untwisted action would give 8f).
The swap matrix (0 1; 1 0), of determinant -1, sends (a,b,c,d) to (-d,-c,-b,-a).

sources.excerpt: Throughout this paper, we always use the “twisted” action of GL2(Z) on binary cubic forms, i.e., an element γ ∈ GL2(Z) acts on a binary cubic form f(x, y) by (γf)(x, y) = 1/det(γ) f((x, y)γ).

nodes.title: Cubic rings, their discriminant, and maximality at a prime
nodes.statement: A cubic algebra over a commutative ring R is a commutative R-algebra A (with 1) that is free of rank 3 as an R-module (Mathlib: Module.Free R A, Module.Finite R A, Module.finrank R A = 3); a cubic ring is a cubic Z-algebra. The discriminant of A with respect to a basis b is Disc_b(A) = det(Tr_{A/R}(b_i b_j)), Mathlib's Algebra.discr R b; a change of basis by P multiplies it by (det P)^2, so it is a well-defined element of R/(R^x)^2, and for R = Z an integer independent of the basis. A ring A that is free of finite rank over Z is maximal at a prime p if every subring B with A subset B subset A[1/p] that is finitely generated as a Z-module equals A; it is maximal if it is maximal at every prime.
hypotheses: Rank 3 and freeness are part of the notion; over a PID or a local ring the quotient A/R.1 is then free of rank 2 (quotient-by-scalars-is-free).
Maximality at p is tested only against overrings inside A[1/p] (index a power of p); this is Bhargava-Shankar-Tsimerman's R_1 = R' intersect (R tensor Z[1/p]).
For a free Z-module A of finite rank the map A -> A[1/p] is injective, so A is identified with its image.
proofSteps: Define discr via Algebra.discr; the change-of-basis formula is Mathlib's Algebra.discr_of_matrix_mulVec, and over Z the unit determinant is +-1, so the discriminant is basis-independent.
Define IsMaximalAt p A by quantifying over the subrings of Localization.Away (p : A) containing the image of A and finitely generated over Z; IsMaximal A is maximality at every prime.
The ring of integers of a number field is maximal: a subring of K finite over Z consists of integral elements, hence lies in the integral closure (Mathlib NumberField.RingOfIntegers).
acceptance: Disc(Z^3) = 1 in the standard basis; Disc(Z[2^{1/3}]) = -108 in the power basis.
Z[x]/(x^3) is not maximal at 2: Z + Z x + Z (x^2/2) is a ring strictly between it and its localization.

sources.locator: Section 2, printed p. 4, and Section 3, printed p. 6

nodes.title: For a free algebra of rank 3 over a PID or a local ring, 1 extends to a basis
nodes.statement: Let R be a principal ideal domain or a local ring and A an R-algebra that is free of rank n >= 1 as an R-module. Then R -> A, r |-> r.1, is injective, the quotient A/R.1 is free of rank n - 1, and 1 extends to an R-basis <1, a_2, ..., a_n> of A. For n = 3 there is a basis b of A indexed by Fin 3 with b 0 = 1.
hypotheses: R is a PID or a local ring (over an arbitrary base the quotient is only projective, and the parametrization must be phrased with rank-2 projective modules; that generality is not used by any consumer and is not planned here).
proofSteps: Injectivity: if r.1 = 0 then r annihilates the nonzero free module A, so r = 0.
Local case: 1 is nonzero modulo mA (else A = mA and Nakayama gives A = 0); extend its image to a basis of A/mA and lift; by Nakayama the lift is a basis.

PID case: A/R.1 is finitely generated and torsion-free (if r a = s.1 with r != 0 then a is integral over R and equals s/r in A tensor Frac(R); a PID is integrally closed, so s/r is in R), hence free by the structure theorem (Mathlib Module.free_of_finite_type_torsion_free'); a basis of the quotient lifts, together with 1, to a basis of A.
acceptance: For A = Z[x]/(x^3 - 2): the basis <1, x, x^2> has first vector 1.
For R = Z/4 (local) and A = R^3 the vector (1,1,1) extends to a basis.

nodes.title: The cubic ring R(f) of a binary cubic form
nodes.statement: For a binary cubic form f = (a,b,c,d) over a commutative ring R, let R(f) be the commutative R-algebra with R-basis <1, omega, theta> and multiplication omega theta = -ad, omega^2 = -ac - b omega + a theta, theta^2 = -bd - d omega + c theta. It is constructed as R[X_0, X_1]/(X_0 X_1 + ad, X_0^2 + ac + b X_0 - a X_1, X_1^2 + bd + d X_0 - c X_1). It is associative and commutative, free of rank 3 with the stated basis; the constants -ad, -ac, -bd are the only ones compatible with associativity for a normal basis (omega theta in R). Moreover: gamma . f gives an isomorphic R-algebra for gamma in GL2(R); R(n f) is identified with R + n R(f); for a = 1, R(f) = R[omega] with omega^3 + b omega^2 + c omega + d = 0; and R(f) tensor_R S = R(f_S) for any R-algebra S.
hypotheses: Sign convention pinned (Bhargava-Shankar-Tsimerman (10)-(11)): omega^2 = -ac - b omega + a theta. Gross-Lucianovic and HCL III use the basis <1, i, j> = <1, -omega, -theta>, with i^2 = -ac + b i - a j; the index form of their basis is -f.
No hypothesis on R.
proofSteps: Associativity: (omega theta) theta = omega theta^2 and omega^2 theta = omega (omega theta) are linear equations in the three constants n, m, l of a normal basis, with the unique solution n = -ad, m = -ac, l = -bd; with these values all associativity relations among basis elements hold (a polynomial identity check).

Freeness: the quotient of R[X_0, X_1] by the three relations has R-basis 1, X_0, X_1 because the relations are a Groebner basis for the degree order (each monomial of degree 2 is rewritten into degree <= 1, and the overlaps reduce to 0 by the associativity check).
Change of normal basis by gamma in GL2(R) replaces f by gamma . f (Gan-Gross-Savin, proof of Proposition 4.2), giving the isomorphism R(gamma . f) = R(f).
For a = 1: omega^2 = -c - b omega + theta, so theta = omega^2 + b omega + c and omega theta = -d gives omega^3 + b omega^2 + c omega + d = 0 (Gross-Lucianovic, Example 3).

Content: the R-algebra map omega |-> n omega, theta |-> n theta from R(n f) to R(f) respects the relations (each relation scales by n^2) and has image R + n R(f) (HCL III, p. 1332; Gan-Gross-Savin, Proposition 5.2).
Base change: the relations are defined over Z[a,b,c,d], so the presentation commutes with tensor product.
acceptance: R(x^2 y - x y^2) = Z^3 via omega |-> (-1,0,0), theta |-> (0,-1,0) (BST, proof of Proposition 10).
R(0) = R + R omega + R theta with all products of omega, theta zero.

sources.excerpt: Conversely, given a binary cubic form f(x, y) = ax3 + bx2y + cxy2 + dy3, form a potential cubic ring having multiplication laws (10). The values of ℓ, m, n are subject to the associative law relations ... which possesses a unique solution for n, m, ℓ, namely n = −ad m = −ac ℓ = −bd.
sources.match: The multiplication table and the uniqueness of the constants.

sources.excerpt: Finally, the form p(e1, e2) = e3 1 + be2 1e2 + ce1e2 2 + de3 2, with a = 1, corresponds to the cubic ring A = R + Ri + Rj with i2 = −c + bi −j and ij = −d. Since j = −i2 + bi −c, the ring A is generated by α = −i over R.
sources.match: The monogenic case a = 1.

nodes.title: The discriminant of R(f) equals the discriminant of f
nodes.statement: For every binary cubic form f over a commutative ring R, the discriminant of R(f) with respect to its normal basis <1, omega, theta> equals disc(f) = b^2c^2 - 4ac^3 - 4b^3d - 27a^2d^2 + 18abcd.
hypotheses: R is any commutative ring; the identity is a polynomial identity in Z[a,b,c,d].
proofSteps: Traces in the basis <1, omega, theta>: Tr(1) = 3, Tr(omega) = -b, Tr(theta) = c, Tr(omega^2) = b^2 - 2ac, Tr(theta^2) = c^2 - 2bd, Tr(omega theta) = -3ad (from the multiplication table; Gan-Gross-Savin list the same values for the basis <1,-omega,-theta>).

The determinant of the 3 x 3 trace matrix expands to disc(f) (a direct polynomial computation, as Bhargava-Shankar-Tsimerman state); the conceptual route through the uniqueness of the degree-4 SL2-invariant up to scalar is not needed.
acceptance: f = x^2 y - x y^2: R(f) = Z^3 and both discriminants are 1.

sources.excerpt: Proposition 10 The discriminant of an integral binary cubic form f is equal to the discriminant of the corresponding cubic ring R(f). Proof: An explicit calculation using (10) and (11) easily verifies Proposition 10.
sources.match: The statement and the proof by explicit calculation.

sources.excerpt: Using a good basis, we find Tr(1) = 3, Tr(α) = b, Tr(β) = −c, Tr(α2) = b2 −2ac, Tr(β2) = c2 −2bd, Tr(αβ) = −3ad. From this we obtain the identity disc(A/Z) = 1.
sources.match: The trace values used in the computation.

nodes.title: The index form of a cubic algebra with a basis containing 1
nodes.statement: Let A be an R-algebra with an R-basis b = <1, b_1, b_2>. For u, v in A let D_b(u, v) be the determinant of the coordinate vectors of 1, u, v in b. The index form of b is the binary cubic form I_b(x, y) = D_b(xi, xi^2) for xi = x b_1 + y b_2, i.e. 1 ^ xi ^ xi^2 = I_b(x,y) (1 ^ b_1 ^ b_2) in the top exterior power; its coefficients are (D(b_1, b_1^2), D(b_2, b_1^2) + 2 D(b_1, b_1 b_2), 2 D(b_2, b_1 b_2) + D(b_1, b_2^2), D(b_2, b_2^2)). It depends only on the images of b_1, b_2 in A/R.1; a change of basis of A/R.1 by gamma in GL2(R) replaces I_b by gamma . I_b (twisted action); the normal basis <1, omega, theta> of R(f) has index form f; and over Z, |I_b(m, n)| is the index of Z[m b_1 + n b_2] in A when it is nonzero.
hypotheses: The determinant is taken in the coordinates of the same basis b, which is what produces the twist (det gamma)^{-1}.
Orientation convention: with Bhargava-Shankar-Tsimerman's table the normal basis has index form +f; with Gross-Lucianovic's basis <1, i, j> = <1, -omega, -theta> the index form is -f.
proofSteps: Polarization of the trilinear expression D(xi, xi^2) gives the four coefficients.
Translation invariance: adding scalars to b_1, b_2 changes xi by a scalar and xi^2 by a scalar plus a multiple of xi, which do not change the determinant with first row the coordinates of 1.
Change of basis: if (b'_1, b'_2) = (b_1, b_2) gamma modulo R, then xi' at (x, y) equals xi at (x,y) gamma^T-arranged coordinates, and D_{b'} = (det gamma)^{-1} D_b; hence I_{b'} = gamma . I_b.
For the normal basis of R(f) the coefficients are computed from the multiplication table: I(x,y) = det(1; xi; xi^2) = f(x, y) (the footnote of Gross-Lucianovic).
Index formula (Gan-Gross-Savin, Lemma 5.3): <1, xi, xi^2> spans Z[xi], and its coordinate matrix in b has determinant I_b(m, n).
acceptance: For the basis <1, e_0, e_1> of Z^3 (e_i idempotents) the index form is x y^2 - x^2 y.
Negating b_1 and b_2 negates the index form (the twisted action of -1).

nodes.title: Normal bases of a cubic algebra and their multiplication tables
nodes.statement: Let A be an R-algebra with basis <1, b_1, b_2>. There are unique r, s in R such that b'_1 = b_1 + r, b'_2 = b_2 + s satisfy b'_1 b'_2 in R (a normal, or good, basis). For a normal basis <1, omega, theta> with index form f = (a, b, c, d) the multiplication table is omega theta = -ad, omega^2 = -ac - b omega + a theta, theta^2 = -bd - d omega + c theta; in particular A is isomorphic to R(f) by omega |-> omega, theta |-> theta.
hypotheses: A is associative and commutative; the basis contains 1.
proofSteps: Write b_1 b_2 = n + s b_1 + t b_2 with n, s, t in R; then (b_1 - t)(b_2 - s) = n + st is in R, so b'_1 = b_1 - t, b'_2 = b_2 - s is normal (Gross-Lucianovic, proof of Proposition 2.1: i = omega_2 - t, j = omega_3 - s). Uniqueness: if (b'_1 + u)(b'_2 + v) is also in R then v b'_1 + u b'_2 is in R, so u = v = 0 because <1, b'_1, b'_2> is a basis.

In a normal basis write omega^2 = m + beta omega + alpha theta and theta^2 = l + delta omega + gamma theta; the coefficients of the index form are then read off (the determinant computation of the index form), identifying (alpha, beta, gamma, delta) with (a, -b, c, -d).
Associativity forces the constants n, m, l = -ad, -ac, -bd (as in the construction of R(f)).
acceptance: Z[x]/(x^3 - 2) with basis <1, x, x^2> is already normal (x . x^2 = 2); its index form is x^3 - 2y^3 up to the sign conventions.

sources.excerpt: By Lemma 1.1, we may choose a basis ⟨1, ω2, ω3⟩of A over R containing 1. Then for some r, s, t in R we may write ω2ω3 = r + sω2 + tω3 ... Let i = ω2 −t and j = ω3 −s. Then ⟨1, i, j⟩is a basis for which the product ij = r + st lies in R.
sources.match: Existence of a normal basis and the multiplication table.

nodes.title: Delone-Faddeev: GL2(R)-classes of binary cubic forms parametrize cubic rings
nodes.statement: Let R be a principal ideal domain or a local ring (e.g. Z, Z_p, Q, Q_p, R, F_p). The map f |-> R(f) induces a bijection between the GL2(R)-orbits (twisted action) on binary cubic forms over R and the isomorphism classes of cubic R-algebras. The inverse sends A to the index form of any basis <1, b_1, b_2> (which exists by quotient-by-scalars-is-free); disc(R(f)) = disc(f), so the discriminant (in R/(R^x)^2; in Z for R = Z) is preserved. Concretely: every cubic R-algebra A is isomorphic to R(f) for some f; and R(f) is isomorphic to R(g) if and only if g = gamma . f for some gamma in GL2(R).
hypotheses: R a PID or a local ring (Gross-Lucianovic's hypothesis); over Z this is Delone-Faddeev (for nonzero discriminant) and Gan-Gross-Savin (in general).
The action is the twisted action; with the untwisted action the statement is false (the scalar u would act by u^3).
proofSteps: Existence: choose a basis <1, b_1, b_2> (quotient-by-scalars-is-free), normalize it (normal-bases-of-a-cubic-ring), and send omega |-> b_1, theta |-> b_2; the multiplication tables agree, giving A = R(I_b).

Well-definedness of the inverse on isomorphism classes: an isomorphism A -> A' carries bases to bases, and two bases of A/R.1 differ by gamma in GL2(R), changing the index form to gamma . I (index-form-of-a-based-cubic-ring).
R(gamma . f) = R(f) (cubic-ring-of-a-binary-cubic-form); combining: R(f) = R(g) iff g is in the orbit of f.
Discriminant: discriminant-of-the-cubic-ring-of-a-form.
acceptance: disc is preserved: the orbit of x^2 y - x y^2 (disc 1) corresponds to Z^3.
The zero form corresponds to Z + Z omega + Z theta with all products 0 (content infinity); x^3 corresponds to Z[x]/(x^3).

Over F_p the five GL2(F_p)-orbit types of nonzero forms with distinct factorization patterns (111), (12), (3), (1^2 1), (1^3) give F_p^3, F_p x F_{p^2}, F_{p^3}, F_p[t]/(t^2) x F_p, F_p[t]/(t^3) (Bhargava-Shankar-Tsimerman, Section 4).

sources.excerpt: Theorem 9 ([18],[22]) There is a natural bijection between the set of GL2(Z)-equivalence classes of integral binary cubic forms and the set of isomorphism classes of cubic rings.

sources.excerpt: Proposition 2.1. Let N be a free R-module of rank 2. There is a bijection between the set of orbits of the action of GL(N) ≃GL2(R) on the R-module M = Sym3(N) ⊗(∧2 N)−1 and the set of isomorphism classes of cubic rings A over R.

nodes.title: Automorphisms of R(f) are the stabilizer of f in GL2(R)
nodes.statement: For a binary cubic form f over a PID or local ring R, the group of R-algebra automorphisms of R(f) is isomorphic to the stabilizer of f in GL2(R) under the twisted action: an automorphism sigma induces the matrix gamma of its action on R(f)/R in the basis <omega, theta>, and gamma . f = f; conversely each element of the stabilizer lifts uniquely to an automorphism fixing the normal basis structure.
hypotheses: Twisted action; R a PID or local ring.
proofSteps: An automorphism sends the normal basis to a basis with first vector 1 whose image modulo R differs from <omega, theta> by gamma; its index form is gamma . f = f since automorphisms preserve the index form. The normalized translate is the image basis itself (automorphisms preserve normality), so sigma is determined by gamma.
Conversely gamma in Stab(f) gives, via the proof of Delone-Faddeev, an isomorphism R(f) = R(gamma . f) = R(f).
acceptance: For f = x^2 y - x y^2, R(f) = Z^3 has automorphism group S_3, and the stabilizer of x^2 y - x y^2 in GL2(Z) has order 6.
For irreducible f defining a non-Galois cubic field the stabilizer is trivial.

sources.excerpt: Proposition 12 For an integral binary cubic form f, the group of ring automorphisms of R(f) is naturally isomorphic to the stabilizer of f in GL2(Z). Proof: This follows directly from the proof of Theorem 9

nodes.title: Reducible forms correspond to cubic rings with zero divisors
nodes.statement: (a) For a nonzero integral binary cubic form f, R(f) is an integral domain if and only if f(x, y) != 0 for all (x, y) in Z^2 \ {0}, i.e. f has no linear factor over Q (f is irreducible over Q). (b) Over a field K, R(f) is a field if and only if f != 0 and f has no zero in P^1(K). In particular the irreducible integral forms correspond to the orders R(f) whose fraction algebra R(f) tensor Q is a cubic field.
hypotheses: f != 0 in (a); for f = 0 the ring has nilpotents.
proofSteps: If f has a zero, move it to (1:0) by GL2 (a = 0 after the substitution); then omega theta = -ad = 0 with omega, theta nonzero.

Conversely, if R(f) has zero divisors alpha beta = 0, the characteristic polynomial of alpha has zero constant term, so either alpha or alpha^2 + c_1 alpha + c_2 spans with 1 a quadratic subring; a primitive such element extends to a normal basis <1, omega, theta> with a = 0, so f has a linear factor (BST, proof of Proposition 11).
Over a field the same argument shows: no zero of f in P^1(K) iff no zero divisors iff R(f) is a field (a finite-dimensional domain is a field).
acceptance: f = y(x^2 + y^2) gives omega theta = 0.
f = x^3 - 2 y^3 gives the domain Z[2^{1/3}].

nodes.title: Nonzero discriminant corresponds to etale cubic algebras
nodes.statement: For a binary cubic form f over a field K, R(f) is an etale K-algebra if and only if disc(f) != 0. Over Z, disc(f) != 0 if and only if R(f) tensor Q is a product of number fields (an order in an etale cubic Q-algebra); forms of discriminant 0 are the degenerate locus.
hypotheses: K any field.
proofSteps: disc(f) = Disc R(f) is the determinant of the trace form (discriminant-of-the-cubic-ring-of-a-form).

A finite-dimensional commutative K-algebra is etale iff it is a finite product of finite separable field extensions iff its trace form is nondegenerate: separable extensions have nondegenerate trace form (Mathlib traceForm_nondegenerate), and a nonzero nilpotent or an inseparable residue extension lies in the kernel of the trace form.
acceptance: x^3 over K: disc 0 and R(f) = K[t]/(t^3) is not etale.
x^2 y - x y^2: disc 1 and R(f) = K^3.
