nodes.title: The Davenport-Heilbronn sets U_p of binary cubic forms
nodes.statement: For a prime p, U_p is the set of integral binary cubic forms f such that (i) f is not congruent to 0 modulo p, and (ii) no GL2(Z)-translate gamma . f has p^2 | a and p | b. U_p is GL2(Z)-invariant, is defined by congruence conditions modulo p^2 (membership depends only on f mod p^2), and contains every form with p^2 not dividing disc(f). The same definition over Z_p (with GL2(Z_p)) gives an open compact subset of V_3(Z_p) whose intersection with V_3(Z) is U_p.
hypotheses: p prime; the twisted and untwisted actions give the same divisibility conditions over Z since det = +-1.
proofSteps: Invariance: immediate from the definition (orbits are closed under GL2(Z)).
Dependence modulo p^2: conditions (i) and (ii) only involve the coefficients modulo p^2 after substitution by integral matrices.
p^2 not dividing disc: condition (ii) forces p^2 | disc (disc(g) with p^2 | a, p | b is divisible by p^2 term by term), and (i) likewise; so p^2 not dividing disc(f) implies f in U_p.
acceptance: x^3 + 2y^3 is in U_3; x^3 + y^3 is not (the substitution y -> y - x gives 3x^2 y - 3 x y^2 + y^3).
The zero form is in no U_p.

nodes.title: A cubic ring not maximal at p has an overring of index p of two special shapes
nodes.statement: If a cubic ring R = R(f) is not maximal at p, there is a basis <1, omega, theta> of R such that Z + Z(omega/p) + Z theta or Z + Z(omega/p) + Z(theta/p) is a ring. Equivalently, in terms of the form: either all coefficients of f are divisible by p, or some GL2(Z)-translate of f has p^2 | a and p | b.
hypotheses: p prime; R free of rank 3 over Z.
proofSteps: Take R' strictly containing R with index divisible by p and R_1 = R' intersect R[1/p]; by elementary divisors R_1 = Z + Z(omega/p^i) + Z(theta/p^j) with i >= j >= 0.
Normalize the basis; R_1 being a ring is the congruences a = 0 mod p^{2i-j}, b = 0 mod p^i, c = 0 mod p^j, d = 0 mod p^{2j-i} (BST (14)).
If j = 0 replace (i, j) by (i-1, 0), else by (i-1, j-1); the congruences persist, and after finitely many steps i = 1: the two cases (i, j) = (1, 0) and (1, 1).
Reading (14) for (1,0): p^2 | a, p | b; for (1,1): p | a, b, c, d.
acceptance: R(x^3 + y^3): the translate 3x^2 y - 3xy^2 + y^3 has p^2 | a = 0 and 3 | b, so Z[x]/(x^3+1) is not maximal at 3.

sources.excerpt: Lemma 13 Suppose R is not maximal at p. Then there is a Z-basis ⟨1, ω, θ⟩of R such that at least one of the following is true: • Z + Z · (ω/p) + Z · θ forms a ring • Z + Z · (ω/p) + Z · (θ/p) forms a ring.
sources.match: The lemma; the form translation is the congruences (14).

nodes.title: Davenport-Heilbronn: R(f) is maximal at p if and only if f is in U_p
nodes.statement: For an integral binary cubic form f and a prime p, the cubic ring R(f) is maximal at p if and only if f is in U_p. Hence R(f) is maximal if and only if f is in U_p for every prime p. (The identification of the maximal cubic domains with the rings of integers of cubic fields is ST.3/maximal-irreducible-cubic-rings-are-rings-of-integers-of-cubic-fields.)
hypotheses: p prime; f integral.
proofSteps: If f is not in U_p: in case (i) f = p g and R(f) = Z + p R(g) is contained in R(g) with index p^2 (content relation of cubic-ring-of-a-binary-cubic-form); in case (ii) the basis with p^2 | a, p | b makes Z + Z(omega/p) + Z theta a ring (congruences (14) with (i,j) = (1,0)). So R(f) is not maximal at p.
If R(f) is not maximal at p then f is not in U_p (nonmaximal-cubic-rings-have-small-overrings).
Maximality at all primes: the definition of IsMaximal.
acceptance: x^3 + 2y^3 is in U_2 and U_3, and Z[2^{1/3}] is the ring of integers of Q(2^{1/3}).
x^3 + y^3 is not in U_3 and Z[x]/(x^3 + 1) is not maximal at 3 (index 3 in Z x Z[(1+sqrt(-3))/2]).

sources.excerpt: Theorem 14 (Davenport–Heilbronn [17]) The cubic ring R(f) is maximal at p if and only if f ∈Up. The cubic ring R(f) is maximal if and only if f ∈Up for all p.
sources.match: The theorem.

nodes.title: Index-p subrings of R(f) correspond to zeros of f mod p
nodes.statement: For an integral binary cubic form f and a prime p, the number of subrings of R(f) of index p equals the number omega_p(f) of zeros of f modulo p in P^1(F_p) (with the convention that f = 0 mod p has p + 1 zeros).
hypotheses: p prime.
proofSteps: If S subset R' = R(f') has index p, then S = Z + pR' + Z theta for theta well defined in (R'/Z)/p; extending to a normal basis <1, omega, theta> of R', S = <1, p omega, theta> is a ring iff d' = 0 mod p, i.e. the image of theta is a zero of f' mod p.
Then f(x, y) = a' p^2 x^3 + b' p x^2 y + c' x y^2 + (d'/p) y^3 is the form of the basis <1, p omega, theta> (BST, proof of Propositions 15-16).
acceptance: f = x^2 y - x y^2 mod p has 3 zeros: Z^3 has exactly 3 subrings of index p for every p (Z + p e_i-type subrings).

sources.excerpt: Proposition 15 For an integral binary cubic form f, the number of index p subrings of R(f) is equal to ωp(f), the number of zeroes in P1(Fp) of f modulo p.
sources.match: The statement; the proof is the first half of the proof on pp. 7-8.

nodes.title: Index-p overrings of R(f) correspond to liftable double zeros of f mod p
nodes.statement: For an integral binary cubic form f and a prime p, the number of cubic rings in R(f) tensor Q containing R(f) with index p equals the number of double zeros alpha in P^1(F_p) of f mod p such that f(alpha') = 0 mod p^2 for all lifts alpha' of alpha.
hypotheses: p prime.
proofSteps: If R subset R' with index p, write R = Z + pR' + Z theta and normalize; with f the form of the basis <1, p omega, theta> of R, the module spanned by 1, omega, theta is a ring iff p^2 | a and p | b, i.e. the image of p omega is a double zero with f(p omega) = 0 mod p^2 (BST, proof of Proposition 16).
The form of R' is then f' = (a/p^2) x^3 + (b/p) x^2 y + c x y^2 + d p y^3.
acceptance: x^3 + y^3 mod 3 has the double zero (1 : -1) with f(1, -1 + 3t) = 0 mod 9: Z[x]/(x^3+1) has exactly one overring of index 3.

sources.excerpt: Proposition 16 For an integral binary cubic form f, the number of cubic rings in R(f) ⊗Q containing R(f) with index p is equal to the number of double zeroes α ∈P1(Fp) of f modulo p such that f(α′) ≡0 (mod p2) for all α′ ≡α mod p.

nodes.title: Pairs of ternary quadratic forms, the GL3 x GL2 action and the cubic resolvent form
nodes.statement: For a commutative ring R, an (integer-valued) ternary quadratic form is Q(x) = sum_{i<=j} a_ij x_i x_j with a_ij in R (Gram matrix with a_ii on the diagonal and a_ij/2 off it), and W(R) = (Sym^2 R^3 tensor R^2)* is the module of pairs (A, B). The group GL3(R) x GL2(R) acts by (g_3, g_2) . (A, B) = (r A' + s B', t A' + u B') with A' = g_3 A g_3^T, B' = g_3 B g_3^T and g_2 = (r s; t u). Attached invariants: 4 Det(Q) = 4 a_11 a_22 a_33 + a_12 a_13 a_23 - a_11 a_23^2 - a_22 a_13^2 - a_33 a_12^2; the cubic resolvent form f_{(A,B)}(x, y) = 4 Det(A x - B y), a binary cubic form over R; the discriminant Disc(A, B) = disc(f_{(A,B)}); the fifteen SL2-invariants lambda^{ij}_{kl} = a_ij b_kl - a_kl b_ij; and, over Z, the content ct(A, B) = gcd of the lambda^{ij}_{kl}. One has f_{(g . (A,B))} = (det g_3)^2 (f_{(A,B)} composed with the substitution by (r -s; -t u)), hence Disc(g . (A,B)) = (det g_3)^8 (det g_2)^6 Disc(A, B).
hypotheses: Integer-valued convention (Bhargava HCL III (11), (19)): diagonal coefficients integral, off-diagonal Gram entries half-integral; 4 Det has integer coefficients.

Sign convention pinned: the resolvent form is 4 Det(Ax - By) (Bhargava-Shankar); HCL III writes 4 Det(Ax + By), which differs by (x, y) |-> (x, -y) and is inconsistent with its own multiplication table (ArithmeticStatistics/E205).
Over Z, GL3(Z) = {+-1} x SL3(Z) and -1 acts trivially on pairs, so GL3(Z) x GL2(Z)-orbits are the GL2(Z) x SL3(Z)-orbits of Bhargava-Shankar.
proofSteps: Define the six-coefficient ternary forms with evaluation, linear combination and composition t |-> Q(M^T t) (coefficients by polarization at e_i and e_i + e_j); the pair action is then explicit; its axioms are polynomial identities.
Transformation of 4 Det: Det(g A g^T) = det(g)^2 Det(A); for the GL2 part, 4 Det((r A + s B) x - (t A + u B) y) = f(r x - t y, -s x + u y) (expand).
Disc: disc of a binary cubic form scales by c^4 under multiplication by c and by det(M)^6 under substitution by M.
acceptance: For A_1 = x_1 x_3 - x_2^2 and B = a x_1^2 + b x_1 x_2 + c x_2^2 + d x_2 x_3 + e x_3^2 the resolvent form is x^3 + c x^2 y + (bd - 4ae) x y^2 + (a d^2 + b^2 e - 4ace) y^3 (monic).
Proportional pairs (Q, Q) have all lambda = 0 and discriminant 0.

nodes.title: Quartic rings and their cubic resolvent rings
nodes.statement: A quartic ring is a commutative ring free of rank 4 over Z. Following HCL III Definitions 19-20, a cubic resolvent of a quartic ring Q is a cubic ring C together with an isomorphism xi : wedge^3(Q/Z) -> wedge^2(C/Z) and a quadratic map phi : Q/Z -> C/Z such that (29) xi(x ^ y ^ xy) = phi(x) ^ phi(y) for all x, y in Q, and (34) the binary cubic form that C corresponds to under Delone-Faddeev is Disc(phi) (equivalently, xi(x ^ x^2 ^ x^3) = phi(x) ^ phi(x)^2, identity (25)). In bases <1, alpha_1, alpha_2, alpha_3> of Q and <1, omega_1, omega_2> of C, with phi(sum t_i alpha_i) = B(t) omega_1 + A(t) omega_2 modulo Z, the data is a pair (A, B) in W(Z) and the conditions read: det(1, x, y, xy) = B(x) A(y) - A(x) B(y) for all x, y in Q (coordinates of x on alpha_1, alpha_2, alpha_3), and the index form of <1, omega_1, omega_2> is -4 Det(Ax - By) (in the orientation of index-form-of-a-based-cubic-ring). The content ct(Q) is the largest n such that Q = Z + n Q' for a ring Q' of rank 4.
hypotheses: Base Z (the coordinate-free definition works over Z_p and F_p verbatim; HCL III, Appendix).
The orientation xi is part of the data; with the pinned orientation the sign in (29) is +.
Degenerate quartic rings (discriminant 0) are included: the definition does not use S_4-closures.
proofSteps: State the based conditions (determinant identity (12) and the index-form identity) and the coordinate-free Definition 20; show that changing bases of Q/Z and C/Z by (g_3, g_2) replaces (A, B) by (g_3, g_2) . (A, B), so the based notion descends to the coordinate-free one.
Discriminants: Disc Q = Disc C = Disc(A, B) follow from the explicit multiplication table (quartic-ring-of-a-pair) and Delone-Faddeev.
Content: define as the supremum; it is finite for nondegenerate rings and infinity only for the trivial ring Z + Z x_1 + Z x_2 + Z x_3 with all x_i x_j = 0.
acceptance: Z^4 has the cubic resolvent Z^3.
A based cubic resolvent has index form -4 Det(Ax - By), never +4 Det(Ax - By) when the latter is nonzero.
Z^4 has content 1.

sources.excerpt: Let Q be a quartic ring, R a cubic ring, and ξ : ∧3(Q/Z) →∧2(R/Z) an isomorphism. Then we call a quadratic map φ : Q/Z →R/Z a resolvent mapping if (a) the identity (29) holds for all x, y ∈Q; and (b) the binary cubic form associated to R under the Delone-Faddeev correspondence is Disc(φ)

nodes.title: The quartic ring Q(A,B) and cubic resolvent ring R(A,B) of a pair
nodes.statement: For a pair (A, B) of ternary quadratic forms over a commutative ring R, Q(A, B) is the R-algebra with basis <1, alpha_1, alpha_2, alpha_3> and alpha_i alpha_j = c^0_ij + sum_k c^k_ij alpha_k, where for every permutation (i, j, k) of (1, 2, 3) with sign epsilon: c^i_ii = epsilon lambda^{ik}_{ij} + C_i, c^j_ii = epsilon lambda^{ii}_{ik}, c^i_ij = epsilon (1/2) lambda^{ik}_{jj} + (1/2) C_j, c^k_ij = epsilon lambda^{jj}_{ii}, with C_1 = lambda^{23}_{11}, C_2 = -lambda^{13}_{22}, C_3 = lambda^{12}_{33}, and c^0_ij = sum_r (c^r_jk c^k_ri - c^r_ij c^k_rk) for any k != i. All c^k_ij are integral polynomials in the coefficients (the halves cancel: c^1_12 = c^2_12 = c^1_13 = 0, c^3_13 = lambda^{23}_{11}, c^2_23 = lambda^{12}_{33}, c^3_23 = -lambda^{13}_{22}); the basis is normal (c^1_12 = c^2_12 = c^1_13 = 0). The cubic resolvent ring is R(A, B) = R(-4 Det(Ax - By)) (Delone-Faddeev); with phi(sum t_i alpha_i) = B(t) omega_1 + A(t) omega_2 the triple is a based cubic resolvent, and Disc Q(A,B) = Disc R(A,B) = Disc(A,B).
hypotheses: The index condition in the formula for c^0_ij is k != i; HCL III prints k != j, for which the expression depends on k and the table is not associative (ArithmeticStatistics/E204).

The sign of the resolvent form: with the table above and HCL III's normal basis of the resolvent, identity (25) holds for 4 Det(Ax - By), not 4 Det(Ax + By) as printed in (26) (ArithmeticStatistics/E205).
proofSteps: The structure constants are forced by Lemma 9 (identity (12)) with phi = (B, A): equating the coefficients of the degree-4 polynomials p = q in r_1, ..., s_3 (HCL III (17)-(18)) gives the linear system with the unique solution (21)-(22); associativity then forces (23).

Associativity of the resulting table, the independence of c^0_ij from k != i and integrality were checked by expansion for generic and random integral pairs; they are polynomial identities in Z[a_ij, b_ij].
Disc Q(A,B) = Disc(A,B): explicit polynomial identity (HCL III Proposition 10), also checked by expansion.

The cubic resolvent: identity (25) Ind_Q(1, x, x^2, x^3) = Ind_R(1, phi(x), phi(x)^2) determines the resolvent form as the index form of R, namely -4 Det(Ax - By) in the orientation of index-form-of-a-based-cubic-ring (HCL III Proposition 11, with the sign corrected); Proposition 12's check that R(A,B) is a resolvent is the based identity (29) together with this.
Construct Q(A,B) as R[X_1, X_2, X_3] modulo the six relations X_i X_j - c^0_ij - sum_k c^k_ij X_k; freeness of rank 4 is the Groebner-basis argument as for cubic rings.
acceptance: The zero pair gives the ring with all alpha_i alpha_j = 0.
Disc Q(A,B) = Disc(A,B) for (x_1 x_3 - x_2^2, x_1^2 + x_2 x_3).

sources.excerpt: For any permutation (i, j, k) of (1, 2, 3), we have c i ii = ±λik ij + Ci, c j ii = ±λii ik, c i ij = ±1/2λik jj + 1/2Cj, c k ij = ±λjj ii , where we have used ± to denote the sign of the permutation (i, j, k) of (1, 2, 3)

nodes.title: Bhargava: pairs of ternary quadratic forms parametrize quartic rings with cubic resolvents
nodes.statement: There is a canonical bijection between GL3(Z) x GL2(Z)-orbits on W(Z) = (Sym^2 Z^3 tensor Z^2)* and isomorphism classes of pairs (Q, R) with Q a quartic ring and R a cubic resolvent ring of Q; it sends (A, B) to (Q(A,B), R(A,B)) and a pair (Q, R) to the pair of ternary quadratic forms representing the resolvent map phi : Q/Z -> R/Z in bases. It preserves discriminants: Disc(A, B) = Disc(Q) = Disc(R). In based form: every pair (A, B) is the resolvent pair of a based quartic ring and cubic resolvent, unique up to based isomorphism, and changing the bases realizes exactly the GL3(Z) x GL2(Z)-orbit.
hypotheses: Base Z (the same proof works over Z_p and F_p with the appendix's definition).
Cubic resolvents in the sense of quartic-ring-and-cubic-resolvent; degenerate pairs included.
proofSteps: (A,B) |-> (Q(A,B), R(A,B)) is a based cubic resolvent (quartic-ring-of-a-pair).

Conversely, for a based cubic resolvent the identity (12) determines the structure constants of the normal basis as in (21)-(23), so Q is Q(A,B) (HCL III Proposition 10), and (34) determines R as R(A,B) by Delone-Faddeev (Proposition 11; in the degenerate case by the appendix's definition).

The two constructions are mutually inverse on based objects; changing bases of Q/Z and R/Z by (g_3, g_2) acts on (A,B) by the action of pairs-of-ternary-quadratic-forms, so isomorphism classes correspond to orbits.
Discriminants: quartic-ring-of-a-pair.
acceptance: Z^4 corresponds to the orbit of a pair of conics through four points of P^2(Q) in general position, with R = Z^3.
The trivial ring Z + Z x_1 + Z x_2 + Z x_3 (all products 0) corresponds to the pairs spanning a space of dimension <= 1.

sources.excerpt: Theorem 1. There is a canonical bijection between the set of GL3(Z) × GL2(Z)-orbits on the space (Sym2Z3⊗Z2)∗of pairs of integral ternary quadratic forms and the set of isomorphism classes of pairs (Q, R), where Q is a quartic ring and R is a cubic resolvent ring of Q.
sources.match: The theorem.

sources.excerpt: Proposition 13. The bijection in Theorem 1 is discriminant-preserving. That is, if (Q, R) is the pair of rings associated to a pair (A, B) of ternary quadratic forms as in Theorem 1, then Disc(A, B) = Disc(Q) = Disc(R).
sources.match: Discriminant preservation.

nodes.title: Every quartic ring has a cubic resolvent; primitive (in particular maximal) quartic rings have exactly one
nodes.statement: (a) Every quartic ring Q has at least one cubic resolvent ring. (b) The number of cubic resolvent rings of Q (as pairs (R, phi) up to isomorphism) depends only on the content n = ct(Q) and equals sigma(n) = sum_{d | n} d, the number of index-n sublattices of Z^2. (c) In particular a primitive quartic ring (content 1), hence every maximal quartic ring and every ring of integers of a quartic field, has a unique cubic resolvent ring up to isomorphism, namely the cubic invariant ring R_inv(Q). (d) Two pairs give the same quartic ring iff they are related by GL3(Z) x GL2^{+-1}(Q).
hypotheses: Q nontrivial for (b)-(d) (the trivial ring has infinite content).
Maximal quartic rings of nonzero discriminant are Gorenstein and have content 1.
proofSteps: The structure constants of a normal basis of Q determine the fifteen lambda^{ij}_{kl} by (21), and associativity gives the Pluecker syzygies (27) (HCL III Section 3.8).
Lemma 16: fifteen constants satisfying (27), not all zero, are the lambda-invariants of a unique SL2(C)-orbit, which contains an integral point when the constants are integers (elementary divisors).

Lemma 17: the GL3(Z) x GL2(Z)-orbits with prescribed integral lambda of gcd n correspond to the index-n sublattices of the maximal lattice X_Z of integral forms in the pencil; there are sigma(n) of them.
Combine with bhargava-parametrization-of-quartic-rings; content: the gcd of the lambda equals ct(Q) by the formulas (21)-(23).
Maximal rings: a ring Z + nQ' with n > 1 is not maximal (contained in Q'), so maximal rings are primitive.
acceptance: A maximal quartic order has exactly one resolvent.
Z + 2 Z^4 (content 2) has sigma(2) = 3 cubic resolvents.

sources.excerpt: ... it is equal to the number ∑d|n d of sublattices of Z2 having index n. ... Corollary 5. Every quartic ring has a cubic resolvent ring. A primitive quartic ring has a unique cubic resolvent ring up to isomorphism. In particular, every maximal quartic ring has a unique cubic resolvent ring.
sources.match: Parts (a)-(c).

sources.excerpt: Lemma 17. Let λij kℓ∈Z be any 15 integers satisfying the relations (27), and let n be their gcd. Then the number of GZ-orbits WZ in VZ such that λij kℓ(WZ) = λij kℓfor all i ≤j, k ≤ℓ, (i, j) < (k, ℓ) is equal to the number of index n sublattices of Z2
sources.match: The counting lemma.

nodes.title: Maximality of Q(A,B) at p in terms of the lambda-invariants
nodes.statement: If a quartic ring Q is not maximal at p, there is a Z-basis <1, alpha_1, alpha_2, alpha_3> of Q such that Z + Z(alpha_1/p) + Z alpha_2 + Z alpha_3, or Z + Z(alpha_1/p) + Z(alpha_2/p) + Z alpha_3, or Z + Z(alpha_1/p) + Z(alpha_2/p) + Z(alpha_3/p) is a ring. For Q = Q(A, B) these read, after a GL3(Z) x GL2(Z)-change of the pair: (i) lambda^{11}_{22}, lambda^{11}_{23}, lambda^{11}_{33}, lambda^{12}_{13} = 0 mod p and lambda^{11}_{12}, lambda^{11}_{13} = 0 mod p^2; (ii) lambda^{11}_{13}, lambda^{11}_{23}, lambda^{12}_{13}, lambda^{12}_{23}, lambda^{13}_{22}, lambda^{22}_{23} = 0 mod p and lambda^{11}_{12}, lambda^{11}_{22}, lambda^{12}_{22} = 0 mod p^2; (iii) all lambda = 0 mod p. Q(A, B) is maximal at p iff (A, B) is in the set U_p of pairs for which none of (i)-(iii) can be achieved; the U_p are defined by congruence conditions modulo p^2.
hypotheses: p prime; quartic rings of nonzero discriminant for the geometric reading of (i), (ii) (double intersection points, double lines) in HCL III Section 4.2.
proofSteps: Elementary divisors give an overring Q' = Z + Z(alpha_1/n_1) + Z(alpha_2/n_2) + Z(alpha_3/n_3) with n_3 | n_2 | n_1 and p | n_1; being a ring is the congruences n_k c^k_ij = 0 mod n_i n_j (42). Removing primes other than p and lowering exponents as in the cubic case reaches n_1 = p (HCL III Lemma 22).
Translate the three shapes into congruences on the lambda through the explicit c^k_ij (quartic-ring-of-a-pair).
Conversely each of (i)-(iii) exhibits the overring, so Q(A,B) is not maximal.
acceptance: A pair with p | all coefficients gives a nonmaximal Q (case (iii)).
Pairs with Disc(A,B) not divisible by p^2 give Q maximal at p.

sources.excerpt: Lemma 22. If Q is any quartic ring that is not maximal at p, then there exists a Z-basis 1, α1, α2, α3 of Q such that ... (i) Z + Z · (α1/p) + Z · α2 + Z · α3 forms a ring; (ii) Z + Z · (α1/p) + Z · (α2/p) + Z · α3 forms a ring; (iii) Z + Z · (α1/p) + Z · (α2/p) + Z · (α3/p) forms a ring.

sources.excerpt: (i) λ11 22, λ11 23, λ11 33, λ12 13 are multiples of p, and λ11 12, λ11 13 are multiples of p2, (ii) λ11 13, λ11 23, λ12 13, λ12 23, λ13 22, λ22 23 are all multiples of p, and λ11 12, λ11 22, λ12 22 are mul- tiples of p2, (iii) all the λij kℓ’s are multiples of p.

nodes.title: Splitting symbols of pairs and the structure of Q(A,B)/p
nodes.statement: For a pair (A, B) over Z (or Z_p, F_p) whose conics A = 0, B = 0 meet in four points of P^2 over F_p-bar counted with multiplicity, let ((A,B), p) = (f_1^{e_1} f_2^{e_2} ...) record the residue degrees and multiplicities of the intersection points. Then (A,B) is in T_p(sigma) iff Q(A,B)/(p) = F_{p^{f_1}}[t_1]/(t_1^{e_1}) + ..., except for sigma = (1^4), where Q(A,B)/p may also be F_2[x,y]/(x^2, xy + y^2), F_p[x,y]/(x^2, y^2) or F_p[x,y]/(xy, x^2 + n y^2). In particular Disc(A,B) is nonzero mod p iff the conics meet in four distinct points iff Q(A,B)/p is etale over F_p; for maximal Q(A,B), ((A,B), p) is the splitting type of p.
hypotheses: p prime; nondegenerate reductions (A, B mod p spanning a pencil without common component).
proofSteps: The ring Q(A,B)/p depends only on the GL3(F_p) x GL2(F_p)-orbit of (A,B) mod p (base change of quartic-ring-of-a-pair).
Write the multiplication table at one representative of each of the eleven orbit types (HCL III Section 4.1, 'direct calculation').
Nonzero discriminant mod p: four distinct intersection points, and Disc(Q/p) = Disc(A,B) mod p is nonzero, so Q/p is etale.
acceptance: Four F_p-rational points in general position give F_p^4.
A double line in the pencil gives one of the non-reduced types (over-ramified cases).

sources.excerpt: In fact, a direct calculation shows that (A, B) ∈Tp(fe1 1 fe2 2 · · · ) (36) if and only if Q(A, B)/(p) ∼= Fpf1[t1]/(te1 1 ) ⊕Fpf2[t2]/(te2 2 ) ⊕· · · , (37) except in the case Tp(14)

nodes.title: Quadruples of quinary alternating 2-forms and the GL4 x SL5 action
nodes.statement: For a commutative ring R, V(R) = R^4 tensor wedge^2 R^5 is the module of quadruples A = (A_1, ..., A_4) of alternating 5 x 5 matrices over R (recorded by their entries above the diagonal). The group GL4(R) x SL5(R) acts by (g_4, g_5) . A = (sum_s (g_4)_{rs} g_5 A_s g_5^T)_r. The 4 x 4 sub-Pfaffian map Q(X) = (Q_1(X), ..., Q_5(X)), Q_i(X) = (-1)^{i-1} Pf(X with row and column i deleted), is a quadratic covariant: X Q(X) = 0 for every alternating X, and Q(cX) = c^2 Q(X). The SL5-invariants {ijklm} = Q(A_i, A_j)^T A_k Q(A_l, A_m) (Q(.,.) the symmetric bilinear form with Q(X,X) = 2Q(X)) determine the multiplication table of the quintic ring R(A); the unique GL4 x SL5-invariant is the degree-40 discriminant Disc(A).
hypotheses: The discriminant is not written out as a polynomial (degree 40); it is characterized in HCL IV Section 3 and equals Disc R(A).
proofSteps: Define the entries, the matrices, the action and the sub-Pfaffians explicitly; the action axioms are matrix identities.
X Q(X) = 0: the Pfaffian expansion of the 6 x 6 alternating matrix with a repeated row (checked by expansion; verified symbolically for the sign convention (-1)^{i-1}).
The invariants P^+ and P^- of HCL IV (11)-(14) and the brackets {ijklm} (18) are polynomial SL5-invariants of degree 5.
acceptance: For the matrix with x_12 = x_34 = 1 (0-indexed entries (1,2), (3,4)) the sub-Pfaffian vector is (1, 0, 0, 0, 0).
The diagonal of each A_r is zero.

sources.locator: Theorem 1 and Section 4, printed pp. 54 and 66
sources.excerpt: Given a 5 × 5 skew-symmetric matrix X, let Q(X) denote as before the column vector [Q1, . . . , Q5]t of (signed) 4×4 sub-Pfaffians of X. Then Q is evidently a quadratic form on the vector space of 5 × 5 skew-symmetric matrices.

nodes.title: Bhargava: quadruples of quinary alternating forms parametrize quintic rings with sextic resolvents
nodes.statement: (a) There is a canonical bijection between GL4(Z) x SL5(Z)-orbits on V(Z) = Z^4 tensor wedge^2 Z^5 and isomorphism classes of pairs (R, S) with R a quintic ring and S a sextic resolvent ring of R (HCL IV Theorems 1 and 8; for nondegenerate pairs Disc(A) = Disc(R) = (1/16) Disc(S)^{1/3}); the sextic resolvent is defined by HCL IV Definitions 10-11 (a sextic ring S with a Z-linear map phi : R/Z -> wedge^2(S/Z) such that R(phi) = R and S(phi) = S). (b) Every quintic ring is R(A) for some A, so every quintic ring has a sextic resolvent (Theorem 17, Corollary 18). (c) If R is maximal, A is unique up to GL4(Z) x SL5(Z), so a maximal quintic ring has a unique sextic resolvent (Theorem 17, Corollary 19). (d) The classical resolvent map of Cayley is 4 times the sub-Pfaffian covariant (Theorem 9).
hypotheses: The multiplication tables of R(A) (HCL IV Section 4, (16)-(25)) and S(A) (Section 6) are part of the statement; they are specified by the source and not re-derived here.
proofSteps: From A, Lemma 4 expresses the determinants built from conjugates through the invariants P^+, P^- and the brackets {ijklm}, which determines the normalized structure constants of R(A) (Section 4) and of S(A) (Section 6).

The fundamental map g : wedge^2 S~ -> R~ realizes the inverse (Sections 5 and 7), giving Theorem 8 for nondegenerate elements; the appendix-style Definitions 10-11 extend it to all elements (Section 9).

Existence and uniqueness for maximal rings: the invariant theory of Section 10 (Theorem 12 and Lemmas 13-16) constructs an integral A with prescribed structure constants and shows uniqueness when R is maximal (minimal integral model), giving Theorem 17 and Corollaries 18-19.
acceptance: Z^5 corresponds to the quadruple whose sub-Pfaffians vanish at five points of P^3 in general position.
A maximal quintic ring has exactly one sextic resolvent.

sources.excerpt: Theorem 1. There is a canonical bijection between the GL4(Z)×SL5(Z)- orbits on the space Z4 ⊗∧2Z5 of quadruples of 5 × 5 skew-symmetric matrices and the set of isomorphism classes of pairs (R, S), where R is a quintic ring and S is a sextic resolvent ring of R.
sources.match: Part (a).

sources.excerpt: Every quintic ring R is of the form R(A) for some element A ∈Z4 ⊗∧2Z5. If R is a maximal ring, then ... A ... is unique up to Γ-equivalence. ... Corollary 3. Every quintic ring has at least one sextic resolvent ring. A maximal quintic ring has a unique sextic resolvent ring up to isomorphism.
sources.match: Parts (b)-(c).

nodes.title: Maximality of R(A) at p is a congruence condition U_p on quadruples
nodes.statement: For A in V(Z), R(A) is maximal iff A is in U_p for every prime p, where U_p is the union of the seventeen sets U_p(sigma) of elements of splitting type sigma whose ring is maximal at p (defined by congruence conditions modulo p^2); R(A) is maximal exactly when A is a minimal integral model (smallest nonzero discriminant in its GL4(Q) x SL5(Q)-orbit meeting V(Z)).
hypotheses: p prime; nondegenerate A.
proofSteps: The analogue of HCL III Lemma 22 for quintic rings (overrings of index p of three shapes) translated into congruences on the structure constants (HCL IV Section 12).
Theorem 12 and Lemma 16 (minimal integral models) give maximality iff minimality.
acceptance: Elements with p^2 not dividing Disc(A) are in U_p.

nodes.title: The PGL2-action on binary quartic forms, orbits with given invariants, and stabilizers
nodes.statement: Let R be a commutative ring and V(R) the binary quartic forms over R (ST.0), with the twisted action gamma * f = (det gamma)^{-2} f((x,y) gamma) of GL2(R) (ST.0), on which the centre acts trivially. It therefore induces an action of PGL2(R) = GL2(R)/centre (Mathlib's Matrix.ProjGenLinGroup). The invariants I and J are PGL2(R)-invariant, so the orbit space PGL2(R)\V(R) maps to R x R; its fibre over (I, J) is the set of orbits of forms with invariants I, J. The stabilizer of f is Stab_{PGL2(R)}(f). Over Z (and any ring whose units have square 1) the PGL2-orbits are the orbits of GL2 under plain substitution.
hypotheses: The twist exponent is -2, so that I and J are invariant (ST.0 records the untwisted weights (det gamma)^4, (det gamma)^6).
PGL2 is the quotient by the full centre (scalar matrices), not PSL2.
proofSteps: Define the action through a set-theoretic section of GL2(R) -> PGL2(R); well-definedness is ST.0's twistedSMul_scalar (scalars act trivially); the action axioms follow from twistedSMul_mul.
Invariance of I and J: the twisted action multiplies I by (det gamma)^4 (det gamma)^{-4} (ST.0 relative invariance).
Over Z: det gamma = +-1 so the twist is trivial and the orbits agree with those of the plain action.
acceptance: Scalars act trivially.
diag(2, 1) in PGL2(Q) sends (a, b, c, d, e) to (4a, 2b, c, d/2, e/4).
x^3 y - y^4 (J = 27) and its negative (J = -27) lie in different orbits.

sources.excerpt: For any ring R, let VR denote the space of binary quartic forms with coefficients in R. The center of GL2(R) acts trivially under the “twisted action” of GL2(R) on VR defined by γ · f(x, y) := (det γ)−2f((x, y) · γ), yielding an action of PGL2(R) on VR.
sources.match: The action and its descent to PGL2.

sources.excerpt: Note that the PGL2(Z)-orbits on VZ are the same as the GL2(Z)-orbits on VZ, since (−1 −1) ∈GL2(Z) acts trivially on VZ.
sources.match: Integral orbits.

nodes.title: Soluble and locally soluble binary quartic forms
nodes.statement: A binary quartic form f over a field K is K-soluble if z^2 = f(x, y) has a solution with x, y, z in K and (x, y) != (0, 0). Over a number field K, f is (everywhere) locally soluble if f is K_v-soluble for every completion K_v: at every finite place (Mathlib's adicCompletion at each height-one prime of O_K) and at every infinite place (Mathlib's InfinitePlace.Completion). Over Q this means R-soluble and Q_p-soluble for every prime p; an integral form is locally soluble if its rational form is. The reducible locus consists of the integral forms with a rational linear factor (a zero in P^1(Q)); irreducible forms have a != 0 and f(X, 1) irreducible over Q. Solubility is invariant under PGL2(K), stable under field extension, and holds whenever f has a zero in P^1(K) or its leading coefficient is a square.
hypotheses: (x, y) != (0, 0) is required; z may be 0.
For forms of nonzero discriminant, K-solubility is equivalent to the genus-one curve z^2 = f(x, y) having a K-point, but the definition does not refer to curves.
proofSteps: PGL2-invariance: (det gamma)^{-2} f((x,y) gamma) = z^2 has the solution ((x,y) gamma^{-1}, z det gamma).
Base change: a solution over K maps to one over L.
Zeros of f give solutions with z = 0; f(1, 0) = a a square gives (1, 0, sqrt a).
acceptance: -x^4 - y^4 is not R-soluble.
x^3 y + y^4 is Q-soluble.
Lind's quartic 2x^4 - 34y^4 is locally soluble over Q but not Q-soluble.

nodes.title: The Hessian and sextic covariants of a binary quartic
nodes.statement: For g = (a, b, c, d, e), the quartic covariant is g_4 = (3b^2 - 8ac) X^4 + 4(bc - 6ad) X^3 Y + 2(2c^2 - 24ae - 3bd) X^2 Y^2 + 4(cd - 6be) X Y^3 + (3d^2 - 8ce) Y^4 (= -(1/3) times the Hessian determinant of g where 3 is invertible), and the sextic covariant is g_6 = (b^3 + 8a^2 d - 4abc) X^6 + 2(16a^2 e + 2abd - 4ac^2 + b^2 c) X^5 Y + 5(8abe + b^2 d - 4acd) X^4 Y^2 + 20(b^2 e - ad^2) X^3 Y^3 - 5(8ade + bd^2 - 4bce) X^2 Y^4 - 2(16ae^2 + 2bde - 4c^2 e + cd^2) X Y^5 - (d^3 + 8be^2 - 4cde) Y^6. Under the twisted action they transform as g_4(gamma * g) = gamma * g_4(g) (weight -2 twist, like g) and g_6(gamma * g)(x,y) = (det gamma)^{-3} g_6(g)((x,y) gamma).
hypotheses: Cremona-Fisher normalization; the seminvariants are p = 3b^2 - 8ac = g_4(1,0), r = b^3 + 8a^2 d - 4abc = g_6(1,0).
proofSteps: Define by the explicit coefficients.
Equivariance: Cremona-Fisher Lemma 5 (a proper equivalence (M, lambda) sends g_4 to lambda^2 g_4^M and g_6 to lambda^3 mu^3 g_6^M); a polynomial identity.
The Hessian relation: expand F_xx F_yy - F_xy^2.

nodes.title: The cubic invariant z(g) in the square classes of the etale algebra of E_{I,J}
nodes.statement: Let K be a field of characteristic not 2 or 3 and I, J in K with 4I^3 - J^2 != 0. Let E_{I,J} : y^2 = x^3 - 27 I x - 27 J (a short Weierstrass curve, the Jacobian of z^2 = g(x,y)) and A_{I,J} = K[T]/(T^3 - 27 I T - 27 J), which is Tau Ceti's W.A for W = E_{I,J}; M_{I,J} = A^x/(A^x)^2 is W.M. For a binary quartic g with invariants I, J put phi = -T/3 (a root of X^3 - 3IX + J) and G(x, y) = (4 phi g(x,y) + g_4(x,y))/3 in A_{I,J}. Then N(G(x, y)) = g_6(x, y)^2; G(x, y) is a unit iff g_6(x, y) != 0; and the class z(g) = [G(x, y)] in M_{I,J} does not depend on the choice of (x, y) with g_6(x, y) != 0 (such a point exists when K is not F_5). z commutes with base change along field homomorphisms (the restriction of square classes, Tau Ceti's localRes).
hypotheses: char K not 2, 3; #K != 5 for the existence of a point with g_6 != 0 (P^1(F_5) has 6 points and g_6 has degree 6).
The curve is E_{I,J} : y^2 = x^3 - 27 I x - 27 J, isomorphic to Bhargava-Shankar's y^2 = x^3 - (I/3) x - J/27 by (x, y) |-> (x/9, y/27).
proofSteps: N(G) = g_6^2: the norm of a linear element u + v phi is u^3 - 3 I u v^2 - J v^3; substituting and using the syzygy gives g_6^2 (checked symbolically: Res(3G, X^3 - 3IX + J) = 27 g_6^2).
Independence: Cremona-Fisher Lemma 1, G(x_1, y_1) G(x_2, y_2) = F(x_1, y_1, x_2, y_2)^2 with F in A[x_1, y_1, x_2, y_2] explicit; hence the classes at two admissible points agree.
Existence of an admissible point for #K != 5: g_6 has at most 6 zeros in P^1(K) (it is nonzero when the discriminant is nonzero: Res(g, g_6) = Delta^3/3^9 up to the normalization).
Base change: the formula is polynomial in the coefficients.
acceptance: For x^3 y - x y^3 (I = 3, J = 0, a linear factor) z = 1.
N(G) is always a square.

nodes.title: z(g) is constant on PGL2(K)-orbits
nodes.statement: If g has invariants I, J and gamma is in PGL2(K), then z(gamma * g) = z(g).
hypotheses: Same hypotheses as the construction of z.
proofSteps: G(gamma * g)(x, y) = (det gamma)^{-2} G(g)((x, y) gamma) by the equivariance of g and g_4 (Cremona-Fisher Lemma 5); (det gamma)^{-2} is a square, and (x,y) gamma is admissible for g when (x, y) is admissible for gamma * g (equivariance of g_6).
acceptance: A diagonal substitution rescales G by a square.

sources.excerpt: Proposition 6 Suppose that the two quartics g and g′ are properly equivalent. Then z(g) = z(g′) in L∗/L∗2. Proof. Immediate from Proposition 2 and Lemma 5.

nodes.title: Forms with a linear factor: trivial cubic invariant and a single orbit
nodes.statement: Let g have invariants I, J with 4I^3 - J^2 != 0. (a) z(g) = 1 if and only if g has a linear factor over K (a zero in P^1(K)). (b) Every such g is PGL2(K)-equivalent to the normal form q_0 = (1/27) Y (27 X^3 - 9 I X Y^2 - J Y^3) = X^3 Y - (I/3) X Y^3 - (J/27) Y^4; hence the forms with a linear factor and invariants I, J form one orbit.
hypotheses: char K not 2, 3.
proofSteps: (a, =>) At a zero (x, y) of g, g_4(x, y) != 0 and g_6(x,y) != 0 (resultants Delta^2/3^2, Delta^3/3^9), and the syzygy gives G(x, y) = g_4(x,y)/3 = (3 g_6/g_4)^2, a square (Cremona-Fisher Lemma 3).

(a, <=) With r = g_6(1, 0) != 0 after a proper change, z = G(1,0) has characteristic polynomial Z^3 - pZ^2 + qZ - r^2; if z = z_1^2 then h(Z^2) = -h_1(Z) h_1(-Z) and -(u + b)/(4a) is a root of g (Cremona-Fisher Proposition 8).
(b) Move the linear factor to Y, translate X to kill c, and rescale with (M, lambda) of determinant 1 (Cremona-Fisher Proposition 7).
acceptance: x^3 y - x y^3 has z = 1 and is the normal form with I = 3, J = 0.

sources.excerpt: Proposition 7 Let g be a quartic with invariants I, J which has a linear factor in K[X, Y ]. Then g is properly equivalent to 1/27 Y (27X3 −9IXY 2 −JY 3) = −1/27 Y 4F(−3X/Y). Hence any two quartics with the same invariants and which both have linear factors are properly equivalent.

nodes.title: Equal cubic invariants give a zero of p_1 g_2 - a_1 h_2
nodes.statement: Let g_1, g_2 have the same invariants I, J, with seminvariants a_i = g_i(1,0), p_i = g_{i,4}(1,0), r_i = g_{i,6}(1, 0), and suppose r_1, r_2 != 0. If z(g_1) = z(g_2), then the binary quartic p_1 g_2 - a_1 h_2 (h_2 the Hessian covariant of g_2) has a zero in P^1(K).
hypotheses: char K not 2, 3.
proofSteps: z(g_1) = z(g_2) gives w with w^2 = z_1^{-1} z_2 and N(w) = r; comparing coefficients in h(X^2) = -h_0(X) h_0(-X) with h_0 = N(X - w) = X^3 - uX^2 + vX - r gives (u^2 - p)^2 - 8ru - 4q = 0, i.e. 3 r_1 u is a root of g~(X) = X^4 - 2 s_1 X^2 - 216 r_1^2 r_2 X + s_1^2 - 36 r_1^2 s_2.
g~(X) = (1/a) g(X + b, -4a) for g = p_1 g_2 - a_1 h_2 with coefficients (a, b, ...) when a != 0 (computer algebra), so g has a zero; if a = 0 then (1, 0) is a zero.
acceptance: For g_1 = g_2 the comparison form p g - a h vanishes at a point of P^1(K).

sources.excerpt: Lemma 9 Let g1, g2 ∈BQ(K) have the same invariants I, J. ... and suppose that r1, r2̸ = 0. If z(g1) = z(g2) then the quartic eg(X) = X4 −2s1X2 −216r2 1r2X + s2 1 −36r2 1s2 has a root in K

nodes.title: A zero of p_1 g_2 - a_1 h_2 gives a PGL2(K)-equivalence
nodes.statement: Let g_1, g_2 have the same invariants with r_1 = g_{1,6}(1, 0) != 0. If p_1 g_2 - a_1 h_2 has a zero in P^1(K), then g_1 and g_2 are PGL2(K)-equivalent.
hypotheses: char K not 2, 3.
proofSteps: Move the zero to (1, 0) by a proper change of g_2: p_1 a_2 = a_1 p_2.
If a_1 = 0 then p_1 != 0, so a_2 = 0 and both forms have a linear factor: equivalent by linear-factor-forms.

Otherwise t = a_2/a_1 = p_2/p_1 and the seminvariant syzygy gives r_2^2 = t^3 r_1^2, so t is a square; a proper diagonal change makes t = 1 and a shift makes b_2 = b_1; equal invariants then force g_2 = g_1 (Cremona-Fisher Lemma 10).
acceptance: For g_1 = g_2 the identity equivalence is found.

nodes.title: Cremona-Fisher: the cubic invariant determines the PGL2(K)-orbit
nodes.statement: Let K be a field of characteristic not 2 or 3, K != F_5, and g_1, g_2 binary quartics with the same invariants I, J, 4I^3 - J^2 != 0. Then z(g_1) = z(g_2) if and only if g_1 and g_2 are PGL2(K)-equivalent.
hypotheses: Includes the cases I = 0 or J = 0, where equivalence by GL2 x GL1 with the same invariants need not be proper; the theorem is about PGL2(K) (proper) equivalence.
proofSteps: <=: cubic-invariant-is-an-orbit-invariant.

=>: if z = 1 both have linear factors (linear-factor-forms). Otherwise neither has a linear factor; after proper changes r_1, r_2 != 0; auxiliary-quartic-root-from-equal-cubic-invariants gives a zero of p_1 g_2 - a_1 h_2, and linear-factor-of-the-comparison-quartic-gives-equivalence concludes.

nodes.title: The binary quartic q(P) attached to a point of E_{I,J}
nodes.statement: For P in E_{I,J}(K) define q(O) = X^3 Y - (I/3) X Y^3 - (J/27) Y^4 (the linear-factor normal form) and, for P = (xi, eta), q(P) = X^4 - (xi/6) X^2 Y^2 - (eta/27) X Y^3 + ((36 I - xi^2)/432) Y^4. Then q(P) has invariants I and J, is K-soluble (its leading coefficient is 1, or it has the linear factor Y), and q(-P) is PGL2(K)-equivalent to q(P). In Bhargava-Shankar's normalization y^2 = x^3 - (I/3) x - J/27 the same quartic is (1/4) X^4 - (3/2) xi' X^2 Y^2 + 2 eta' X Y^3 + (I/3 - (3/4) xi'^2) Y^4 with (xi', eta') = (xi/9, eta/27), up to PGL2(K).
hypotheses: char K not 2, 3.
proofSteps: Invariants: direct computation using eta^2 = xi^3 - 27 I xi - 27 J (checked symbolically, also for the Bhargava-Shankar formula).
Solubility: (1, 0, 1) is a solution for affine P; q(O) vanishes at (1, 0).
q(-P): the substitution Y -> -Y (determinant -1, trivial twist) changes the sign of the eta-term.
acceptance: q(O) vanishes at (1, 0).
On y^2 = x^3 - 27x the 2-torsion point (0, 0) gives X^4 + Y^4/12.
The leading coefficient of q(P) at an affine point is 1.

nodes.title: Bhargava-Shankar Theorem 3.2: E(K)/2E(K) and PGL2(K)-orbits of soluble quartics
nodes.statement: Let K be a field of characteristic not 2 or 3 and I, J in K with 4I^3 - J^2 != 0. The map P |-> PGL2(K) . q(P) induces a bijection between E_{I,J}(K)/2E_{I,J}(K) and the set of PGL2(K)-orbits of K-soluble binary quartic forms with invariants I and J; the identity class corresponds to the orbit of forms with a linear factor over K. Equivalently, z restricted to soluble orbits is a bijection onto the image of Tau Ceti's mu, and z o q = mu.
hypotheses: char K not 2, 3; for K = F_5 (excluded from the construction of z) the statement is verified by exhaustive computation.
proofSteps: Well-defined and injective: z(q(P)) = mu(P) (cubic-invariant-of-the-quartic-of-a-point), z is injective on orbits (cubic-invariant-determines-the-orbit) and ker mu = 2E(K) (Tau Ceti ker_μ_eq); so q(P) ~ q(Q) iff mu(P) = mu(Q) iff P - Q in 2E(K).

Surjective onto soluble orbits: a soluble g with a zero is in the linear-factor orbit = q(O); otherwise a proper change gives leading coefficient 1 and b = 0, and then (xi, eta) = (-6c, -27d) lies on E_{I,J} and q(xi, eta) = g (Cremona-Fisher Theorem 13(2), using the formulas for I, J).
Identity: q(O) is the linear-factor form (linear-factor-forms).
K = F_5: finitely many forms, points and matrices; check directly.
acceptance: Over R: #E(R)/2E(R) = #E(R)[2]/2, which is 1 if Delta < 0 and 2 if Delta > 0; so there are that many PGL2(R)-orbits of R-soluble forms with given invariants.
Over F_p (p >= 5): #E(F_p)/2E(F_p) = #E(F_p)[2], and every nondegenerate quartic over F_p is soluble.

nodes.title: Cremona-Fisher: proper equivalences correspond to bilinear factors
nodes.statement: Let g_1, g_2 be binary quartics with the same invariants and Hessians h_1, h_2, and F_{g_1,g_2}(X_1, Y_1, X_2, Y_2) = g_1(X_1,Y_1) h_2(X_2,Y_2) - g_2(X_2,Y_2) h_1(X_1,Y_1). Then g_1 and g_2 are PGL2(K)-equivalent iff F has a K-rational bilinear factor (X_1 Y_1) A (X_2 Y_2)^T with A in GL2(K); the factor with matrix A gives the equivalence M = A^T (0 1; -1 0). Moreover F_{g,g} = -3 (X_1 Y_2 - Y_1 X_2) R(X_1X_2, X_1Y_2 + X_2Y_1, Y_1Y_2) with R a ternary cubic form that is, up to a nonzero constant, the norm from L = K[phi] of an L-linear form; hence over K-bar, F_{g,g} has exactly three further bilinear factors, one for each root phi_i of X^3 - 3IX + J, and such a factor is K-rational iff phi_i is in K.
hypotheses: char K not 2, 3.
proofSteps: If g_2 = det(M)^{-2} g_1^M then F_{g_1,g_2} = det(M)^{-2} F_{g_1,g_1}(X_1, Y_1, (X_2,Y_2)M), and F_{g_1,g_1} has the factor X_1 Y_2 - Y_1 X_2.
Conversely a bilinear factor, specialized at (X_1, Y_1) = (1, 0) (after making r_1 != 0), gives a zero of p_1 g_2 - a_1 h_2, and linear-factor-of-the-comparison-quartic-gives-equivalence applies.

The factorization of F_{g,g} and of R as a norm from L = K[phi] (Cremona-Fisher Section 6, identities (1)-(2), verified by computer algebra) identifies the nontrivial bilinear factors with the conjugates of an L-linear factor.
acceptance: For g = X^4 - Y^4 the proper self-equivalences over Q(i) are 4 in number.

sources.excerpt: Then g1 and g2 are properly equivalent if and only if Fg1,g2 has a K-rational bi-linear factor. Moreover, if this factor has associated matrix A ∈GL2(K), then g2 is the transform of g1 via the proper equivalence (M, det(M)−1) where M = AT (0 1; −1 0).
sources.match: The criterion.

sources.excerpt: exactly four proper equivalences between any two quartics with the same invariants, coming from the four bi-linear factors of Fg1,g2. In particular there are always exactly three non-trivial proper equivalences from a quartic g to itself; these are defined over the resolvent cubic extension L.

nodes.title: Bhargava-Shankar Theorem 3.2: Stab_{PGL2(K)}(f) is isomorphic to E(K)[2]
nodes.statement: Let K be a field of characteristic not 2 or 3 and f a binary quartic over K with invariants I, J and 4I^3 - J^2 != 0 (not necessarily K-soluble). Then Stab_{PGL2(K)}(f) is isomorphic to E_{I,J}(K)[2]. It is an elementary abelian 2-group of order 1 + #{roots of X^3 - 3IX + J in K}; over R it has order 4 if Delta(f) > 0 and 2 if Delta(f) < 0 (never 1).
hypotheses: char K not 2, 3; the discriminant is nonzero.
proofSteps: Order: stabilizer elements are the proper self-equivalences; by bilinear-factor-criterion-for-proper-equivalence they correspond to the K-rational bilinear factors of F_{f,f}: the trivial one and one for each K-rational root of the resolvent.
Exponent 2: a self-equivalence is given by M = (-alpha_2 alpha_1; -alpha_3 alpha_2) (Cremona-Fisher Section 6), of trace 0, so M^2 = -det(M) I is scalar.

E(K)[2]: its order is 1 + #{roots of x^3 - 27Ix - 27J in K} (Tau Ceti card_ker_nsmul_two), and the roots correspond to those of X^3 - 3IX + J under T = -3 phi. Elementary abelian 2-groups of equal order 1, 2 or 4 are isomorphic.
Over R: the resolvent has three real roots iff its discriminant 27 Delta is positive.
acceptance: Over R: order 4 if Delta > 0, 2 if Delta < 0; these give Bhargava-Shankar's GL2(R)-stabilizer orders 8 and 4 (Lemma 2.2) and n_0 = 4, n_1 = 2, n_{2+-} = 4.
x^4 - y^4 over Q: resolvent X^3 + 36X has one rational root (0), so the stabilizer has order 2.

sources.excerpt: Furthermore, the stabilizer in PGL2(K) of any (not necessarily K-soluble) binary quartic form f in VK, having nonzero discriminant and invariants I and J, is isomorphic to E(K)[2], where E is the elliptic curve defined by y2 = x3 −I/3x −J/27.
sources.match: The theorem.

nodes.title: Which square classes are cubic invariants: linear representatives and the conic
nodes.statement: Let K be a field of characteristic not 2 or 3 with #K != 5, I, J with 4I^3 - J^2 != 0, and m in A_{I,J}^x with square norm. Then the following are equivalent: (a) m = z(g) for a binary quartic g with invariants I, J; (b) m is represented by a unit linear in T (m w^2 = u + v phi for a unit w); (c) the ternary quadratic form Q_m(t) = coefficient of T^2 in m (t_0 + t_1 T + t_2 T^2)^2 (reduced modulo T^3 - 27IT - 27J) has a nontrivial zero. Q_m is regular: its Gram determinant is -N(m) up to the normalization of T. If v != 0 and N(u + v phi) = r^2, Simon's quartic (1/(12 v))(X^4 - 6u X^2 Y^2 + 8r X Y^3 + (12 I v^2 - 3 u^2) Y^4) has invariants I, J and cubic invariant (u + v phi)/(9 v^2).
hypotheses: char K not 2, 3, #K != 5.
proofSteps: (a) => (b): z(g) is represented by G(x, y), which is linear in phi.
(b) => (a): if v = 0 the norm condition makes m a square, take the linear-factor form; otherwise Simon's quartic works (invariants and z checked symbolically; Cremona-Fisher Theorem 13(3)).

(b) <=> (c): m w^2 linear iff the T^2-coefficient of m w^2 vanishes; a nontrivial zero t of Q_m may be taken to be a unit of A: the zeros form a smooth conic (Q_m regular) with at least #K + 1 >= 8 points, while the non-units form at most three lines of P^2(K) each meeting the conic in at most 2 points.
Regularity: det Q_m = -N(m) for a depressed cubic (checked symbolically).
acceptance: For m = 1 the conic has the zero t = (1, 0, 0).
For I = 3, J = 0 and m = u + v phi linear, Simon's quartic has invariants (3, 0).

sources.excerpt: (3) The image of z consists of those classes in H that may be represented by an element of L that is linear in ϕ. ... Otherwise, following (Simon, 2002, §1.4) we put g(X, Y ) = 1/(12v) (X4 −6uX2Y 2 + 8rXY 3 + (12Iv2 −3u2)Y 4).

nodes.title: Locally soluble quartics and Tau Ceti's 2-Selmer group (Bhargava-Shankar Proposition 3.3)
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field and I, J in K with 4I^3 - J^2 != 0. The cubic invariant z induces a bijection between the PGL2(K)-orbits of everywhere locally soluble binary quartic forms over K with invariants I, J and Tau Ceti's 2-Selmer group selmerGroup_2 of E_{I,J} (relative to O_K and the family of completions at the infinite places); the orbit of forms with a linear factor goes to 1. Equivalently (Mathlib-only form): z is injective on these orbits, and a square class m of square norm is the cubic invariant of a locally soluble global form iff for every place v the restriction of m is the cubic invariant of a K_v-soluble form with invariants I, J.
hypotheses: K a number field; Tau Ceti's selmerGroup_2 is defined by the norm condition and the local conditions localRes m in range(mu over K_v) at all finite places and at the infinite completions.
At complex places every form is soluble and the local condition is automatic.
proofSteps: Into the Selmer group: for locally soluble g, z(g) has square norm, and at each place v, localRes z(g) = z_v(g) (cubic-invariant-of-a-binary-quartic, base change) is in z_v(soluble orbits) = range(mu_v) (binary-quartic-parametrization-of-E-mod-2E over K_v, Tau Ceti localRes_comp_μ); this is membership in selmerGroup_2 (Tau Ceti mem_selmerGroup₂_iff).
Injective: cubic-invariant-determines-the-orbit (K is infinite).

Surjective: for m in selmerGroup_2, at each place m_v = mu_v(P_v) = z_v(q(P_v)) is represented by a linear unit, so the conic Q_m is isotropic over every K_v (image-of-the-cubic-invariant over K_v); it is regular, so by Hasse-Minkowski for ternary forms (GlobalQuadraticForms Layer 5) it is isotropic over K; hence m = z(g) for some g with invariants I, J (image-of-the-cubic-invariant over K). Then z_v(g) = m_v = z_v(q(P_v)), so g is PGL2(K_v)-equivalent to the soluble q(P_v) (injectivity over K_v): g is locally soluble.
Identity: linear-factor-forms.
acceptance: Over Q for E = 571a1 (I = 44608, J = 18842960): the three nontrivial Selmer elements are represented by the quartics g_1, g_2, g_3 of Fisher's Example 3.4, and the product of their cubic invariants is a square.
Lind's quartic 2x^4 - 34y^4 (I = -816, J = 0) is locally soluble with no rational point: its cubic invariant lies in selmerGroup_2 of y^2 = x^3 + 22032 x but not in the image of mu.

nodes.title: A primitive vector over a PID is a column of a matrix in SL3
nodes.statement: Let O be a principal ideal domain and v in O^3 with coordinates generating the unit ideal (a primitive vector). Then for every j there is M in SL3(O) whose j-th column is v; in particular SL3(O) acts transitively on P^2(Frac O) (on primitive vectors up to units).
hypotheses: O a PID (Z, Z_p, Z_(p)).
proofSteps: O^3/Ov is finitely generated and torsion-free (v primitive), hence free of rank 2 over the PID (Mathlib Module.free_of_finite_type_torsion_free'); so v extends to a basis of O^3.
The matrix of this basis has unit determinant u; scale another basis vector by u^{-1} and permute columns to place v in position j.
acceptance: v = (1290, 383, 1000) (the point 2(3,5) of y^2 = x^3 - 2 in projective coordinates) is a column of a matrix in SL3(Z).

nodes.title: Ternary cubic forms and their invariants c_4, c_6
nodes.statement: A ternary cubic over a commutative ring R is U = a x^3 + b y^3 + c z^3 + a_2 x^2 y + a_3 x^2 z + b_1 x y^2 + b_3 y^2 z + c_1 x z^2 + c_2 y z^2 + m x y z. Its invariants c_4(U) (25 terms, degree 4) and c_6(U) (103 terms, degree 6) are the integer polynomials in the coefficients determined by Fisher's normalization H(lambda U + mu H) = 3(c_4 lambda^2 mu + 2 c_6 lambda mu^2 + c_4^2 mu^3) U + (lambda^3 - 3 c_4 lambda mu^2 - 2 c_6 mu^3) H, where H(U) = -(1/2) det(Hessian of U); c_4 = -216 abcm + 144 abc_1c_2 + ... + m^4 and c_6 = 5832 a^2b^2c^2 - 3888 a^2 b b_3 c c_2 + ... - m^6. For the Weierstrass cubic y^2 z - x^3 - A x z^2 - B z^3 they are c_4 = -48A and c_6 = -864B, the usual invariants of y^2 = x^3 + Ax + B; and c_4^3 - c_6^2 = 1728 Delta. Substitution: (U o M)(x, y, z) = U(M^T (x, y, z)).
hypotheses: The polynomials are written out explicitly (derived from the Hessian identity and checked on the Weierstrass family); their leading terms agree with Fisher's printed partial expansions.
proofSteps: Compute H(U), the first and second directional derivatives of H at U in the direction H(U), and read off c_4, c_6 from the lambda^2 mu and lambda mu^2 coefficients (exact polynomial division by the coefficient a; checked symbolically).
Evaluate on the Weierstrass cubic.
acceptance: Fermat cubic x^3 + y^3 + z^3: c_4 = 0, c_6 = 5832.

sources.excerpt: The ternary cubic U(x, y, z) = ax3 + by3 + cz3 + a2x2y + a3x2z +b1xy2 + b3y2z + c1xz2 + c2yz2 + mxyz has Hessian H(U) = (−1/2) × det(...). Putting c4 = c4(U), c6 = c6(U) and H = H(U) we find H(λU + µH) = 3(c4λ2µ + 2c6λµ2 + c2 4µ3)U + (λ3 −3c4λµ2 −2c6µ3)H.

nodes.title: c_4 and c_6 are SL3-invariants of weights 4 and 6
nodes.statement: For a ternary cubic U and a 3 x 3 matrix M over a commutative ring, c_4(U o M) = det(M)^4 c_4(U) and c_6(U o M) = det(M)^6 c_6(U).
hypotheses: Polynomial identities in the coefficients of U and the entries of M.
proofSteps: Both sides are polynomials; the identities are multiplicative in M, so it suffices to check them for elementary transvections and diagonal matrices over Q (these generate GL3(Q), which is Zariski dense), and they then hold over every commutative ring (Cremona-Fisher-Stoll Theorem 2.8(i); Fisher, Section 4).

nodes.title: Projection of a plane cubic from the point (0:1:0): the binary quartic f_2^2 + 4 f_1 f_3
nodes.statement: Let U be a ternary cubic with b = 0, i.e. with (0:1:0) on U = 0, written U = f_1(x,z) y^2 - f_2(x,z) y - f_3(x,z) with f_1 = b_1 x + b_3 z, f_2 = -(a_2 x^2 + m x z + c_2 z^2), f_3 = -(a x^3 + a_3 x^2 z + c_1 x z^2 + c z^3). Its projection quartic is the binary quartic F_U = f_2^2 + 4 f_1 f_3 in (x, z) (the discriminant in y of U along the line through (0:1:0) with slope (x : z)). If U is integral then F_U is integral, and I(F_U) = c_4(U), J(F_U) = 2 c_6(U). For the Weierstrass cubic of y^2 = x^3 + Ax + B, F = 4(x^3 z + A x z^3 + B z^4), with invariants (-48A, -1728B) = (2^4 I, 2^6 J) for I = -3A, J = -27B.
hypotheses: The generalized quartic y^2 + f_2 y = f_1 f_3 of Cremona-Fisher-Stoll (3.4) becomes F_U after completing the square (times 4), which is how integrality at 2 is kept.
proofSteps: Lines through (0:1:0) are {z x_0 = x z_0}; substituting, U restricted to the line is the quadratic f_1 y^2 - f_2 y - f_3 whose discriminant is F_U; the residual intersection points are rational iff F_U is a square.

I(F_U) = c_4(U) and J(F_U) = 2 c_6(U) for b = 0: polynomial identities (checked symbolically; Cremona-Fisher-Stoll: 'a generic computation shows that the genus one models (3.4) and (3.5) have the same discriminant', here with c_4, c_6 themselves).
acceptance: Weierstrass cubic: F = (0, 4, 0, 4A, 4B).
Integrality is compatible with base change to Q.

nodes.title: The projected quartic from P has invariants (2^4 I, 2^6 J) and cubic invariant mu(P)
nodes.statement: Let E : y^2 = x^3 + Ax + B over a field K of characteristic not 2, 3, P = (xi, eta) in E(K), and M in SL3(K) with M^T e_2 = (xi, eta, 1) (row 1 of M is P). Then F = projection quartic of (Weierstrass cubic o M) has invariants I(F) = -48A, J(F) = -1728B, and its cubic invariant is the class of 36 xi - T in A_{-48A, -1728B}, i.e. mu(P') for the image P' = (36 xi, 216 eta) of P on y^2 = x^3 + 1296 A x + 46656 B = E_{-48A,-1728B} (the variable change of ratio 6). The same holds for P = O with class 1, and at 2-torsion points with the corrected representative.
hypotheses: char K not 2, 3.
proofSteps: Invariants: invariance-of-ternary-cubic-invariants (det M = 1) and projection-of-a-plane-cubic-from-a-rational-point with the Weierstrass values.

The line through P and O meets E in P, O, -P; the corresponding point of z^2 = F is K-rational, and at that point G takes the value (a square times) 36 xi - T (explicit computation; checked numerically on y^2 = x^3 - 43x + 42, where the classes of P = (-3, +-12), O, (1,0), (6,0) and 2P all agree componentwise with xi - e_i).
Alternatively: F is K-soluble with invariants (2^4 I, 2^6 J), so F ~ q(P'') for some P'' (binary-quartic-parametrization-of-E-mod-2E); the computation above identifies P'' = P' modulo 2E.
acceptance: For A = -43, B = 42 and P = (-3, 12) the square classes of z(F) and (xi - e_i) are both (-1, -1, 1).

nodes.title: Every Q_p-soluble quartic with invariants (-48A, -1728B) has a Z_p-integral representative
nodes.statement: Let p be a prime, A, B in Z_p with 4A^3 + 27B^2 != 0, and f a Q_p-soluble binary quartic over Q_p with I(f) = -48A and J(f) = -1728B. Then f is PGL2(Q_p)-equivalent to a binary quartic with coefficients in Z_p (with the same invariants).
hypotheses: p arbitrary (including 2 and 3): the factor 4 in F = f_2^2 + 4 f_1 f_3 is what makes the argument uniform at 2.
This is the n = 2 case of the Cremona-Fisher-Stoll Minimisation Theorem (minimal level 0 for soluble models), in the normalization with invariants (2^4 I, 2^6 J).
proofSteps: By binary-quartic-parametrization-of-e-mod-2e over Q_p (for E_{-48A,-1728B}), f ~ q(P') for some P' = (36 xi, 216 eta), P = (xi, eta) in E_{A,B}(Q_p), or f has a linear factor (P = O).

nodes.title: Local integral representatives at every prime give a global one
nodes.statement: Let f be a binary quartic over Q such that for every prime p there is gamma_p in PGL2(Q_p) with gamma_p * f integral over Z_p. Then there is gamma in PGL2(Q) with gamma * f integral over Z.
hypotheses: Twisted action; scalars act trivially, so lattices up to scaling suffice.
proofSteps: For almost all p, f is already Z_p-integral (finitely many denominators); take gamma_p = 1 there.

Lift gamma_p to GL2(Q_p); the lattices Z_p^2 gamma_p determine a Z-lattice Lambda in Q^2 with Lambda tensor Z_p = Z_p^2 gamma_p (Lambda = Q^2 intersect the local lattices; Q^2 is dense in Q_p^2 and the local lattices are open).
Lambda is free (Z a PID): Lambda = Z^2 gamma for gamma in GL2(Q); then gamma_p = k_p gamma with k_p in GL2(Z_p).
gamma * f = k_p^{-1} * (gamma_p * f) is Z_p-integral for every p (GL2(Z_p) preserves V(Z_p)), hence integral.
acceptance: For f with a single bad prime p the global gamma can be taken to be the local one when it has rational entries.

nodes.title: Bhargava-Shankar Theorem 3.5: 2-Selmer elements are PGL2(Q)-classes of locally soluble integral quartics with invariants 2^4 I, 2^6 J
nodes.statement: Let E = E_{A,B} : y^2 = x^3 + Ax + B with A, B in Z, 4A^3 + 27B^2 != 0, and I = I(E) = -3A, J = J(E) = -27B. Then the elements of the 2-Selmer group of E are in bijection with the PGL2(Q)-equivalence classes of locally soluble integral binary quartic forms with invariants 2^4 I = -48A and 2^6 J = -1728B. The bijection sends the class of g to z(g), an element of Tau Ceti's selmerGroup_2 of E_{2^4 I, 2^6 J} : y^2 = x^3 + 1296 A x + 46656 B, transported to E by the variable change x |-> 36x, y |-> 216y. The integral forms with a rational linear factor and these invariants form one PGL2(Q)-class, corresponding to the identity. Stabilizers: Stab_{PGL2(Q)}(g) is isomorphic to E(Q)[2] for every such g.
hypotheses: A, B integers (the minimal-pair condition is not needed; it pins the curve within its isomorphism class, as in EllipticCurves Layer 8).
The rescaling by 2^4, 2^6 is forced: Lemma 3.4's divisibility hypotheses hold for (2^4 I, 2^6 J) and not in general for (I, J).
PGL2(Q)-classes of rational forms, each represented by integral forms; two integral forms in one class need not be GL2(Z)-equivalent (the weights m(f) of ST.4 count this).
proofSteps: Apply locally-soluble-quartics-and-the-two-selmer-group over Q to I' = 2^4 I, J' = 2^6 J: locally soluble orbits with these invariants correspond to selmerGroup_2 of E_{I',J'}, the linear-factor orbit to 1.
Each such orbit contains an integral form: integral-representatives-of-locally-soluble-quartics (I' = -48A, J' = -1728B).
Transport to E_{A,B}: E_{I',J'} is E_{A,B} rescaled by u = 1/6; the explicit Selmer group, mu and the local conditions are compatible with this variable change (request to EllipticCurves Layer 6).
Stabilizers: stabilizer-of-a-binary-quartic-is-two-torsion, and E_{I',J'}(Q)[2] = E(Q)[2].
acceptance: y^2 = x^3 - x (A = -1, B = 0): Sel_2 has order 4 = #E(Q)[2]; the classes are those of the integral quartics q(P') for the three 2-torsion points and the linear-factor class.
Scaling check: the quartics with invariants (I, J) themselves (without 2^4, 2^6) need not have integral representatives.

nodes.title: The embedding phi of binary quartic forms into pairs of ternary quadratic forms and the map psi on orbits
nodes.statement: Let A_1 = x_1 x_3 - x_2^2 (Gram matrix antidiag(1/2, -1, 1/2)) and, for f = (a, b, c, d, e) in V_Z, B_f = a x_1^2 + b x_1 x_2 + c x_2^2 + d x_2 x_3 + e x_3^2 (Gram matrix (a, b/2, 0; b/2, c, d/2; 0, d/2, e)). Then phi(f) = (A_1, B_f) in W_{Z,1} = {(A_1, B)} (Bhargava-Shankar (30)). phi is injective, its image is the set of (A_1, B) with B_13 = 0, and every F_{Z,1}-class of W_{Z,1} (F_{Z,1} the lower unitriangular matrices of GL2(Z), acting by (A_1, B) |-> (A_1, B + r A_1)) has a unique representative in the image. phi preserves discriminants, and 4 Det(A_1 x - B_f y) = x^3 + c x^2 y + (bd - 4ae) x y^2 + (a d^2 + b^2 e - 4ace) y^3 is the monic cubic resolvent of f (same I, J). With rho(gamma) = (det gamma)^{-1} (a^2, ab, b^2; 2ac, ad + bc, 2bd; c^2, cd, d^2) for gamma = (a b; c d), rho : GL2(Z) -> SO(A_1, Z) is a homomorphism and phi(gamma . f) = rho(gamma) . phi(f) modulo F_{Z,1}. The induced map psi : PGL2(Z)\V_Z -> (GL2(Z) x SL3(Z))\W_Z is the composite of the orbit bijection with forgetting the slice.
hypotheses: rho is written in the coordinate order that makes phi equivariant for the action g . B = g B g^T; the matrix printed as (31) in Bhargava-Shankar has the coordinates in the reverse order (ArithmeticStatistics/E203).
The resolvent form is 4 Det(A x - B y); the 'Det(Ax - By)' printed on p. 16 has leading coefficient 1/4 (ArithmeticStatistics/E201).
proofSteps: phi and the slice: explicit; the (1,3)-entry of B + r A_1 is B_13 + r/2 in half-integral units, so exactly one r makes it 0.
Discriminant and resolvent: expand 4 Det(A_1 x - B_f y) (checked symbolically); its I, J equal I(f), J(f) and its discriminant is disc(f).
rho is a homomorphism into SO(A_1): rho(gamma) A_1 rho(gamma)^T = A_1 and det rho(gamma) = 1 (polynomial identities).
Equivariance: rho(gamma) B_f rho(gamma)^T - B_{gamma . f} is a multiple of A_1, checked on the generators (1 1; 0 1), (0 1; 1 0), (1 0; 0 -1) of GL2(Z) and symbolically for general gamma.
acceptance: phi(x^3 y) = (A_1, x_1 x_2) with resolvent x^3.
The x_1^2-coefficient of rho(T) . B_{y^4} equals that of B_{(x+y)^4}, namely 1 (the printed order gives 0).

nodes.title: rho maps GL2(Z) onto SO(A_1, Z)
nodes.statement: An element M of SL3(Z) preserves A_1 = x_1 x_3 - x_2^2 (M A_1 M^T = A_1) if and only if M = rho(gamma) for some gamma in GL2(Z); rho has kernel {+-1}, so it induces an isomorphism PGL2(Z) = SO(A_1, Z).
hypotheses: The coordinate order of rho as in the embedding node.
proofSteps: Over a field K of characteristic not 2: M in SO(A_1)(K) preserves the conic A_1 = 0, parametrized by (s : t) |-> (s^2 : st : t^2); M restricted to the conic is (Q_1 : Q_2 : Q_3) with Q_2^2 = Q_1 Q_3 and Q_1, Q_3 coprime binary quadratics, so Q_1 = L_1^2, Q_3 = L_2^2, Q_2 = L_1 L_2 up to a scalar, and M agrees with rho(gamma) (gamma given by the linear forms L_1, L_2) on the conic, which spans P^2; hence M = lambda rho(gamma), and det = 1 with M A_1 M^T = A_1 forces lambda = 1.

Integrality: if rho(gamma) is integral with gamma = (a b; c d) scaled to be a primitive integral matrix, then ad - bc divides a^2, b^2, c^2, d^2, so every prime dividing ad - bc divides a, b, c, d; hence ad - bc = +-1 and gamma is in GL2(Z).
Kernel: rho(gamma) = 1 forces gamma scalar, and scalars in GL2(Z) are +-1.
acceptance: rho(0 1; 1 0) reverses the coordinates up to sign and preserves A_1.

nodes.title: Bhargava-Shankar Proposition 2.16: the fibres of psi over nondegenerate classes are uniformly bounded
nodes.statement: Let N be an upper bound for #{(x, y) in Z^2 : g(x, y) = 1} over all integral binary cubic forms g of nonzero discriminant (N = 12 by Delone and Evertse; N = 10 by Bennett). An element of (GL2(Z) x SL3(Z))\W_Z of nonzero discriminant has at most 2N preimages in PGL2(Z)\V_Z under psi.
hypotheses: Nonzero discriminant.
The source states the bound 12 = N; its argument gives 2N (ArithmeticStatistics/E202). Any uniform bound suffices for Bhargava-Shankar Theorem 2.20 and the uniformity estimate.
proofSteps: By orbit-bijection-for-the-embedding it suffices to bound the F_{Z,1} x SO(A_1, Z)-classes in W_{Z,1} inside a GL2(Z) x SL3(Z)-orbit w; fix (A_1, B_0) in w and let g = 4 Det(A_1 x - B_0 y) (monic).

An element (A_1, B) = (g_2, g_3) . (A_1, B_0) of the slice has first form p A_1 + q B_0 transformed to A_1, so 4 Det(p A_1 + q B_0) = 1, i.e. g(p, -q) = 1 for the first row (p, q) of g_2 (4 Det is multiplied by det(g_3)^2 = 1).

Two such elements with the same first row differ by g_2' g_2^{-1} = (1 0; r s) with s = +-1 and by an element of SO(A_1, Z): for s = 1 they are F_{Z,1} x SO(A_1, Z)-equivalent, for s = -1 they differ by (A_1, B) |-> (A_1, -B) (the forms f and -f).
Hence the number of classes is at most 2 #{(x, y) : g(x, y) = 1} <= 2N.

nodes.title: Chebyshev-type bounds for the prime-counting function and for tails of prime sums
nodes.statement: (a) There is an absolute constant C such that π(x) ≤ C·x/log x for every real x ≥ 2, where π(x) is the number of primes p ≤ x. (b) For every real s > 1 there is a constant C_s such that Σ_{p prime, p > N} p^{−s} ≤ C_s·N^{1−s}/log N for every real N ≥ 2. (c) Consequently, for every integer k ≥ 2 there is C_k with Σ_{p prime, M < p ≤ r} r^n/p^k ≤ C_k·r^n/(M^{k−1} log M) for all reals 2 ≤ M ≤ r and every n ≥ 0.
hypotheses: x, N, M ≥ 2 so that the logarithms are positive; the sums run over rational primes
The constants are absolute (C) or depend only on s (C_s) or k (C_k); in particular they are independent of N, M, r and n
proofSteps: (a) Split the primes p ≤ x at √x. Every prime in (√x, x] has log p > (1/2) log x, so π(x) − π(√x) ≤ 2θ(x)/log x ≤ 2 log 4 · x/log x by Chebyshev's bound θ(x) ≤ (log 4)x (Chebyshev.theta_le_log4_mul_x, with θ written as a sum over primes by Chebyshev.theta_eq_sum_primesLE); and π(√x) ≤ √x ≤ 2x/log x for x ≥ 2.

(b) Decompose (N, ∞) into dyadic blocks (2^j N, 2^{j+1} N], j ≥ 0. By (a) the block contains at most C·2^{j+1}N/log(2^{j+1}N) ≤ 2C·2^j N/log N primes, each contributing at most (2^j N)^{−s}. Summing the geometric series Σ_j 2^{j(1−s)} = (1 − 2^{1−s})^{−1} gives C_s = 2C/(1 − 2^{1−s}).
(c) is (b) with s = k, multiplied by r^n, after dropping the upper limit r.
acceptance: Order check: the bounds are exactly what the proofs of Bhargava-Shankar Theorem 2.20 (O(X^{1/6}/log X) primes below X^{1/6} and Σ_{p > X^{1/6}} p^{−2} = O(1/(X^{1/6} log X))) and of the geometric sieve (16) use; the trivial bound Σ_{p > N} p^{−2} ≤ 1/(N − 1) would lose the logarithm and make the error term in Theorem 2.20 of the same order X^{5/6} as the main term.
Numerical sanity check: π(10^6) = 78498 ≤ 2 log 4 · 10^6/log 10^6 + 10^3 ≈ 201,700.

nodes.title: Lattice points of a dilated compact region lying on a subvariety of codimension k
nodes.statement: Let B ⊂ ℝ^n be a compact set and let Y ⊆ 𝔸^n_ℚ be a Zariski-closed subset of codimension ≥ k ≥ 1, i.e. Y = V(𝔞) for an ideal 𝔞 ⊆ ℚ[x_1, …, x_n] with Krull dimension of ℚ[x_1, …, x_n]/𝔞 at most n − k. Then there is a constant C = C(B, Y) such that #{a ∈ rB ∩ ℤ^n : a ∈ Y(ℚ)} ≤ C·r^{n−k} for every real r ≥ 1.
hypotheses: B compact (the source says 'compact region having finite measure'; only boundedness is used)
r ≥ 1: for 0 < r < 1 the left side can be 1 (the origin) while r^{n−k} → 0 (sourceIssue ArithmeticStatistics/E309)
The constant depends on B and Y only, not on r
proofSteps: Reduce to Y irreducible by summing over its finitely many irreducible components. Choose f_1, …, f_k ∈ ℚ[x] such that the irreducible component Y′ of V(f_1, …, f_k) containing Y has codimension k; it suffices to bound the points of Y′.
Induct on n. If no f_i involves x_n the bound follows from the case n − 1 times the O(r) choices of the last coordinate.

Elimination: reorder so that f_k is nonconstant in x_n, and replace each f_i (i < k) involving x_n by the resultant Res_{x_n}(f_i, f_k) (Polynomial.resultant). Since Res_{x_n}(f_i, f_k) = A_i f_i + B_i f_k with A_i ≠ 0 (Polynomial.exists_mul_add_mul_eq_C_resultant), the component of the new zero set containing Y is still Y′, and now f_1, …, f_{k−1} do not involve x_n. After removing leading terms that vanish on Y′, the leading coefficient h_k ∈ ℚ[x_1, …, x_{n−1}] of f_k in x_n does not vanish identically on Y′.

Points with h_k(a) = 0: their first n − 1 coordinates lie on the union Z ⊆ 𝔸^{n−1} of the components meeting Y′ ∩ {h_k = 0} of V(f_1, …, f_{k−1}, h_k), which has codimension k in 𝔸^{n−1}; by induction there are O(r^{n−1−k}) of them, times O(r) values of a_n, giving O(r^{n−k}).

Points with h_k(a) ≠ 0: their first n − 1 coordinates lie on the codimension-(k − 1) component Y_{k−1} ⊆ 𝔸^{n−1} of V(f_1, …, f_{k−1}) containing the projection of Y′, so by induction there are O(r^{(n−1)−(k−1)}) = O(r^{n−k}) of them, and for each at most d = deg_{x_n} f_k values of a_n make f_k vanish (Polynomial.card_roots').
acceptance: Degree-one case: for Y the coordinate subspace x_1 = ⋯ = x_k = 0 and B = [−1, 1]^n the count is (2⌊r⌋ + 1)^{n−k}, so the exponent n − k cannot be lowered in general (the source's Remark 3.2).
The count for Y = {x_1^2 + ⋯ + x_n^2 = 0} (codimension 1 over ℚ, but with the single rational point 0) is 1 = O(r^{n−1}), consistent with the lemma.
k = n: a zero-dimensional Y has O(1) points in rB for every r ≥ 1.

sources.excerpt: Lemma 3.1 Let B be a compact region in R^n having finite measure. Let Y be a variety in R^n of codimension k ≥ 1. Then we have #{a ∈ rB ∩ Y ∩ Z^n} = O(r^{n−k}), where the implied constant depends only on B and on Y.

sources.excerpt: We now show, via elimination theory, that we may reduce to the case where k − 1 of the fi, say f1, . . . , fk−1, all do not involve some ﬁxed variable, say xn.

nodes.title: A closed subscheme of 𝔸^n_ℤ of codimension k has O(p^{n−k}) points over 𝔽_p
nodes.statement: Let Y = Spec ℤ[x_1, …, x_n]/𝔞 be a closed subscheme of 𝔸^n_ℤ of codimension ≥ k, i.e. the Krull dimension of ℤ[x_1, …, x_n]/𝔞 is at most n + 1 − k. Then there are constants M_0 = M_0(Y) and C = C(Y) such that #Y(𝔽_p) = #{a ∈ 𝔽_p^n : g(a) = 0 for all g ∈ 𝔞} ≤ C·p^{n−k} for every prime p > M_0.
hypotheses: The codimension is taken in 𝔸^n_ℤ, which has dimension n + 1; a vertical fibre 𝔸^n_{𝔽_{p_0}} has codimension 1, so it is excluded for k ≥ 2
Only primes p > M_0 are covered; for the finitely many p ≤ M_0 the trivial bound #Y(𝔽_p) ≤ p^n is used by the consumers
proofSteps: The generic fibre Y_ℚ = V(𝔞ℚ[x]) has dimension at most n − k (a component of Y_ℚ of dimension e closes up in Y to a component of dimension e + 1). Induct on d = n − k, the dimension of Y_ℚ; d = −1 means Y_ℚ = ∅, so 1 ∈ 𝔞ℚ[x], a nonzero integer N lies in 𝔞, and Y(𝔽_p) = ∅ for p ∤ N.

For d ≥ 0 run the elimination of ArithmeticStatistics:ST.2/lattice-points-on-a-subvariety-in-a-dilated-region over ℤ: after clearing denominators the polynomials f_1, …, f_k, the resultants replacing them (Polynomial.resultant, Polynomial.exists_mul_add_mul_eq_C_resultant) and the leading coefficient h_k are integral, and each nonzero one stays nonzero modulo every prime not dividing its content; let M_0 exceed all these contents and the M_0 of the schemes used in the induction.

Points of Y(𝔽_p) with h_k(a) = 0 lie on the closed subscheme Y ∩ V(h_k), whose generic fibre has dimension ≤ d − 1 because h_k does not vanish on any component of Y_ℚ; by induction there are O(p^{n−k−1}) of them.

Points with h_k(a) ≠ 0 project to 𝔽_p-points of the subscheme V(f_1, …, f_{k−1}) ⊆ 𝔸^{n−1}_ℤ, of codimension ≥ k − 1, of which there are O(p^{(n−1)−(k−1)}) by induction on n; over each, f_k(b, x_n) is a nonzero polynomial over 𝔽_p of degree ≤ deg_{x_n} f_k, with at most that many roots (Polynomial.card_roots').

The base case k = 1 (a single nonzero polynomial g ∈ 𝔞 with nonzero reduction) is the Schwartz-Zippel bound #{a ∈ 𝔽_p^n : g(a) = 0} ≤ deg(g)·p^{n−1} (MvPolynomial.schwartz_zippel_totalDegree with S = 𝔽_p).
acceptance: Y = V(x_1, …, x_k): #Y(𝔽_p) = p^{n−k} exactly, for every p.
Y = V(p_0) for a fixed prime p_0 has codimension 1 in 𝔸^n_ℤ, and #Y(𝔽_{p_0}) = p_0^n: this is why only p > M_0 is claimed and why the codimension is taken in 𝔸^n_ℤ.

For Y = V(Δ, ∂Δ/∂e) on binary quartic forms (codimension 2 by ArithmeticStatistics:ST.2/discriminant-loci-of-codimension-two) the lemma gives #Y(𝔽_p) = O(p^3), consistent with the splitting-type description of strongly divisible forms, in which the types (1^3 1), (1^2 1^2) and (2^2) each contribute a constant times p^3 residue classes.

sources.excerpt: Furthermore, there exists a constant M0 > 0 such that Y′ (mod p) has codimension k in A^n_{F_p} for all primes p > M0.
sources.match: The uniformity in p that the proof of Theorem 3.3 needs; the source asserts it without proof (sourceIssue ArithmeticStatistics/E310).

sources.excerpt: since #Y′(F_p) = O(p^{n−k}) and rB can be covered by O((r/p)^n) boxes each of whose sides have length p

nodes.title: The geometric sieve for primes up to the size of the region
nodes.statement: Let B ⊂ ℝ^n be compact and Y ⊆ 𝔸^n_ℤ a closed subscheme of codimension k ≥ 2. There is C = C(B, Y) such that for all reals r ≥ 1 and M ≥ 2, #{(a, p) : a ∈ rB ∩ ℤ^n, p prime, M < p ≤ r, a mod p ∈ Y(𝔽_p)} ≤ C·r^n/(M^{k−1} log M).
hypotheses: k ≥ 2 (for k = 1 the prime sum Σ 1/p diverges)
Pairs (a, p) are counted, so a point reducing into Y modulo several primes counts several times
proofSteps: Fix a prime p ≤ r. Cover rB by O((r/p)^n) cubes of side p (possible because p ≤ r and B is bounded). Each cube contains at most #Y(𝔽_p) integral points reducing into Y(𝔽_p), and #Y(𝔽_p) ≤ C p^{n−k} for p > M_0 by ArithmeticStatistics:ST.2/uniform-bound-for-points-of-a-subscheme-modulo-p; for the finitely many p ≤ M_0 use #Y(𝔽_p) ≤ p^n and absorb them into the constant (they occur only when M < M_0, and then 1 ≤ M_0^{k−1} log M_0/(M^{k−1} log M)).
So each prime contributes O(r^n/p^k), and Σ_{M < p ≤ r} r^n/p^k = O(r^n/(M^{k−1} log M)) by part (c) of ArithmeticStatistics:ST.2/chebyshev-bounds-for-prime-sums.
acceptance: For Y = V(x_1, x_2) in 𝔸^2 and B = [0, 1]^2 the number of pairs is Σ_{M<p≤r} (⌊r/p⌋ + 1)^2 ≍ r^2 Σ_{p > M} p^{−2}, matching the bound.
Removing the logarithm from Chebyshev's bound would give only O(r^n/M^{k−1}), which is still enough for Bhargava-Shankar Theorem 2.13 but not for the stated (13).

sources.excerpt: Thus the total number of desired pairs (a, p) with p ≤ r is at most #{ (a, p) | a ∈ rB ∩ Z^n, M < p ≤ r, a (mod p) ∈ Y′(F_p)} = Σ_{M<p≤r} O(r^n/p^k) = O(r^n/(M^{k−1} log M)).
sources.match: Exactly the lemma.

nodes.title: The geometric sieve for primes larger than the region
nodes.statement: Let B ⊂ ℝ^n be compact and let Y ⊆ 𝔸^n_ℤ be a closed subscheme of codimension k ≥ 1 (Krull dimension of its coordinate ring ≤ n + 1 − k). There is C = C(B, Y) such that for every real r ≥ 1, #{(a, p) : a ∈ rB ∩ ℤ^n, p prime, p > r, a ∉ Y(ℤ), a mod p ∈ Y(𝔽_p)} ≤ C·r^{n−k+1}.
hypotheses: Points of Y(ℤ) are excluded here and counted separately by ArithmeticStatistics:ST.2/lattice-points-on-a-subvariety-in-a-dilated-region
The primes are larger than the linear size r of the region
proofSteps: Reduce to an irreducible Y′ (a component of Y, or of its reduction, of the same or larger codimension): a ∉ Y(ℤ) implies a ∉ Y′(ℤ) for every component, and a mod p ∈ Y(𝔽_p) puts a mod p in some component; put Y′ in the elimination normal form of ArithmeticStatistics:ST.2/lattice-points-on-a-subvariety-in-a-dilated-region, cut out generically by integral f_1, …, f_k.
k = 1: some f_i does not vanish at a ∉ Y′(ℤ), and 0 ≠ |f_i(a)| = O(r^{deg f_i}) has at most deg f_i prime factors exceeding r; so each of the O(r^n) points contributes O(1) pairs.

k ≥ 2, induction on n, with the elimination normal form (f_1, …, f_{k−1} free of x_n, leading coefficient h_k of f_k not vanishing on Y′). The pairs split into three sets: (19) a ∈ Y_{k−1}(ℤ), f_k(a) ≠ 0 and p | f_k(a): O(r^{(n−1)−(k−1)}) first coordinates by the lattice-point lemma, O(r) values of a_n, O(1) primes each; (20) a ∉ Y_{k−1}(ℤ) with a mod p ∈ Z(𝔽_p), Z the codimension-k locus in 𝔸^{n−1} over which h_k vanishes: induction on n gives O(r^{(n−1)−k+1}) pairs for the first coordinates, times O(r) values of a_n; (21) a ∉ Y_{k−1}(ℤ), a mod p ∈ Y′(𝔽_p) and h_k(a) ≢ 0 mod p: induction gives O(r^{(n−1)−(k−1)+1}) pairs (b, p), and a_n mod p is one of the ≤ deg_{x_n} f_k roots of f_k(b, x_n) mod p (Polynomial.card_roots'), each class meeting an interval of length O(r) = O(p) in O(1) integers.
Adding the three contributions gives O(r^{n−k+1}).
acceptance: For Y′ = V(x_1, x_2) ⊂ 𝔸^2 and B = [−1, 1]^2 the set counted is empty: a prime p > r dividing a_1 and a_2 with |a_i| ≤ r forces a = 0 ∈ Y′(ℤ).

For Y′ = V(x_1, x_2^2 − 2x_3^2) ⊂ 𝔸^3 (n = 3, k = 2) the set (19) consists of the pairs (a, p) with a_1 = 0, a_2^2 − 2a_3^2 ≠ 0 and p > r a prime divisor of a_2^2 − 2a_3^2; each nonzero value is O(r^2), so it has at most one such prime, and the set has at most O(r^2) = O(r^{n−k+1}) elements, the order of the lemma.

sources.locator: Proof of Theorem 3.3, display (17) and the decomposition (18)-(21), p. 12
sources.excerpt: We next turn to the case of counting pairs (a, p) where p > r, and show that #{ (a, p) | a ∈ rB ∩ Z^n, p > r, a ∉ Y′(Z), a (mod p) ∈ Y′(F_p)} = O(r^{n−k+1}).
