nodes.title: Cokernel law of a Haar-random alternating matrix over ℤ_p
nodes.statement: For n even and a finite abelian p-group class G, π_n(G) is the probability that coker(A) ≅ G for A Haar-random in M_n(ℤ_p)^alt. It is computed at finite level: for any e ≥ 1 with p^{e−1}G = 0, π_n(G) = #{Ā ∈ M_n(ℤ/p^e)^alt : coker(Ā) ≅ G} / p^{e·n(n−1)/2}, and this is independent of such e. (A cokernel coker(A) ≅ ℤ_p^s ⊕ F is isomorphic to G iff s = 0 and F ≅ G, which is detected mod p^e.)
hypotheses: p prime
n even
e ≥ 1 with p^{e−1}G = 0
proofSteps: Define the finite count over alternating matrices with entries in ZMod (p^e) and the cokernel as the quotient of (ℤ/p^e)^n by the image of Ā, compared with the standard representative of G.

Independence of e: reduction M_n(ℤ/p^{e+1})^alt → M_n(ℤ/p^e)^alt is surjective with fibres of size p^{n(n−1)/2}, and for p^{e−1}G = 0 the condition coker ≅ G is detected mod p^e (a cyclic summand ℤ/p^f, f ≥ e, or a free summand would give an element of order p^e in the reduction).
acceptance: π_n(0) = #GL_n(𝔽_p)^alt / #M_n(𝔽_p)^alt (e = 1).
π_n(G) = 0 unless G is symplectic.

nodes.title: BKLPR: limiting cokernel law of random alternating matrices
nodes.statement: (a) For each symplectic p-group G, lim_{n→∞, n even} π_n(G) = A_0(G) := #G/#Sp(G) · ∏_{i≥1}(1 − p^{1−2i}), and Σ_G A_0(G) = 1. (b) For r ≥ 0, define A_r(G) := (#G)^{1−r}/#Sp(G) · ∏_{i≥r+1}(1 − p^{1−2i}) for symplectic G; then Σ_G A_r(G) = 1, and A_r is the limit as n → ∞ (n − r even) of the laws of (coker A)_tors for A drawn from the natural probability measure on alternating n × n matrices over ℤ_p of rank n − r (BKLPR Theorem 3.11).
hypotheses: p prime
G a symplectic p-group
proofSteps: (a) Fix G and m = n − dim_{𝔽_p} G[p]. Surjections ℤ_p^n → G pull back the pairing of G to alternating pairings on ℤ_p^n inducing G; Sp(G) acts freely on Sur(ℤ_p^n, G) with these pairings as orbits, so there are #Sur(ℤ_p^n, G)/#Sp(G) of them (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/symplectic-finite-abelian-p-groups, ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/surjection-count).

The probability that the pairing of A equals a fixed one is #GL_m(𝔽_p)^alt/#M_m(𝔽_p)^alt · (#G)^{1−n} (BKLPR Corollaries 3.4–3.5: A ∈ D + D M_n(ℤ_p) D with rank condition), so π_n(G) = #Sur(ℤ_p^n, G)/#Sp(G) · #GL_m^alt/#M_m^alt · (#G)^{1−n}; as n → ∞, #Sur(ℤ_p^n, G)/(#G)^n → 1 and ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/count-of-nondegenerate-alternating-matrices gives the limit.
Total mass: Σ_G π_n(G) = 1 (singular matrices have measure zero), Fatou gives Σ A_0 ≤ 1, and the bound π_n(G) ≤ #G/#Sp(G) plus dominated convergence gives equality.

(b) For r ≥ 1 the measure on rank-(n − r) alternating matrices is the normalised canonical measure on the ℤ_p-points of that scheme (BKLPR Proposition 2.1, Lemma 3.13); its existence and the pushforward identity are the gap 'Canonical measure on ℤ_p-points (Oesterlé–Serre)'. Given it, the proof integrates |det|^r (BKLPR Lemma 3.12) and repeats (a).
acceptance: The p-rank marginal of A_0 is the even-n limit of the kernel law P_p(· | n) (reduce A mod p).

nodes.title: The BKLPR model for the p^∞-Selmer sequence
nodes.statement: For a prime p, the BKLPR distribution Q is the probability measure on pairs (r, T), r ∈ ℤ_{≥0} and T a symplectic p-group class, given by Q(r, T) := (1/2) A_r(T) for r ∈ {0, 1} and Q(r, T) := 0 for r ≥ 2 (A_r from ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/bklpr-alternating-cokernel-limit). A pair (r, T) stands for the split short exact sequence 0 → (ℚ_p/ℤ_p)^r → (ℚ_p/ℤ_p)^r ⊕ T → T → 0 of co-finite type ℤ_p-modules, which models 0 → E(k) ⊗ ℚ_p/ℤ_p → Sel_{p^∞}(E) → Ш(E)[p^∞] → 0; every isomorphism class of such split sequences with finite cokernel arises from exactly one pair. BKLPR define Q as the limit of the laws Q_{2n} of intersections of random maximal isotropic ℤ_p-submodules; their proof of Theorem 1.2 identifies Q_{2n} with this mixture (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/bklpr-random-isotropic-intersection-law).
hypotheses: p prime
proofSteps: Define Q on ℕ × (symplectic classes) by the displayed weights; total mass (1/2)(Σ A_0 + Σ A_1) = 1 by ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/bklpr-alternating-cokernel-limit.
Derived laws: the modelled Selmer group S = (ℚ_p/ℤ_p)^r ⊕ T, its p-torsion rank r + dim T[p], and S[p^e].
acceptance: The law of dim_{𝔽_p} S[p] = r + dim T[p] under Q is the Poonen–Rains distribution (BKLPR §5.5, PR Theorem 5.2 identities).

nodes.title: BKLPR: intersections of random maximal isotropic ℤ_p-submodules realise the model
nodes.statement: Let V = ℤ_p^{2n} with the hyperbolic form Q(x, y) = Σ x_i y_i, OGr_n(ℤ_p) its maximal isotropic direct summands with the canonical probability measure, and Z, W ∈ OGr_n(ℤ_p) independent random. Put R := (Z ∩ W) ⊗ ℚ_p/ℤ_p, S := (Z ⊗ ℚ_p/ℤ_p) ∩ (W ⊗ ℚ_p/ℤ_p) and T := S/R. Then: (i) R ≅ (ℚ_p/ℤ_p)^r with r = rk(Z ∩ W) ∈ {0, 1}, each with probability 1/2 (Proposition 5.6); (ii) T is finite and the sequence splits (Corollaries 5.2–5.3); (iii) the law Q_{2n} of (r, T) converges as n → ∞ to the BKLPR model Q, and the law T_{2n,r} of T given r converges to A_r (Theorems 1.2, 1.6(a)–(b), 1.10(b)); (iv) S[q] ≅ Z/qZ ∩ W/qW for q a power of p (Proposition 5.4).
hypotheses: p prime
Z, W independent and distributed by the canonical measure on OGr_n(ℤ_p)
proofSteps: Canonical measure: OGr_n is a smooth projective ℤ-scheme of relative dimension n(n − 1)/2 with two isomorphic components distinguished by parity (BKLPR Propositions 4.4–4.5); the measure on OGr_n(ℤ_p) is the normalised limit of counts mod p^e (Proposition 2.1). This input is the gap 'Canonical measure on ℤ_p-points (Oesterlé–Serre) and the orthogonal Grassmannian'.
(i): the Schubert loci S_{n,r} with r ≥ 2 have smaller dimension (Proposition 4.9) hence measure zero; the parity of rk(Z ∩ W) is equidistributed by the isomorphism of the two components.
(ii),(iv): divisibility and co-finite type arguments (BKLPR Proposition 5.1, Corollaries 5.2–5.3, Proposition 5.4); routine module theory over ℤ_p.

(iii): represent Z = W_1ᵀ ⊕ graph(A) for a random decomposition and a random alternating A of corank r, so T ≅ (coker A)_tors; the size n − m of A tends to ∞ in probability (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/alternating-matrix-kernel-law and BKLPR Lemma 3.7), so T_{2n,r} → A_r by ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/bklpr-alternating-cokernel-limit; combine with (i).
acceptance: Q_{2n}(r ≥ 2) = 0 for every n.
For q = p, (iv) and PR's Proposition 2.6 recover the Poonen–Rains Selmer model.

nodes.title: Number of maximal isotropic direct summands of (ℤ/p^e)^{2n}
nodes.statement: For q = p^e (e ≥ 1), the hyperbolic quadratic ℤ/qℤ-module (ℤ/q)^{2n} has #OGr_n(ℤ/qℤ) = q^{n(n−1)/2} ∏_{i=1}^{n} (1 + p^{i−n}) maximal isotropic direct summands.
hypotheses: p prime
proofSteps: e = 1: #OGr_n(𝔽_p) = ∏_{j=0}^{n−1}(p^j + 1) = p^{n(n−1)/2}∏_{i=1}^{n}(1 + p^{i−n}) (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/number-of-maximal-isotropic-subspaces).

Lifting: every maximal isotropic direct summand mod p^e lifts to mod p^{e+1} in exactly p^{n(n−1)/2} ways (smoothness of OGr_n of relative dimension n(n − 1)/2, BKLPR Proposition 4.4; concretely, lifts of Z̄ = graph(Ā) over a complement correspond to alternating corrections p^e B with B ∈ M_n(𝔽_p)^alt). The chart description gives the count directly: near a point, maximal isotropic summands transverse to a fixed complement are graphs of alternating maps.

nodes.title: BKLPR: moments of injection counts in the mod-q model
nodes.statement: For q = p^e and m ≥ 0, let I_m(G) be the number of injective homomorphisms (ℤ/qℤ)^m → G. As Z, W range over OGr_n(ℤ/qℤ) (uniformly and independently), the average of I_m(Z ∩ W) equals q^{m(m+1)/2} ∏_{i=0}^{m−1}(1 − p^{i−n}) ∏_{i=n−m}^{n−1}(1 + p^{−i}), which tends to q^{m(m+1)/2} as n → ∞.
hypotheses: q = p^e, e ≥ 1
proofSteps: Fix W (the orthogonal group acts transitively). The average equals the number of injective h : (ℤ/q)^m → W, namely (#W)^m ∏_{i=0}^{m−1}(1 − p^{i−n}), times the probability that a random Z contains im(h).

The Z ⊇ im(h) correspond to maximal isotropic direct summands of im(h)^⊥/im(h), a hyperbolic module of rank 2n − 2m (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/isotropic-reduction-map, over ℤ/q); their number is #OGr_{n−m}(ℤ/q) (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/maximal-isotropic-direct-summands-modulo-prime-powers).
Divide by #OGr_n(ℤ/q) and simplify; let n → ∞.
acceptance: q = p, m = 1: limit p, i.e. the average of #(Z ∩ W) − 1 is p, so the average of #Sel_p is p + 1 (PR Proposition 2.22).
q = p, general m: equivalent to PR Proposition 2.22(a) (BKLPR Remark 5.13).

nodes.title: The Poonen–Rains conjecture for p-Selmer groups over ℚ (as a stated proposition)
nodes.statement: For a prime p, the Poonen–Rains conjecture over ℚ is the proposition PR(p): over the family of elliptic curves E_{A,B} : y² = x³ + Ax + B (A, B ∈ ℤ, 4A³ + 27B² ≠ 0, no prime ℓ with ℓ⁴ | A and ℓ⁶ | B) ordered by the naive height H(E_{A,B}) = max(4|A|³, 27B²) (the family and height of ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0), (a) for every d ≥ 0 the set {E : dim_{𝔽_p} Sel_p(E) = d} has density a_d (the Poonen–Rains weight), and (c) for every m ≥ 1 the m-th moment of #Sel_p(E) exists and equals ∏_{i=1}^{m}(p^{i} + 1) (moments as in ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/height-moments-in-an-arithmetic-family); (b) is (c) with m = 1, average p + 1. It is a conjecture: this node defines the proposition so that theorems can take it as a hypothesis and proved cases can be compared with it. Sel_p(E) is the p-Selmer group of Tau Ceti EllipticCurves Layer 7. Poonen–Rains state it over any global field with an unspecified height on the coefficients; the definition is pinned over ℚ with the height above.
hypotheses: p prime
proofSteps: Compose: the family carrier and height (ST.0, EC Layer 8 minimal short models), Sel_p(E) and its 𝔽_p-dimension (EC Layer 7), the densities and moments (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/height-moments-in-an-arithmetic-family), and the weights (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/poonen-rains-distribution).
The proposition is the conjunction of the density statement for each d and the moment statement for each m.
acceptance: Proved instances of clause (c) with m = 1: p = 2, 3, 5 (Bhargava–Shankar); with m = 2, p = 2 the upper bound 15 (Bhargava–Shankar–Swaminathan) but not the equality.
Clause (a) is not known for any p over the family of all curves.

nodes.title: The BKLPR conjecture for p^∞-Selmer sequences over ℚ (as a stated proposition)
nodes.statement: For a prime p, BKLPR(p) is the proposition: over the family E_{A,B}/ℚ ordered by naive height (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0), for every r ≥ 0 and every finite abelian p-group class G, the set {E : rank E(ℚ) = r and Ш(E)[p^∞] ≅ G} has density Q(r, G) (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/bklpr-model). Since E(ℚ) ⊗ ℚ_p/ℤ_p is divisible the sequence 0 → E(ℚ) ⊗ ℚ_p/ℤ_p → Sel_{p^∞}(E) → Ш(E)[p^∞] → 0 splits, and its isomorphism class is determined by (r, Ш[p^∞]) when Ш[p^∞] is finite; so this is BKLPR Conjecture 1.3 for k = ℚ. It is a conjecture, defined as a proposition.
hypotheses: p prime
proofSteps: Compose the family (ST.0), rank E(ℚ) (EC Layer 6), Ш(E)[p^∞] and Sel_{p^∞} (EC Layer 7 and SelmerIwasawaCohomology:L2), densities (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/height-moments-in-an-arithmetic-family) and Q.
Equivalence with the sequence formulation: a split sequence 0 → (ℚ_p/ℤ_p)^r → S → T → 0 with T finite is determined up to isomorphism by (r, T) (routine).
acceptance: BKLPR(p) predicts density 1/2 · ∏_{i≥1}(1 − p^{1−2i}) for rank 0 with Ш[p^∞] = 0.

nodes.title: For each prime p, 100% of curves E_{A,B}/ℚ have no rational p-torsion
nodes.statement: For every prime p, the set of E_{A,B} with E(ℚ)[p] ≠ 0 has density 0 in the family of elliptic curves over ℚ ordered by naive height.
hypotheses: p prime
proofSteps: p = 2: this is ArithmeticStatistics:ST.4/rational-two-torsion-has-density-zero (an integer root t of x³ + Ax + B gives B = −t³ − At with |t| ≪ X^{1/6}, so O(X^{1/2}) pairs against ≍ X^{5/6} curves).

p odd: E(ℚ)[p] ≠ 0 forces a rational root of the p-division polynomial of E_{A,B}. The generic curve over ℚ(A, B) has no rational p-torsion (its mod-p image is GL_2(𝔽_p); gap 'Generic mod-p image'), so the set is contained in a thin set of (A, B) ∈ ℤ², which by the counting form of Hilbert irreducibility has o(X^{5/6}) points in the box |A| ≪ X^{1/3}, |B| ≪ X^{1/2} (request InverseGaloisAndArithmeticFundamentalGroups:IG.2).
acceptance: The Tate normal forms show infinitely many curves with rational 3-, 5- and 7-torsion, so the set is infinite; it has density zero only.

nodes.title: Consequences of the BKLPR conjecture: rank law, finiteness of Ш[p^∞] and the Poonen–Rains law
nodes.statement: Assume BKLPR(p) (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/bklpr-selmer-conjecture) for a prime p. Then over E_{A,B}/ℚ ordered by height: (i) the sets of curves of rank 0 and of rank 1 each have density 1/2, and rank ≥ 2 has density 0; (ii) Ш(E)[p^∞] is finite for a density-one set of E; (iii) for every d, the set {E : dim_{𝔽_p} Sel_p(E) = d} has density a_d, i.e. clause (a) of PR(p) holds.
hypotheses: BKLPR(p)
proofSteps: (i),(ii): sum the densities Q(r, G) over G (countably many classes; Σ_G Q(r, G) = 1/2 for r ≤ 1, 0 for r ≥ 2) — the density of a countable union needs a tightness step: the densities of the finitely many-G events are lower densities, and 1 − Σ_{r ≤ 1, G} Q(r, G) = 0 bounds the upper density of the complement (routine with ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/height-moments-in-an-arithmetic-family, API familyLowerDensity_compl).

(iii): off the density-zero set of curves with E(ℚ)[p] ≠ 0 (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/rational-p-torsion-has-density-zero), Sel_p(E) ≅ Sel_{p^∞}(E)[p] (BKLPR Proposition 5.9(c); Kummer sequences of EC Layer 7), so dim Sel_p(E) = r + dim Ш[p^∞][p].

Under Q, r + dim T[p] has the Poonen–Rains law (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/bklpr-model, API bklprModel_selmer_p_rank; for r = 0 from the kernel law of alternating matrices, ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/alternating-kernel-law-limit-is-poonen-rains, and for r = 1 from the identity a_{2n+1} = (1/2)Prob(X_{Ш[p],1} = 2n) of ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/delaunay-compatibility-of-the-selmer-model together with the equality of the p-rank marginal of A_1 with Delaunay's X_{Ш[p],1} (gap 'p-rank marginal of A_1')).
Sum the densities over the classes with given r + dim G[p], as in the first step.
acceptance: The conclusion (i) is Goldfeld–Katz–Sarnak's minimalist prediction; it follows from BKLPR(p) for a single p.

nodes.title: Bhargava–Shankar: the average size of the 3-Selmer group is 4
nodes.statement: When the curves of any subfamily of E_{A,B}/ℚ defined by finitely many congruence conditions are ordered by height, the average of #Sel_3(E) exists and equals 4. In particular (the whole family) the average size of Sel_3(E) is 4. Family: elliptic curves E_{A,B} : y² = x³ + Ax + B with A, B ∈ ℤ, 4A³ + 27B² ≠ 0 and no prime ℓ with ℓ⁴ | A and ℓ⁶ | B (one representative of each ℚ-isomorphism class), ordered by H(E_{A,B}) = max(4|A|³, 27B²) (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0 and Tau Ceti EllipticCurves Layer 8); a subfamily defined by finitely many congruence conditions is the set of E_{A,B} with (A, B) in a finite union of residue classes modulo some N (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/family-defined-by-local-conditions). Averages are first moments in the sense of ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/height-moments-in-an-arithmetic-family; Sel_n(E) is the n-Selmer group of EllipticCurves Layer 7.
hypotheses: F a family of E_{A,B}/ℚ defined by finitely many congruence conditions on (A, B)
proofSteps: Parametrisation (source §3): 3-Selmer elements of E_{A,B} correspond to SL_3(ℚ)-classes of locally soluble ternary cubic forms with invariants (I, J) matching (A, B) (up to fixed scalars), with integral representatives and stabiliser E[3]; this is a genus-one orbit parametrisation in the scope of ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1 (gap 'Orbit parametrisations of 3-, 4- and 5-Selmer elements').

Counting (source §§2, 4): the number of SL_3(ℤ)-classes of irreducible integral ternary cubic forms of height < X, via averaging over a fundamental domain for SL_3(ℤ) acting on SL_3(ℝ) and cutting off the cusp, is (vol) · X^{5/6} + o(X^{5/6}); this is the geometry-of-numbers step of ArithmeticStatistics:ST.2 for the representation Sym³(3) of SL_3, with Davenport's lemma imported from GeometryOfNumbersAndQuadraticArithmetic:GN.4.
Sieve to locally soluble forms and to F (source §§5–6): multiply by local masses; the uniformity estimate for infinitely many congruence conditions is the ST.2 tail estimate.
Mass computation: the product of local masses and the Tamagawa number τ(PGL_3) = 3 give 3 nontrivial elements on average; add the identity element: 1 + 3 = 4 = σ(3).
acceptance: The value 4 = 3 + 1 is the Poonen–Rains prediction p + 1 at p = 3 and BS(3) (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/bhargava-shankar-selmer-average-conjecture).
Independent of the congruence family: the average is 4 for every such F (contrast: twist families, BKLOS).

Family: elliptic curves E_{A,B} : y² = x³ + Ax + B with A, B ∈ ℤ, 4A³ + 27B² ≠ 0 and no prime ℓ with ℓ⁴ | A and ℓ⁶ | B (one representative of each ℚ-isomorphism class), ordered by H(E_{A,B}) = max(4|A|³, 27B²) (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0 and Tau Ceti EllipticCurves Layer 8); a subfamily defined by finitely many congruence conditions is the set of E_{A,B} with (A, B) in a finite union of residue classes modulo some N (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/family-defined-by-local-conditions). hypotheses: F a family of E_{A,B}/ℚ defined by finitely many congruence conditions on (A, B)
proofSteps: Parametrisation: locally soluble 4-coverings of E embed in ℙ³ as intersections of two quadrics (Cassels), so 4-Selmer elements correspond to locally soluble G(ℚ)-orbits on pairs of quaternary quadratic forms 2 ⊗ Sym²(4), G = {(g_2, g_4) : det g_2 det g_4 = 1}/{(λ^{−2}I_2, λI_4)}, whose invariants correspond to (A, B) (gap 'Orbit parametrisations of 3-, 4- and 5-Selmer elements'; scope of ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1).

Not a moment of Sel_2: the second moment of #Sel_2 is predicted to be 15, not 7.

Mass computation: 5 nontrivial elements on average plus the identity.

Combined with ST.4's rank inequality the average rank is at most (6 + 15)/20 = 1.05 using 20r − 15 ≤ 5^r; the source's sharper bound 0.885 uses root-number equidistribution (coverage remaining).

nodes.title: Bhargava–Shankar–Swaminathan: the second moment of #Sel_2 is at most 15
nodes.statement: When elliptic curves over ℚ, or those of any subfamily defined by finitely many congruence conditions, are ordered by height, the upper second moment M⁺_2(#Sel_2(E)) is at most 15. (15 = (2 + 1)(4 + 1) is the Poonen–Rains prediction for the second moment; equality is not proved.) Bhargava–Shankar–Swaminathan use the model E_{I,J} : y² = x³ − (I/3)x − J/27 with height (4/27)max(|I|³, J²/4); its comparison with (E_{A,B}, max(4|A|³, 27B²)) is the normalisation comparison owned by ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/invariants-height-and-eligible-pairs and changes no average. Family: elliptic curves E_{A,B} : y² = x³ + Ax + B with A, B ∈ ℤ, 4A³ + 27B² ≠ 0 and no prime ℓ with ℓ⁴ | A and ℓ⁶ | B (one representative of each ℚ-isomorphism class), ordered by H(E_{A,B}) = max(4|A|³, 27B²) (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0 and Tau Ceti EllipticCurves Layer 8); a subfamily defined by finitely many congruence conditions is the set of E_{A,B} with (A, B) in a finite union of residue classes modulo some N (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/family-defined-by-local-conditions). Averages are first moments in the sense of ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/height-moments-in-an-arithmetic-family; Sel_n(E) is the n-Selmer group of EllipticCurves Layer 7.
hypotheses: F a family of elliptic curves over ℚ defined by finitely many congruence conditions
proofSteps: Write #Sel_2(E)² = Σ over pairs of 2-Selmer elements; pairs (σ, τ) correspond to 2-Selmer elements of the Jacobian of a locally soluble genus-one curve z² = f(x, y) attached to σ (source §§2–4: parametrisation of 2-Selmer groups of hyperelliptic Jacobians by pairs of n-ary quadratic forms, orbits of small rank).

Source Theorem 1.2: the average size of Sel_2 of such Jacobians, ordered by the heights of their Jacobian elliptic curves, is at most 6; counting special integral orbits of SL_4 and PSO_A on quadratic forms via equidistribution (source §§5–7).

Assembly (source §7): #Sel_2(E)² = Σ_{σ ∈ Sel_2(E)} #Sel_2(E); the σ = 0 terms average to 3 (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.4/average-size-of-the-2-selmer-group-is-three); for σ ≠ 0 (on average 2 of them) the group Sel_2(E) is compared with the 2-Selmer group of Jac(C_σ), whose average is at most 6; hence M⁺_2 ≤ 3 + 2 · 6 = 15, after slicing over the leading coefficient and summing local masses. These steps are not decomposed here (gap 'Second-moment proof of Bhargava–Shankar–Swaminathan').
acceptance: Consistency: M_1(#Sel_2) = 3 and M⁺_2(#Sel_2) ≤ 15 give, by Cauchy–Schwarz, no contradiction (9 ≤ 15).
The Poonen–Rains moment formula at p = 2, m = 2 equals 15 (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/poonen-rains-moments).

nodes.title: Heath-Brown, Swinnerton-Dyer, Kane: the 2-Selmer rank distribution in quadratic twist families
nodes.statement: Let E : y² = (x − c_1)(x − c_2)(x − c_3) with c_i ∈ ℚ distinct and none of (c_i − c_j)(c_i − c_k) a rational square (equivalently E(ℚ)[2] = E[2] and E has no ℚ-rational cyclic subgroup of order 4), and for b ∈ ℤ \ {0} let E_b : y² = (x − bc_1)(x − bc_2)(x − bc_3) be the quadratic twist by ℚ(√b). Then for every d ≥ 0, lim_{N→∞} #{b ∈ ℤ : 0 < |b| ≤ N, dim_{𝔽_2} Sel_2(E_b) = d + 2}/(2N) = a_d, the Poonen–Rains weight at p = 2 (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/poonen-rains-distribution); the same holds among positive b, and among squarefree b prime to any fixed D divisible by 8 and the bad primes (relative density). For E : y² = x³ − x this is Heath-Brown's theorem.
hypotheses: c_1, c_2, c_3 ∈ ℚ distinct
proofSteps: Swinnerton-Dyer's algebraic step: for b = p_1 ⋯ p_n squarefree prime to D, Sel_2(E_b) is the intersection of two Lagrangian subspaces of a symplectic 𝔽_2-space determined by the classes of p_i in (ℤ/D)^×/(ℤ/D)^{×2} and the Legendre symbols (p_i/p_j); the proportion π_d(n) of such data with dim Sel_2 = d tends to α_d = a_{d−2} as n → ∞ (a Markov chain whose stationary law is the Poonen–Rains law; ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/alternating-kernel-law-limit-is-poonen-rains identifies that law).

Kane's analytic step: the moments of #Sel_2(E_b) over squarefree b ≤ N prime to D converge to the Poonen–Rains moments (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/poonen-rains-moments), using |U ∩ W| = |V|^{−1/2}Σ_{u,w}(−1)^{u·w} and bounds for character sums in Legendre symbols of the prime factors (large sieve, SieveMethodsAndPrimePatterns:SV.2).

Moments determine the law here (parity is fixed by the class of b mod D, Kane Lemma 1, and the moments grow like 2^{m(m+1)/2}); pass from squarefree b prime to D to all b by twisting by divisors of D and noting that twists by squares do not change Sel_2. The analytic estimates are not decomposed (gap 'Kane's character-sum estimates').
acceptance: d = 0 (Sel_2 = E[2] only): density a_0 ≈ 0.2097.
The parity of dim Sel_2(E_b) depends only on the class of b in ∏_{v∈S}ℚ_v^×/ℚ_v^{×2}, and is even for exactly half of the classes (Kane, Lemma 1).

nodes.title: de Jong: the average size of the 3-Selmer group over 𝔽_q(t) is at most 4 + O(1/q)
nodes.statement: Let 𝔽_q be a finite field with 3 ∤ q. When the elliptic curves over 𝔽_q(t) are ordered by height (isomorphism classes of height d, d → ∞), the upper average of #Sel_3(E/𝔽_q(t)) is at most 4 + ε(q), where ε(q) is an explicit rational function of q with ε(q) → 0 as q → ∞. This is the function-field analogue, as an upper bound, of ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/average-size-of-the-3-selmer-group; de Jong speculated that the truth is 4.
hypotheses: q a prime power with 3 ∤ q
elliptic curves over 𝔽_q(t) ordered by height
proofSteps: de Jong counts isomorphism classes of elliptic curves of height d over 𝔽_q(t) and bounds the number of elliptic surfaces over ℙ¹ carrying a relative polarisation of degree 3 (plane cubic models of 3-coverings), then compares the two counts.

The source (de Jong, Moscow Math. J. 2 (2002)) is available only as a DVI file and was not read; the statement is taken from Poonen–Rains §1.2 and Bhargava–Shankar §1 (gap 'de Jong's function-field 3-Selmer bound').
acceptance: As q → ∞ the bound tends to 4 = σ(3), the Poonen–Rains prediction p + 1 at p = 3.

nodes.title: Distribution of p^∞-Selmer coranks in a quadratic twist family
nodes.statement: Let E be an elliptic curve over a number field F and p a prime; write c_p(E/F) := corank_{ℤ_p} Sel_{p^∞}(E/F) (the ℚ_p-dimension of the Pontryagin dual of Sel_{p^∞} tensored with ℚ_p; SelmerIwasawaCohomology:L2). For a squareclass s ∈ F^×/F^{×2} let E^s be the quadratic twist of E by F(√s)/F (E^s ≅ E when s is a square; Tau Ceti EllipticCurves Layer 5). (i) Signed-integer ordering over ℚ (Smith): for r ≥ 0 and H ≥ 1, N_r(H) := #{d ∈ ℤ : 0 < |d| ≤ H, c_p(E^d/ℚ) = r} and the proportion N_r(H)/(2H); every nonzero integer d is counted, squares and non-squarefree d included, and E^d depends only on the squareclass of d. (ii) Squareclass ordering (Bhargava–Klagsbrun–Lemke Oliver–Shnidman, Burungale–Tian): for Σ ⊆ F^×/F^{×2} and X > 0, Σ(X) := {s ∈ Σ : H(s) < X} with H(s) := ∏_{𝔭 : v_𝔭(s) odd} N𝔭, each squareclass counted once (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/quadratic-twist-squareclass-family), and the proportion #{s ∈ Σ(X) : c_p(E^s/F) = r}/#Σ(X). (iii) For a probability vector π = (π_r)_{r≥0}, E has twist-corank law π at p (in ordering (i) or (ii)) if every proportion converges to π_r; lower bounds are stated with liminf. For F = ℚ the squareclass height of the class of a squarefree d is |d|.
hypotheses: E elliptic over a number field F
p prime
proofSteps: Import c_p(E/F) (request SelmerIwasawaCohomology:L2) and the twist E^s (Tau Ceti EllipticCurves Layer 5, WeierstrassCurve.quadraticTwist; request).

Define the counting functions as finite counts: {d : 0 < |d| ≤ H} is finite; Σ(X) is finite by ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/quadratic-twist-squareclass-family (units modulo squares and finiteness of the class group).
Define the law predicates as limits (resp. liminf) of the proportions; the densities are the ones of ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/height-moments-in-an-arithmetic-family specialised to these families.
acceptance: If c_p(E^d/ℚ) = 0 for all d then the law is the point mass at 0.

Signed ordering (i) versus squarefree ordering: the non-squarefree d have positive density (1 − 6/π²) in (i) but E^d = E^{d'} for the squarefree part d'; the two orderings are different families and need a comparison.

nodes.title: Smith's Assumption 1.1 on an elliptic curve over ℚ
nodes.statement: An elliptic curve A/ℚ satisfies Smith's Assumption 1.1 if one of the following holds: (1) A(ℚ)[2] = 0; (2) A(ℚ)[2] ≅ ℤ/2 and, for the unique ℚ-isogeny φ : A → A_0 of degree 2, ℚ(A_0[2]) ≠ ℚ and ℚ(A_0[2]) ≠ ℚ(A[2]); (3) A(ℚ)[2] ≅ (ℤ/2)² and A has no cyclic ℚ-isogeny of degree 4. For a model y² = f(x) with f ∈ ℚ[x] monic separable cubic this is equivalent to: (1) f has no rational root; or (2) f has exactly one rational root e and, writing f(x + e) = x(x² + ax + b), neither b nor b(a² − 4b) is a rational square; or (3) f = (x − e_1)(x − e_2)(x − e_3) with e_i ∈ ℚ and none of (e_i − e_j)(e_i − e_k) ({i, j, k} = {1, 2, 3}) is a rational square. The cubic form is the one used in Lean.
hypotheses: A/ℚ given by y² = f(x), f monic separable cubic
proofSteps: A(ℚ)[2] \ {O} = {(e, 0) : f(e) = 0, e ∈ ℚ} (2-torsion of a Weierstrass curve; Mathlib WeierstrassCurve points).

Case (2): for A : y² = x(x² + ax + b) the 2-isogenous curve is A_0 : y² = x(x² − 2ax + a² − 4b) (Vélu; Tau Ceti EllipticCurves Layer 1), so ℚ(A[2]) = ℚ(√(a² − 4b)) and ℚ(A_0[2]) = ℚ(√b); two quadratic fields coincide iff the product of the radicands is a square.

Case (3): a cyclic subgroup of order 4 is ⟨P⟩ with 2P = (e_i, 0) and x(P) = e_i ± √((e_i − e_j)(e_i − e_k)); ⟨P⟩ is Galois-stable iff x(P) ∈ ℚ; so no cyclic ℚ-isogeny of degree 4 iff no (e_i − e_j)(e_i − e_k) is a square (equivalence stated by Kane, §1).
acceptance: y² = x³ − x satisfies (3) (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/congruent-number-curve-satisfies-smith-hypothesis).
y² = x³ + 4x (Cremona 32a1) has a rational 4-torsion point (2, 4), so it fails (2): b = 4 is a square.

nodes.title: Smith's ℓ^∞-Selmer corank equals the ℤ_ℓ-corank of Sel_{ℓ^∞}
nodes.statement: Let E be an elliptic curve over a number field F and ℓ a prime. For k ≥ 1 let r_{ℓ^k}(E/F) be the largest r such that (ℤ/ℓ^k)^r injects into Sel_{ℓ^k}(E/F)/im(E(F)_tors). Then r_ℓ ≥ r_{ℓ²} ≥ …, the sequence is eventually constant, and its limit r_{ℓ^∞}(E/F) equals corank_{ℤ_ℓ} Sel_{ℓ^∞}(E/F).
hypotheses: E elliptic over a number field F
ℓ prime
proofSteps: Kummer: the sequence 0 → E(F)[ℓ^∞]/ℓ^k → Sel_{ℓ^k}(E/F) → Sel_{ℓ^∞}(E/F)[ℓ^k] → 0 is exact (surjectivity of H¹(F, E[ℓ^k]) → H¹(F, E[ℓ^∞])[ℓ^k] with kernel E(F)[ℓ^∞]/ℓ^k, compatible with local conditions; requests Tau Ceti EllipticCurves Layer 7 and SelmerIwasawaCohomology:L2).
The image of E(F)_tors in Sel_{ℓ^k} is the image of E(F)[ℓ^∞]/ℓ^k (the prime-to-ℓ torsion is ℓ^k-divisible), so Sel_{ℓ^k}/im(E(F)_tors) ≅ Sel_{ℓ^∞}[ℓ^k].

Sel_{ℓ^∞} ≅ (ℚ_ℓ/ℤ_ℓ)^c ⊕ G with G finite (co-finite type; L2), c the corank; so Sel_{ℓ^∞}[ℓ^k] ≅ (ℤ/ℓ^k)^c ⊕ G[ℓ^k] and the largest free ℤ/ℓ^k-rank is c + #{cyclic factors of G of order ≥ ℓ^k}, which equals c once ℓ^k exceeds the exponent of G.
acceptance: If Ш(E/F)[ℓ^∞] is finite then r_{ℓ^∞}(E/F) = rank E(F).
Finite 2-Selmer rank r_2 can exceed the corank: for y² = x³ − x twisted by n = 5 (a congruent number with rank 1) r_2 = 1 = corank, but twists with Ш[2] ≠ 0 have r_2 > r_{2^∞}.

nodes.title: A two-point limiting corank law forces density zero for corank at least 2
nodes.statement: Let c : ℤ \ {0} → ℤ_{≥0} be any function and suppose that #{0 < |d| ≤ H : c(d) = 0}/(2H) → π_0 and #{0 < |d| ≤ H : c(d) = 1}/(2H) → π_1 with π_0 + π_1 = 1. Then #{0 < |d| ≤ H : c(d) ≥ 2}/(2H) → 0. In particular this holds when E has signed twist-corank law (1/2, 1/2, 0, 0, …), the conclusion of Smith I Theorem 1.2.
proofSteps: #{0 < |d| ≤ H : c(d) ≥ 2} = 2H − N_0(H) − N_1(H) (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/p-infinity-selmer-corank-distribution-in-twist-families, API sum_signedTwistCorankCount); divide by 2H and take limits.
Note that the convergence of each N_r(H)/(2H) with r ≥ 2 to 0 would not suffice without π_0 + π_1 = 1 (tightness).
acceptance: For Smith's law: the proportion of |d| ≤ H with corank ≥ 2 tends to 0; Smith's Remark 1.3 gives the rate exp(−c(log log log H)^{1/2}).

nodes.title: Burungale–Tian Theorem 3.3 from Smith's 2^∞-Selmer law: corank zero for 100% of even congruent twists
nodes.statement: Let E : y² = x³ − x and, for n ∈ ℤ \ {0}, E^(n) : ny² = x³ − x (≅ y² = x³ − n²x, the twist of E by ℚ(√n)). Stated input (Smith I, Theorem 1.2, for A = E, which satisfies Assumption 1.1 by ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/congruent-number-curve-satisfies-smith-hypothesis): for every r ≥ 0, lim_{H→∞} #{d ∈ ℤ : 0 < |d| ≤ H, r_{2^∞}(E^d/ℚ) = r}/(2H) = 1/2, 1/2, 0 for r = 0, r = 1, r ≥ 2. Conclusion: for a density-one subset of the positive squarefree integers n ≡ 1, 2, 3 (mod 8), corank_{ℤ_2} Sel_{2^∞}(E^(n)/ℚ) = 0; that is, with S(X) := {0 < n ≤ X : n squarefree, n mod 8 ∈ {1, 2, 3}}, #{n ∈ S(X) : corank = 0}/#S(X) → 1. ST.5 proves the implication; the stated input is Smith's theorem, whose proof belongs to ArithmeticStatisticsPartIISmithMethod (gap 'Smith's 2^∞-Selmer distribution theorem'), which applies this node to obtain Burungale–Tian's Theorem 3.3 unconditionally.
hypotheses: E : y² = x³ − x over ℚ
Smith's law: the signed-integer 2^∞-Selmer corank law of the twists of E is (1/2, 1/2, 0, …)
proofSteps: Translate Smith's r_{2^∞} into corank_{ℤ_2} Sel_{2^∞} (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/smith-selmer-rank-limit-equals-corank) and E^(n) into Smith's A^n (the model y² = x³ − n²x of A^d: y² = x³ + d²ax + d³b with a = −1, b = 0; isomorphism (x, y) ↦ (nx, n²y), Tau Ceti EllipticCurves Layer 5).
Zero density of high corank: #{0 < |d| ≤ H : corank_{ℤ_2} Sel_{2^∞}(E^d) ≥ 2} = o(H) (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/two-point-corank-law-forces-zero-density-of-high-corank).

Parity: for positive squarefree n ≡ 1, 2, 3 (mod 8), corank_{ℤ_2} Sel_{2^∞}(E^(n)/ℚ) is even (request SelmerIwasawaCohomology:L4: 2-parity (−1)^{corank} = w(E^(n)/ℚ) together with w(E^(n)/ℚ) = +1 exactly for n ≡ 1, 2, 3 mod 8). Hence corank ≠ 0 implies corank ≥ 2 on S.

Positive density of S: S has relative density 1/2 in the positive squarefree integers (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/even-parity-classes-have-half-density), hence #S(X) ~ (3/π²)X (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/positive-squarefree-family-over-q).

Conclude: #{n ∈ S(X) : corank ≠ 0} ≤ #{0 < |d| ≤ X : corank ≥ 2} = o(X) = o(#S(X)); equivalently, the density-one set of all nonzero d with corank ≤ 1 restricts to relative density one in S (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/density-one-restricts-to-subfamilies-of-positive-lower-density), and on S corank ≤ 1 with even corank means corank 0.
acceptance: The conclusion concerns 2^∞-Selmer coranks, not finite 2-Selmer ranks: dim Sel_2(E^(n)) − 2 is not 0 for a density-one subset (its law is Poonen–Rains, ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/two-selmer-distribution-in-full-two-torsion-twist-families).

Burungale–Tian Theorem 1.2 (analytic rank 0 for the same density-one set) follows by combining this conclusion with the rank-zero 2-converse; that consumer belongs to CMRankZeroConverse and is not part of ST.5.

nodes.title: Local and global Selmer ratios of an isogeny and the classes T_m(φ)
nodes.statement: Let φ : E → E' be an isogeny of elliptic curves over a number field F. For a place v of F put c_v(φ) := #coker(φ : E(F_v) → E'(F_v)) / #ker(φ : E(F_v) → E'(F_v)) ∈ ℚ_{>0} (finite: the kernel is finite and the cokernel is finite since E'(F_v)/φE(F_v) injects into H¹(F_v, E[φ])). The global Selmer ratio is c(φ) := ∏_v c_v(φ), a finite product because c_v(φ) = 1 for all finite v ∤ deg φ at which E has good reduction; c_v is multiplicative under composition of isogenies (index multiplicativity). For s ∈ F^×/F^{×2} let φ_s : E^s → E'^s be the quadratic twist of φ (twisting by the same cocycle, Tau Ceti EllipticCurves Layer 5). For deg φ = 3, c(φ_s) ∈ 3^ℤ and t(φ_s) := ord_3 c(φ_s); for m ∈ ℤ, T_m(φ) := {s ∈ F^×/F^{×2} : c(φ_s) = 3^m} (signed; BKLOS §9 notation), and |T|_m := T_m ∪ T_{−m} is BKLOS §2's T_m.
hypotheses: E, E' elliptic over a number field F
φ : E → E' an F-isogeny
proofSteps: Define c_v(φ) from the local Kummer map (finite groups) and the product over all places; finiteness of the product support from ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/local-selmer-ratio-via-tamagawa-numbers (c_v = 1 at good v ∤ deg φ).
Define the twisted isogeny φ_s and the classes T_m(φ) as subsets of the squareclass group (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/quadratic-twist-squareclass-family).

nodes.title: Local Selmer ratios via Tamagawa numbers and the formal group (Schaefer)
nodes.statement: Let φ : E → E' be an isogeny of elliptic curves over a local field F. (a) If F is a finite extension of ℚ_p, then c(φ) = (c(E')/c(E)) · |φ'(0)|_F^{−1}, where c(·) = #E(F)/E_0(F) is the Tamagawa number and |φ'(0)|_F is the normalised absolute value of the derivative at the origin of the map of formal groups induced by φ on minimal models; in particular c(φ) = c(E')/c(E) if p ∤ deg φ, and c(φ) = 1 if moreover E has good reduction. (b) For deg φ = 3: if F = ℂ then c(φ) = 1/3; if F = ℝ then c(φ) = 1/3 when E[φ](ℝ) ≅ ℤ/3 and c(φ) = 1 when E[φ](ℝ) = 0.
hypotheses: F a local field

proofSteps: (a) Filter E(F) ⊇ E_0(F) ⊇ E_1(F) = Ê(𝔪) (Tau Ceti EllipticCurves Layer 4: reduction, component group; Layer 1: formal groups). The index of φ on each graded piece multiplies: #coker/#ker is multiplicative in short exact sequences of finite-index maps (snake lemma).

On Ê(𝔪): for a homomorphism of one-dimensional formal groups with φ'(0) ≠ 0, #coker/#ker on 𝔪-points equals |φ'(0)|^{−1} (compare with the filtration Ê(𝔪^r) ≅ 𝔪^r for r large, where φ acts as multiplication by φ'(0)).

nodes.title: Only finitely many quadratic twists have rational odd p-torsion
nodes.statement: Let E be an elliptic curve over a number field F and p an odd prime. Then {s ∈ F^×/F^{×2} : E^s(F)[p] ≠ 0} has at most p² − 1 elements; in particular it has density zero in the squareclass ordering.

nodes.title: A CM elliptic curve has, at every finite place, a twist with good reduction
nodes.statement: Let E be an elliptic curve over a number field F with End_F(E) an order in an imaginary quadratic field K ⊆ F. For every finite place v of F there is a twist of E (by a character of G_{F_v} with values in Aut(E_{F̄}) = O_K^× ∩ End(E)) which has good reduction at v; if j(E) ∉ {0, 1728} this twist is quadratic. (Rubin, Cetraro notes, 5.22, as cited by BKLOS.)
hypotheses: E/F with CM by an order of K ⊆ F
proofSteps: j(E) is an algebraic integer (integrality of CM j-values; request ComplexMultiplicationAndExplicitReciprocity:CM.3), so E has potentially good reduction at v (Tau Ceti EllipticCurves Layer 4: integral j and the Néron–Ogg–Shafarevich criterion).

Hence the inertia group I_v acts on T_ℓ(E) (ℓ ≠ residue characteristic) through a finite quotient, and commutes with End_F(E) ⊗ ℤ_ℓ ⊇ O ⊗ ℤ_ℓ (endomorphisms are defined over F ⊇ K; ComplexMultiplicationAndExplicitReciprocity:CM.1); a finite-order element of the commutant (O ⊗ ℚ_ℓ)^× acting on a rank-one module is a root of unity of K, i.e. an automorphism of E.

The Galois action on T_ℓ(E) takes values in the commutative group (O ⊗ ℤ_ℓ)^×, so its restriction to I_v is a character ψ : I_v → μ(K) ∩ O^× = Aut(E_{F̄}) that factors through the image of inertia in G_{F_v}^{ab}; by local class field theory that image is the image of O_v^× and F_v^× ≅ π^ℤ × O_v^×, so ψ extends to a character χ of G_{F_v} (Tau Ceti ClassFieldTheory Layer 7, local Artin map). The twist of E by χ^{−1} has trivial inertia action on T_ℓ, hence good reduction by Néron–Ogg–Shafarevich. For j ≠ 0, 1728, Aut(E) = {±1} and the twist is quadratic.
Rubin's notes were not read (not public); the statement follows BKLOS's citation (gap 'Rubin's CM lemmas').
acceptance: j(E) ∉ {0, 1728}: a quadratic twist has good reduction at v.
E : y² = x³ + 1 (j = 0, CM by ℤ[ζ_3]) over ℚ(ζ_3): a sextic twist may be needed at v | 2 or 3.

nodes.title: BKLOS: a 3-isogeny between curves with CM by the maximal order has Selmer ratio one
nodes.statement: Let φ : E → E' be a 3-isogeny of elliptic curves over a number field F with End(E) ≅ End(E') ≅ O_K for an imaginary quadratic field K (necessarily K ⊆ F when the CM is defined over F). Then c(φ) = 1.
hypotheses: φ a 3-isogeny over F
End(E) ≅ End(E') ≅ O_K
proofSteps: Finite v ∤ 3: c_v(E) = c_v(E') — by ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/cm-curves-have-a-twist-with-good-reduction some twist of E has good reduction at v; if it is quadratic, apply ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/tamagawa-ratio-under-potentially-good-reduction; otherwise j(E) ∈ {0, 1728}: j = 1728 is impossible (ℤ[i] has no element of norm 3), and for j = 0 also j(E') = 0, so E ≅ E' and φ is √−3 up to automorphism. Hence c_v(φ) = 1 by ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/local-selmer-ratio-via-tamagawa-numbers.
Infinite places are complex (K ⊆ F): c_v(φ) = 1/3 at each of the [F : ℚ]/2 complex places.

Places above 3: c_v(φ) = |φ'(0)|_v^{−1} (Tamagawa numbers equal by the first step). Choose a prime ℓ ≠ 3 and an ℓ-isogeny λ : E' → E (exists since End(E') ≅ O_K and ideal classes have prime representatives; ComplexMultiplicationAndExplicitReciprocity:CM.1); λ ∘ φ = a ∈ O_K, |λ'(0)|_v = 1, and |a'(0)|_v = |a|_v (the normalised action of O_K on the invariant differential, CM.1; Rubin Prop. 3.14). So ∏_{v|3} c_v(φ) = ∏_{v|3} |a|_v^{−1} = (3-part of N_{K/ℚ}(a))^{[F:K]} = 3^{[F:K]}, because deg a = N(a) = 3ℓ.

Non-maximal orders can give c(φ) ≠ 1 (BKLOS Remark 11.3).

Then, ordering t ∈ K^×/K^{×2} by H(t) = ∏_{v_𝔭(t) odd} N𝔭 (each squareclass once), liminf_{X→∞} #{t : H(t) < X, corank_{ℤ_3} Sel_{3^∞}(E^t/K) = 0}/#{t : H(t) < X} ≥ 1/2. E/K with End_K(E) an order O ⊆ O_K

nodes.title: Coefficient-vector forms and the Veronese vector
nodes.statement: Fix integers n ≥ 0 and d ≥ 0 and let M_{d,n} be the set of exponent vectors m = (m_0, …, m_n) ∈ ℕ^{n+1} with m_0 + ⋯ + m_n = d, so that N_{d,n} := #M_{d,n} = binom(n+d, d). For a commutative ring R and a coefficient vector a = (a_m) ∈ R^{M_{d,n}}, the form with coefficient vector a is f_a = Σ_{m ∈ M_{d,n}} a_m X_0^{m_0}⋯X_n^{m_n} ∈ R[X_0, …, X_n], homogeneous of degree d. The Veronese vector of x ∈ R^{n+1} is ν_{d,n}(x) = (x^m)_{m ∈ M_{d,n}} ∈ R^{M_{d,n}}, with unweighted monomials (no multinomial or square-root weights), so that f_a(x) = ⟨a, ν_{d,n}(x)⟩ = Σ_m a_m x^m. For u, w ∈ R^I the 2×2 minors are u_i w_j − u_j w_i (i, j ∈ I); over ℤ their gcd is G(u, w). The source orders monomials lexicographically; indexing by exponent vectors makes that order immaterial.
hypotheses: R a commutative ring
n, d ≥ 0 integers
proofSteps: Define M_{d,n} as the finite set of finitely supported functions {0, …, n} → ℕ with total d (Mathlib Finset.finsuppAntidiag over the full index set).
Define f_a as the finite sum of the monomials X^m with coefficients a_m; it is homogeneous of degree d since every exponent vector has total d (Mathlib MvPolynomial.IsHomogeneous).
Define ν_{d,n}(x)_m = ∏_i x_i^{m_i}; evaluating the monomials gives f_a(x) = Σ_m a_m ν_{d,n}(x)_m (Mathlib MvPolynomial.eval).
Distinct exponent vectors give distinct monomials, so the coefficient of X^m in f_a is a_m and a ↦ f_a is an isomorphism onto the degree-d forms; #M_{d,n} = binom(n+d, d) by stars and bars.
Define the minors of a pair of vectors coordinatewise.
acceptance: For n = 1, d = 2: N_{2,1} = 3 and the all-ones vector gives X_0² + X_0X_1 + X_1², not (X_0 + X_1)².
f_{c·a} = c·f_a, and ν_{d,n}(c·x) = c^d ν_{d,n}(x).
Reduction modulo Q commutes with a ↦ f_a (a ring homomorphism R → S maps f_a to f_{φ∘a}).

nodes.title: The finite-level local density σ(a; Q)
nodes.statement: For integers Q ≥ 1, n, d ≥ 0 and a coefficient vector a ∈ (ℤ/Qℤ)^{M_{d,n}} (or a ∈ ℤ^{M_{d,n}} reduced modulo Q), σ(a; Q) = Q^{−n} · #{b ∈ R_{n+1}(Q) : f_a(b) ≡ 0 mod Q}, where R_{n+1}(Q) = {b ∈ (ℤ/Qℤ)^{n+1} : gcd(Q, b_0, …, b_n) = 1} is the set of primitive residue vectors (ST.0). Equivalently σ(a; Q) = Q^{−n} #{b ∈ R_{n+1}(Q) : a ∈ Λ^{(Q)}_{ν_{d,n}(b)}}. It depends only on a mod Q, is multiplicative in Q over coprime factors (σ(a; Q) = ∏_{p^r ∥ Q} σ(a; p^r)), is positive exactly when f_a has a primitive zero modulo Q, and is a normalized count, not a probability: it can exceed 1.
hypotheses: a a coefficient vector of degree d in n+1 variables, modulo Q
proofSteps: Define σ(a; Q) as Q^{−n} times the number of primitive residue vectors b ∈ R_{n+1}(Q) with f_a(b) = 0 in ℤ/Qℤ.
The reformulation through Λ^{(Q)}_{ν(b)} is f_a(b) = ⟨a, ν_{d,n}(b)⟩ (coefficient-vector-form).
Multiplicativity (5.11): the Chinese remainder theorem identifies (ℤ/Q_1Q_2)^{n+1} with (ℤ/Q_1)^{n+1} × (ℤ/Q_2)^{n+1}, primitive vectors with pairs of primitive vectors and zeros with pairs of zeros.

nodes.title: A polynomial value moves inside the ideal of the perturbation
nodes.statement: Let R be a commutative ring, σ a set of variables, f ∈ R[X_i : i ∈ σ] and x, h ∈ R^σ. Then f(x + h) − f(x) lies in the ideal (h_i : i ∈ σ). In particular, for R = ℤ and h ≡ 0 mod p^c coordinatewise, f(x + h) ≡ f(x) mod p^c; applied to the partial derivatives, ∇f(x + h) ≡ ∇f(x) mod p^c.
hypotheses: R commutative
f a polynomial
x, h vectors in R^σ
proofSteps: Let I = (h_i : i ∈ σ) and π: R → R/I the quotient map.
Evaluation commutes with ring homomorphisms (Mathlib MvPolynomial.eval_map): π(f(x + h)) = (π f)(π(x + h)) = (π f)(π(x)) = π(f(x)), since π(h_i) = 0.
Hence π(f(x + h) − f(x)) = 0, i.e. f(x + h) − f(x) ∈ I (Mathlib Ideal.Quotient.eq_zero_iff_mem).
acceptance: For a constant polynomial the difference is 0.

nodes.title: First-order Taylor congruence for multivariate polynomials
nodes.statement: Let R be a commutative ring, σ a finite set of variables, f ∈ R[X_i : i ∈ σ] and x, h ∈ R^σ. Then f(x + h) − f(x) − Σ_i h_i ∂f/∂X_i(x) lies in the ideal generated by the products h_i h_j (i, j ∈ σ). In particular, over ℤ, if b ≡ x mod p^c then f(b) ≡ f(x) + ⟨∇f(x), b − x⟩ mod p^{2c}.
hypotheses: R commutative
σ finite
f a polynomial
proofSteps: Induct on f (Mathlib MvPolynomial.induction_on): constants have zero derivative and zero difference; the statement is additive in f.
For f·X_k, write f(x+h) = f(x) + Σ_i h_i ∂_i f(x) + ρ with ρ in the ideal J = (h_i h_j); by the Leibniz rule (Mathlib MvPolynomial.pderiv_mul) ∂_i(f X_k)(x) = ∂_i f(x) x_k + δ_{ik} f(x).
Then (f X_k)(x+h) − (f X_k)(x) − Σ_i h_i ∂_i(f X_k)(x) = (Σ_i h_i ∂_i f(x)) h_k + ρ(x_k + h_k) ∈ J.
acceptance: f = X_0² over ℤ: (x+h)² − x² − 2xh = h².
For f of degree ≤ 1 the remainder is 0.

nodes.title: First moment of σ(·; p^r) over primitive coefficient vectors
nodes.statement: Let d ≥ 1, n ≥ 0, p prime, r ≥ 1 and N = N_{d,n}. Then (1/#R_N(p^r)) Σ_{a ∈ R_N(p^r)} σ(a; p^r) = (1 − p^{−(n+1)})(1 − p^{−(N−1)})/(1 − p^{−N}). In particular, for d ≥ 2 and n ≥ 1 (so N ≥ n + 2) the average lies in [1 − 2p^{−(n+1)}, 1], which is the source's 1 + O(p^{−n−1}) (stated there for d ≥ 2, n ≥ 3).
hypotheses: p prime
proofSteps: Swap the sums: Σ_a σ(a; p^r) = p^{−rn} Σ_{b ∈ R_{n+1}(p^r)} #{a ∈ R_N(p^r) : ⟨a, ν_{d,n}(b)⟩ ≡ 0 mod p^r} (coefficient-vector-form, eval_form).

For primitive b, ν_{d,n}(b) is primitive (it contains b_i^d for a unit b_i), so a ↦ ⟨a, ν(b)⟩ maps (ℤ/p^r)^N onto ℤ/p^r with kernel of size p^{r(N−1)}; the kernel elements with a ≡ 0 mod p are p·a′ with ⟨a′, ν(b)⟩ ≡ 0 mod p^{r−1}, p^{(r−1)(N−1)} of them. So the inner count is p^{r(N−1)}(1 − p^{−(N−1)}), independent of b.
Insert #R_m(p^r) = p^{rm}(1 − p^{−m}) (ST.0, (5.10)) for m = n + 1 and m = N and simplify.
acceptance: n = 1, d = 1 (N = 2), r = 1: the formula gives 1 − 1/p, matching the direct count (every primitive linear form in two variables has exactly p − 1 primitive zeros modulo p).
The average does not depend on r.
n = 0: the formula gives 0 (a primitive one-variable form a X_0^d has no primitive zero).

nodes.title: Coefficient vectors vanishing at two primitive points modulo p^r
nodes.statement: Let d ≥ 1, n ≥ 1, p prime, r ≥ 1, N = N_{d,n} (so N ≥ 2) and b_1, b_2 ∈ R_{n+1}(p^r). Let v ∈ {0, …, r} be the capped p-adic valuation of the minors of (ν_{d,n}(b_1), ν_{d,n}(b_2)), i.e. p^v = gcd(G(ν(b_1), ν(b_2)), p^r) for integral lifts. Then #L(b_1, b_2; p^r) := #{a ∈ R_N(p^r) : f_a(b_1) ≡ f_a(b_2) ≡ 0 mod p^r} = p^{r(N−2)+v} − p^{(r−1)(N−2)+min(v, r−1)}. This one formula covers both of the source's cases (b_1, b_2 proportional modulo p^r is v = r), and gives p^{r(N−2)+v}(1 − p^{−(N−2)}) ≤ #L ≤ p^{r(N−2)+v}, which is (5.13).
hypotheses: b_1, b_2 primitive modulo p^r
proofSteps: Lift b_1, b_2 to primitive c_1, c_2 ∈ ℤ^{n+1}, chosen linearly independent (possible since n + 1 ≥ 2: add p^r e_j to c_2 if needed); ν(c_1), ν(c_2) are primitive (they contain c_{i,j}^d) and linearly independent (ν_{d,n} is injective on lines for d ≥ 1).

By GN.0 (Browning–Le Boudec–Sawin, Lemma 3.9) the lattice Λ^{(p^r)}_{ν(c_1)} ∩ Λ^{(p^r)}_{ν(c_2)} has index p^{2r}/gcd(G(ν(c_1), ν(c_2)), p^r) in ℤ^N. It contains p^r ℤ^N, so the number of residues a mod p^r with ⟨a, ν(b_1)⟩ ≡ ⟨a, ν(b_2)⟩ ≡ 0 is p^{rN}/index = p^{r(N−2)+v}.

The residues with a ≡ 0 mod p are a = p a′ with a′ mod p^{r−1} satisfying the same two congruences modulo p^{r−1}; the same count at level r − 1 gives p^{(r−1)(N−2)+min(v, r−1)} (for r = 1 this is the single residue 0).
Subtract; the bounds follow from min(v, r − 1) ≤ v.
acceptance: r = 1, b_1 and b_2 independent modulo p: #L = p^{N−2} − 1.
b_2 = g b_1 with g a unit modulo p^r: v = r and #L = p^{r(N−1)} − p^{(r−1)(N−1)}, the one-point count of Lemma 5.4.

nodes.title: The Veronese map preserves the minor valuation of a pair of primitive vectors
nodes.statement: Let d ≥ 1, p prime, r ≥ 1 and b_1, b_2 ∈ R_{n+1}(p^r). Then the capped p-adic valuations (at most r) of the minors of (ν_{d,n}(b_1), ν_{d,n}(b_2)) and of (b_1, b_2) are equal. Equivalently, for primitive integral lifts, gcd(G(ν_{d,n}(c_1), ν_{d,n}(c_2)), p^r) = gcd(G(c_1, c_2), p^r); running over all p and r this is Lemma 3.11 of the source, G(ν_{d,n}(x), ν_{d,n}(y)) = G(x, y) for linearly independent primitive x, y ∈ ℤ^{n+1}.
hypotheses: b_1, b_2 primitive modulo p^r
proofSteps: Criterion: for u primitive modulo p^r with u_0 a unit and any w, all minors of (u, w) vanish modulo p^e (e ≤ r) iff w ≡ λu mod p^e for some λ (λ = w_0/u_0): the minors u_0w_j − u_jw_0 give w_j ≡ (w_0/u_0)u_j, and the other minors are combinations of these after multiplying by the unit u_0: u_0(u_iw_j − u_jw_i) = u_i(u_0w_j − u_jw_0) − u_j(u_0w_i − u_iw_0).
If b_2 ≡ λ b_1 mod p^e then ν(b_2) ≡ λ^d ν(b_1) mod p^e, since every monomial has degree d.

Conversely let ν(b_2) ≡ μ ν(b_1) mod p^e with e ≥ 1 and (after renumbering) b_{1,0} a unit. The coordinates X_0^d and X_0^{d−1}X_j give b_{2,0}^d ≡ μ b_{1,0}^d and b_{2,0}^{d−1}b_{2,j} ≡ μ b_{1,0}^{d−1}b_{1,j}. If p | b_{2,0} then p | μ and ν(b_2) ≡ 0 mod p, contradicting the primitivity of ν(b_2); so b_{2,0} is a unit and b_{2,j} ≡ (b_{2,0}/b_{1,0}) b_{1,j} mod p^e.
By the criterion applied to (ν(b_1), ν(b_2)) (ν(b_1) is primitive) and to (b_1, b_2), both valuations are the largest e ≤ r for which b_2 is proportional to b_1 modulo p^e.
acceptance: d = 1: ν is the identity and the statement is trivial.
x = (1, 0), y = (1, p) in ℤ², d = 2: ν(x) = (1, 0, 0), ν(y) = (1, p, p²) and both gcds equal p.

sources.excerpt: Lemma 3.11. Let d, n ≥ 1. Let x, y ∈ Z^{n+1}_prim be two linearly independent vectors. Then G(ν_{d,n}(x), ν_{d,n}(y)) = G(x, y).

nodes.title: Sum of gcd(G(b_1, b_2), p^r) over pairs of primitive vectors
nodes.statement: For n ≥ 2, p prime and r ≥ 1: Σ_{b_1, b_2 ∈ R_{n+1}(p^r)} gcd(G(b_1, b_2), p^r) ≤ p^{2r(n+1)}((1 − p^{−(n+1)})² + 2p^{1−n}). With the trivial lower bound #R_{n+1}(p^r)² this is (5.14): the sum is p^{2r(n+1)}(1 + O(p^{1−n})), uniformly in r.
hypotheses: p prime
proofSteps: For fixed b_1 and 1 ≤ j ≤ r, the b_2 with p^j | G(b_1, b_2) are those with b_2 ≡ λb_1 mod p^j for some λ ∈ (ℤ/p^j)^× (criterion in veronese-minor-valuation); there are at most p^j · p^{(r−j)(n+1)} = p^{r(n+1)−jn} of them.
Write gcd(G, p^r) = 1 + Σ_{1 ≤ j ≤ r, p^j | G}(p^j − p^{j−1}) ≤ 1 + Σ_{1 ≤ j ≤ r, p^j | G} p^j and sum over pairs: the total is at most #R_{n+1}(p^r)² + #R_{n+1}(p^r)·p^{r(n+1)} Σ_{j≥1} p^{−j(n−1)}.
acceptance: r = 1: the pairs with p | G are the proportional pairs, (p^{n+1} − 1)(p − 1) of them, and the bound holds with room.
The bound is uniform in r.

sources.locator: arXiv v1, proof of Lemma 5.5, pp.54–55
sources.excerpt: for given b1 ∈ R_{n+1}(p^r), a little thought reveals that the number of b2 ∈ R_{n+1}(p^r) such that (b1, b2) ∈ F^{(e)}(p^r) is at most p^{r(n+1)−en}. This yields #F^{(e)}(p^r) ≪ p^{2r(n+1)−en}.
sources.match: Proof step 1; the sum is (5.14).

nodes.title: Second moment of σ(·; p^r)
nodes.statement: For d ≥ 1, n ≥ 2, p prime, r ≥ 1 and N = N_{d,n}: Σ_{a ∈ R_N(p^r)} σ(a; p^r)² ≤ p^{rN}((1 − p^{−(n+1)})² + 2p^{1−n}). Dividing by #R_N(p^r) = p^{rN}(1 − p^{−N}) gives the upper half of (5.15): the mean of σ² is at most 1 + O(p^{1−n}).
hypotheses: p prime
proofSteps: By two-point-incidence-count, #L(b_1, b_2; p^r) ≤ p^{r(N−2)} gcd(G(ν(b_1), ν(b_2)), p^r).
By veronese-minor-valuation, gcd(G(ν(b_1), ν(b_2)), p^r) = gcd(G(b_1, b_2), p^r).
Apply primitive-pair-minor-gcd-sum; the exponent is −2rn + r(N−2) + 2r(n+1) = rN.
acceptance: For d = 1 (linear forms, N = n + 1) σ(a; p^r) = 1 − p^{−n} for every primitive a, and the bound holds.
The bound is uniform in r.

sources.locator: arXiv v1, proof of Lemma 5.5, (5.12) and (5.15), pp.54–55
sources.match: The expansion and the second-moment estimate.

nodes.title: Variance of σ(·; p^r) over primitive coefficient vectors
nodes.statement: For d ≥ 1, n ≥ 2, p prime and r ≥ 1: (1/#R_N(p^r)) Σ_{a ∈ R_N(p^r)} (σ(a; p^r) − 1)² ≤ 4p^{1−n}, where N = N_{d,n}. This is the source's bound ≪ p^{−(n−1)} (stated for d ≥ 2, n ≥ 3) with an explicit constant, uniform in r.
hypotheses: p prime
proofSteps: Expand: mean((σ − 1)²) = mean(σ²) − 2 mean(σ) + 1.

Insert mean(σ) = (1 − x)(1 − y)/(1 − z) (local-density-first-moment) and mean(σ²) ≤ ((1 − x)² + 2w)/(1 − z) (local-density-second-moment), where x = p^{−(n+1)}, y = p^{−(N−1)}, z = p^{−N}, w = p^{1−n}.
The numerator is x² + 2w + 2y − 2xy − z ≤ 2w + 2p^{−n} + p^{−2n−2} ≤ 3.1·w, using N ≥ n + 1; the denominator 1 − z ≥ 7/8 since N ≥ 3. Hence the mean is at most (3.1·8/7) w < 4w.
acceptance: d = 1 (linear forms): σ(a; p^r) = 1 − p^{−n} for every primitive a, so the variance is p^{−2n} ≤ 4p^{1−n}.
In the proof of Proposition 5.2 (Part II) this bound is used for every prime p ∣ W with the uniform constant.

nodes.title: Capped valuation of vectors and the gradient strata R^{(e)}(p^r)
nodes.statement: Let p be prime and r ≥ 1. For a vector v ∈ (ℤ/p^rℤ)^I, its capped valuation v_p(v) is the largest e ∈ {0, …, r} with v ≡ 0 mod p^e. For a form f let ∇f = (∂f/∂X_i)_{i=0..n}. For 0 ≤ e ≤ r and N = N_{d,n}, the gradient stratum is R^{(e)}_N(p^r) = {a ∈ R_N(p^r) : ∃ x ∈ R_{n+1}(p^r) with f_a(x) ≡ 0 mod p^r and v_p(∇f_a(x)) = e}. The strata for e = 0, …, r cover F^loc(p^r) = {a ∈ R_N(p^r) : f_a has a primitive zero modulo p^r} (5.18); they are defined existentially and overlap in general, so their cardinalities do not add up to #F^loc(p^r).
hypotheses: p prime
0 ≤ e ≤ r
proofSteps: Define v_p(v) = max{e ≤ r : p^e divides every coordinate}, via Mathlib Nat.findGreatest on the residues' representatives.
Define ∇f_a through the partial derivatives (Mathlib MvPolynomial.pderiv) and R^{(e)} by the existential condition.
(5.18): a zero x of f_a has some valuation e ∈ {0, …, r} of ∇f_a(x), and conversely a ∈ R^{(e)} has the zero x.
acceptance: Linear forms: ∇f_a = a is primitive, so R^{(0)} is all of R_N(p^r) (n ≥ 1) and R^{(e)} = ∅ for e ≥ 1.
X_0X_1 in three variables lies in R^{(0)}(9) and R^{(2)}(9) (zeros (1,0,0) and (0,0,1)): the strata overlap.

sources.excerpt: given a prime number p and integers r, N ≥ 1 we define the p-adic valuation v_p(v) of a vector v ∈ (Z/p^rZ)^N as the largest integer e ∈ {0, . . . , r} such that we have v ≡ 0 mod p^e.
sources.match: The capped valuation.

sources.excerpt: R^{(e)}_{N_{d,n}}(p^r) = {a ∈ R_{N_{d,n}}(p^r) : ∃x ∈ R_{n+1}(p^r) f_a(x) ≡ 0 mod p^r, v_p(∇f_a(x)) = e}. (5.17) It will be very important for our purpose to note that F^loc_{d,n}(p^r) = ∪_{e=0}^r R^{(e)}_{N_{d,n}}(p^r).

nodes.title: High gradient valuation is rare: #R^{(e)}(p^r) ≤ 2p^{rN−e}
nodes.statement: For d ≥ 1, n ≥ 1, p prime and 1 ≤ e ≤ r: #R^{(e)}_{N}(p^r) ≤ 2p^{rN−e}, where N = N_{d,n}. (Stated in the source for d ≥ 2, n ≥ 3, with the cardinality sign omitted; see E641.)
hypotheses: p prime
1 ≤ e ≤ r
proofSteps: If a ∈ R^{(e)} with witness x, then x mod p^e lies in D_a(p^e) = {x ∈ R_{n+1}(p^e) : f_a(x) ≡ 0, ∇f_a(x) ≡ 0 mod p^e}, since e ≥ 1.

D_a(p^e) is stable under x ↦ gx for g ∈ (ℤ/p^e)^× (f_a(gx) = g^d f_a(x), ∇f_a(gx) = g^{d−1}∇f_a(x)), and the p^{e−1}(p − 1) multiples of a primitive x are distinct; so 1_{D_a(p^e) ≠ ∅} ≤ #D_a(p^e)/(p^{e−1}(p − 1)) ≤ 2#D_a(p^e)/p^e.
Swap the sums: #R^{(e)} ≤ (2/p^e) Σ_{x ∈ R_{n+1}(p^e)} #{a mod p^r : f_a(x) ≡ 0 and ∇f_a(x) ≡ 0 mod p^e}.

Fix x and renumber so that x_0 is a unit. Split off the coordinates c^{(i)} of a at the monomials X_0^{d−1}X_i (i = 0..n): f_a(x) = x_0^{d−1}Σ_i c^{(i)}x_i + g_a(x) and ∂_i f_a(x) = c^{(i)}x_0^{d−1} + ∂_i g_a(x) for i ≥ 1, where g_a does not involve c. The n + 1 conditions f_a(x) ≡ 0 and ∂_i f_a(x) ≡ 0 (1 ≤ i ≤ n) mod p^e fix c mod p^e (drop the ∂_0 condition for an upper bound), so at most p^{r(N−n−1)}·p^{(r−e)(n+1)} vectors a qualify.
acceptance: d = 1: the strata e ≥ 1 are empty, consistent with the bound.
In the proof of Proposition 5.2 (Part II) the bound gives Σ_{e ≥ 2} p^{κ(e+1)n}#R^{(e)} ≪ p^{rN−2+3κn} for κ < 1/n.

nodes.title: Hensel lifting at a fixed gradient valuation (Browning–Matthiesen)
nodes.statement: Let p be prime, s ≥ 1, F ∈ ℤ[t_1, …, t_s], A ∈ ℤ, a ∈ ℤ^s and integers m, ℓ, δ ≥ 0 with m ≥ 2δ + 1 and δ ≤ m − ℓ. Put R_δ(p^m, A; p^ℓ) = {t ∈ (ℤ/p^mℤ)^s : F(t) ≡ A mod p^m, v_p(∇F(t)) = δ, t ≡ a mod p^ℓ}. Then for every k ∈ ℤ, #R_δ(p^m, A; p^ℓ)/p^{m(s−1)} = #R_δ(p^{m+1}, A + kp^m; p^ℓ)/p^{(m+1)(s−1)}. In the form used by Browning–Le Boudec–Sawin (s = n + 1, A = k = 0, δ = e, ℓ = e + 1, a = x with v_p(∇F(x)) = e): for every s′ ≥ 2e + 2, #{b mod p^{s′} : b ≡ x mod p^{e+1}, F(b) ≡ 0 mod p^{s′}}/p^{s′n} equals the same quantity at level s′ − 1.
hypotheses: p prime
δ ≤ m − ℓ
proofSteps: For t ∈ R_δ(p^m, A; p^ℓ) and t′ ∈ ℤ^s: F(t + p^{m−δ}t′) ≡ F(t) + p^{m−δ}⟨t′, ∇F(t)⟩ ≡ A mod p^m by first-order-taylor-congruence (2(m − δ) ≥ m and p^δ | ∇F(t)); ∇F(t + p^{m−δ}t′) ≡ ∇F(t) mod p^{m−δ} by polynomial-congruence-under-perturbation, and m − δ ≥ δ + 1, so the valuation δ is kept; t + p^{m−δ}t′ ≡ a mod p^ℓ since ℓ ≤ m − δ. So R_δ(p^m, A; p^ℓ) is a union of cosets modulo p^{m−δ}.

For t mod p^{m+1} reducing into R_δ(p^m, A; p^ℓ), the vectors t + p^{m−δ}t′ (t′ mod p) run through p^s cosets modulo p^{m+1−δ}, and t + p^{m−δ}t′ ∈ R_δ(p^{m+1}, A + kp^m; p^ℓ) iff p^{−m}(F(t) − A) + p^{−δ}⟨t′, ∇F(t)⟩ ≡ k mod p, which has exactly p^{s−1} solutions t′ mod p because p^{−δ}∇F(t) is nonzero modulo p.
Counting cosets: #R_δ(p^{m+1}, A + kp^m; p^ℓ) = p^{s−1}·#R_δ(p^m, A; p^ℓ).
For the BLS form: every b ≡ x mod p^{e+1} has v_p(∇F(b)) = e (perturbation congruence), so the displayed set is R_e(p^{s′}, 0; p^{e+1}); apply the lemma with m = s′ − 1 ≥ 2e + 1.
acceptance: δ = 0: each nonsingular solution modulo p^m has exactly p^{s−1} lifts modulo p^{m+1} (classical Hensel).
The hypothesis m ≥ 2δ + 1 cannot be dropped: s = 1, F = t², p odd, δ = 1, m = 2, ℓ = 0, A = k = 0 gives p − 1 solutions at level 2 and none at level 3.

sources.excerpt: Lemma 3.3. Let m, ℓ, δ ∈ Z⩾0, with m ⩾ 2δ + 1, 0 ⩽ δ ⩽ m − ℓ. Suppose we are given a polynomial F ∈ Z[t1, . . . , ts], A ∈ Z and a ∈ Z^s.
sources.match: Hypotheses of the lemma.

sources.excerpt: Then we have #Rδ(p^m, A; p^ℓ)/p^{m(s−1)} = #Rδ(p^{m+1}, A + kp^m; p^ℓ)/p^{(m+1)(s−1)}, uniformly for k ∈ Z/pZ.
sources.match: Conclusion of the lemma.

sources.locator: arXiv v1, proof of Lemma 5.7, p.57
sources.excerpt: we use Hensel’s lemma (in the form of [6, Lemma 3.3] with #C_{a,x}(p^{e+1}; p^s) = #R_e(p^s, 0; p^{e+1}) for example) to deduce that for any s ≥ 2e + 2, we have #C_{a,x}(p^{e+1}; p^s)/p^{sn} = #C_{a,x}(p^{e+1}; p^{s−1})/p^{(s−1)n}.
sources.match: The form used in Lemma 5.7.

nodes.title: Lower bound for σ(a; p^r) on a gradient stratum
nodes.statement: For d ≥ 1, n ≥ 0, p prime, r ≥ 1, 0 ≤ e ≤ r and a ∈ R^{(e)}_N(p^r): σ(a; p^r) ≥ p^{−(e+1)n}. (Source: d ≥ 2, n ≥ 3.)
hypotheses: p prime
0 ≤ e ≤ r
proofSteps: Choose a witness x ∈ R_{n+1}(p^r) with f_a(x) ≡ 0 mod p^r and v_p(∇f_a(x)) = e. If e = r, x alone gives σ ≥ p^{−rn} ≥ p^{−(r+1)n}.
For e < r: σ(a; p^r) ≥ #C_{a,x}(p^{e+1}; p^r)/p^{rn}, where C_{a,x}(p^c; p^s) = {b ∈ R_{n+1}(p^s) : b ≡ x mod p^c, f_a(b) ≡ 0 mod p^s} (such b are automatically primitive).

Case r ≤ 2e + 1: for b ≡ x mod p^{e+1}, f_a(b) ≡ f_a(x) + ⟨∇f_a(x), b − x⟩ ≡ 0 mod p^r (first-order-taylor-congruence with p^e | ∇f_a(x) and p^{e+1} | b − x); so C = {b ≡ x mod p^{e+1}}, #C = p^{(r−e−1)(n+1)} and σ ≥ p^{r−e−1}·p^{−(e+1)n}.

Case r ≥ 2e + 2: by fixed-gradient-valuation-hensel-lifting applied r − 2e − 1 times, #C(p^r)/p^{rn} = #C(p^{2e+1})/p^{(2e+1)n}, and by the previous case #C(p^{2e+1}) = p^{e(n+1)}; so σ ≥ p^{e−(e+1)n} ≥ p^{−(e+1)n}.
acceptance: e = 0 (a nonsingular zero): σ(a; p^r) ≥ p^{−n} for every r.
In the proof of Proposition 5.2 (Part II) this gives σ(a; p^r)^{−κ} ≤ p^{κ(e+1)n} on R^{(e)}.

sources.excerpt: Lemma 5.7. Let d ≥ 2 and n ≥ 3. Let also p be a prime number and r ≥ 1. For e ∈ {0, . . . , r} and a ∈ R^{(e)}_{N_{d,n}}(p^r), we have σ(a; p^r) ≥ 1/p^{(e+1)n}.
sources.match: The theorem.

sources.locator: arXiv v1, proof of Lemma 5.7, p.57
sources.excerpt: Applying this equality r − (2e + 1) times, we derive σ(a; p^r) ≥ #C_{a,x}(p^{e+1}; p^{2e+1})/p^{(2e+1)n}, which completes the proof since we have #C_{a,x}(p^{e+1}; p^{2e+1}) = p^{e(n+1)} by the previous case.
sources.match: Proof step 4.

nodes.title: Convex concentration of a bounded mass distribution
nodes.statement: Let g ∈ ℝ, 1/2 < ε < 1 and x_1, …, x_k ∈ ℝ with 0 ≤ x_i ≤ εg and Σ_i x_i = g. Then Σ_i x_i² ≤ (ε² + (1 − ε)²)g² = (1 − 2ε(1 − ε))g².
hypotheses: 0 ≤ x_i ≤ εg
Σ x_i = g
proofSteps: If g ≤ 0 the hypotheses force every x_i = 0 and g = 0. Let g > 0 and let x_1 be a largest coordinate.
If x_1 < g/2: Σ x_i² ≤ x_1 Σ x_i < g²/2 ≤ (ε² + (1 − ε)²)g², since ε² + (1 − ε)² ≥ 1/2.
If x_1 ≥ g/2: Σ_{i≥2} x_i² ≤ (Σ_{i≥2} x_i)² = (g − x_1)², so Σ x_i² ≤ x_1² + (g − x_1)², which is increasing in x_1 on [g/2, εg] and equals (ε² + (1 − ε)²)g² at x_1 = εg.
(The source argues by convexity: the maximum over the polytope {x ∈ [0, εg]^k : Σx = g} is at a vertex, and the vertices are the k(k − 1) permutations of (εg, (1 − ε)g, 0, …, 0); see E642.)
acceptance: k = 2, x = (εg, (1 − ε)g): equality.
ε = 0.99: Σ x_i² ≤ 0.9802 g², the constant used in Proposition 5.10.

sources.excerpt: Lemma 5.9. Fix 1/2 < ǫ < 1. Suppose 0 ≤ x_i ≤ ǫg, . . . 0 ≤ x_k ≤ ǫg and Σ_{i=1}^k x_i = g. Then ||x||² = Σ_{i=1}^k x_i² ≤ g²(ǫ² + (1 − ǫ)²) = g²(1 − 2ǫ(1 − ǫ)).
sources.match: The lemma.

nodes.title: Numerical core of the model-count concentration
nodes.statement: For every C ≥ 0 there is g_0 such that for all g ≥ g_0 and every finite family of pairs of positive integers (k_j, n_j) with Σ_j k_j n_j = g in which no j has both k_j = 1 and n_j ≥ 0.99g: (1/2)Σ_j k_j n_j² log n_j + Cg² < 0.495 g² log g.
hypotheses: k_j, n_j ≥ 1
Σ_j k_j n_j = g
no block with k_j = 1 and n_j ≥ 0.99g
proofSteps: Put x_j = k_j n_j. Case A, every x_j < 0.99g: since k_j ≥ 1 and n_j ≤ g, k_j n_j² log n_j ≤ x_j² log g, and convex-concentration-inequality with ε = 0.99 gives Σ_j x_j² ≤ 0.9802g²; so the left side is at most 0.4901 g² log g + Cg².

Case B, some x_{j0} ≥ 0.99g: then k_{j0} ≥ 2 (a block with k = 1 has x = n < 0.99g), so n_{j0} ≤ g/2 and k_{j0}n_{j0}² log n_{j0} = x_{j0}n_{j0} log n_{j0} ≤ (g²/2) log g; the other blocks have Σ_{j≠j0} x_j ≤ 0.01g and n_j ≤ 0.01g, so Σ_{j≠j0} k_j n_j² log n_j ≤ Σ_{j≠j0} x_j n_j log g ≤ 10^{−4} g² log g. The left side is at most 0.25005 g² log g + Cg².
In both cases the left side is below 0.495 g² log g once 0.0049 log g > C, i.e. for g ≥ g_0 = ⌈exp(C/0.0049)⌉ + 1 (log n_j ≥ 0 by Mathlib Real.log_nonneg).
acceptance: A single block (k, n) = (1, g) is excluded by hypothesis, and indeed (1/2)g² log g exceeds the bound: the threshold separates it.
Blocks (2, g/2): (1/2)·2·(g/2)² log(g/2) ≈ 0.25 g² log g < 0.495 g² log g.

sources.locator: arXiv v1, proof of Proposition 5.10, p.32
sources.excerpt: Define x_i := [K_i : Q]n_i. Suppose x_i < 0.99g for all 1 ≤ i ≤ k. By Lemma 5.9, Σ_{i=1}^k [K_i : Q]n_i² log n_i ≤ Σ_{i=1}^k [K_i : Q]²n_i² log g = Σ x_i² log g ≤ (1 − 2 · 0.99 · 0.01)g² log g
sources.match: Case A.

sources.locator: arXiv v1, proof of Proposition 5.10, p.32
sources.excerpt: If [K_{i0} : Q] ≥ 2, then n_{i0} ≤ g/2 and the above is at most ≈ (1/2)g² log g. Therefore, [K_{i0} : Q] = 1 and n_{i0} ≥ 0.99g.
sources.match: Case B, with the corrected factor 1/2 of E643.

nodes.title: Large model-ring orbit counts force a large imaginary-quadratic block (corrected)
nodes.statement: Fix a prime p. There is g_0 = g_0(p) such that for every g ≥ g_0 and every model ring R_{L,n} = ∏_i M_{n_i}(O_{L_i}) with conjugate-transpose involution, where the L_i are distinct CM fields generated by p-Weil numbers with totally real subfields K_i and Σ_i [K_i:ℚ]n_i = g, the following holds: if the number n_{L,n} of R_{L,n}^×-orbits on the positive symmetric units of R_{L,n} (action a ↦ γ* a γ) satisfies log n_{L,n} ≥ 0.495 g² log g, then some i_0 has [K_{i_0}:ℚ] = 1 and n_{i_0} ≥ 0.99g. (Printed: threshold 0.99 g² log g and no restriction on g; corrected through the factor 1/2 of (55), E643.)
hypotheses: p a fixed prime
Σ_i [K_i:ℚ]n_i = g
proofSteps: GN.3 (Lipnowski–Tsimerman (55), corrected by the factor 1/2): log n_{L,n} ≤ (1/2)Σ_i [K_i:ℚ]n_i² log n_i + C_p g² with C_p depending only on p.
Apply weighted-square-concentration to the blocks (k_i, n_i) = ([K_i:ℚ], n_i) with C = C_p: if no i has [K_i:ℚ] = 1 and n_i ≥ 0.99g, then log n_{L,n} < 0.495 g² log g for g ≥ g_0.
acceptance: A single block L = ℚ(√−d) of class number one with n = g: log n_{L,n} = (1/2)g² log g + O_p(g²) exceeds the threshold and the conclusion holds with i_0 that block.
The printed threshold 0.99 g² log g is never reached once the coefficient 1/2 is restored, so the printed statement is vacuous for large g.

sources.excerpt: Proposition 5.10. Suppose n_{L,n}, the number of ∗-conjugation orbits of R^×_{L,n} on the positive symmetric elements of R^×_{L,n}, satisfies log n_{L,n} ≥ 0.99g² log g. Then there is some i0 for which n_{i0} ≥ 0.99g and [K_{i0} : Q] = 1.
sources.match: The proposition, with the corrected threshold.

sources.excerpt: the number of ∗-conjugation orbits of R^×_{L,n} on the positive symmetric elements of R^×_{L,n} is at most Σ_{i=1}^k [K_i : Q]n_i² log n_i + Σ_{i=1}^k O([K_i : Q]²n_i²)

nodes.title: Conditionally, most ppavs over 𝔽_p have a large elliptic or real-Weil isogeny factor (corrected Theorem 0.2)
nodes.statement: Let p be a prime such that p satisfies the corrected conclusion of Lipnowski–Tsimerman Lemma 5.11: there are an elliptic curve E_0/𝔽_p and C_0 with log n_{E_0^g} ≥ (1/2)g² log g − C_0 g² for all g ≥ 1 (true when p splits in one of the nine imaginary quadratic fields of class number one, a set of primes of density ≥ 1 − 2^{−9}). Assume (H1) Lipnowski–Tsimerman Conjecture 5.2: there is C_p such that for every g-dimensional abelian variety A/𝔽_p admitting a principal polarization and isogenous to A_1^{n_1} × ⋯ × A_k^{n_k} with A_i pairwise non-isogenous simple and End⁰(A_i) ≅ L_i a CM field, |log n_A − log n_{L,n}| ≤ C_p g², where n_A is the number of isomorphism classes of principal polarizations on A (Aut(A)-orbits) and n_{L,n} is the orbit count of the model ring R_{L,n} = ∏ M_{n_i}(O_{L_i}); (H2) the same inequality for A isogenous to A_1^{n_1} × ⋯ × A_k^{n_k} × B_0^m with m ≥ 1, where B_0 is the simple abelian surface over 𝔽_p with Frobenius polynomial (x² − p)² and End⁰(B_0) = D, the quaternion algebra over ℚ(√p) ramified exactly at its two infinite places, with model count n_{L,n}·n_D(m), n_D(m) the number of GL_m(O_D)-orbits on the positive definite quaternion-hermitian matrices in GL_m(O_D) (O_D a maximal order, ∗ the conjugate transpose with the canonical involution of D). Call a g-dimensional principally polarized abelian variety (A, λ) over 𝔽_p bad if A has no isogeny factor E^h with E/𝔽_p an elliptic curve and h ≥ 0.99g, and no isogeny factor B_0^m with 2m ≥ 0.99g. Then the proportion of bad classes among the A(p, g) isomorphism classes of g-dimensional ppavs over 𝔽_p (uniform measure) is at most exp(−0.005 g² log g + O_p(g²)); in particular it tends to 0 as g → ∞. (Printed Theorem 0.2 / Corollary 5.13 assume Conjecture 5.2 only and conclude an elliptic factor E^h; that deduction has a gap for B_0-factors, E644.)
hypotheses: p satisfies the corrected conclusion of Lemma 5.11
H1 (Conjecture 5.2)
H2 (its analogue with B_0-factors)
proofSteps: (Part II AbelianSchemesAndArithmeticModuliPartIIFiniteFields, corrected Theorem 0.1) The number B(p, g) of isomorphism classes of g-dimensional abelian varieties over 𝔽_p satisfies log B(p, g) ≤ C′_p g².

(Part II, prime-field endomorphism algebras; AbelianSchemesAndArithmeticModuli A6 Poincaré reducibility) Every simple abelian variety over 𝔽_p has End⁰ a CM field of degree 2·dim, except the isogeny class of B_0; so every A falls under H1 or H2 and g = Σ_i [K_i:ℚ]n_i + 2m. A block with [K_i:ℚ] = 1 is a power of an elliptic curve.

(GN.3, corrected (55), and the quaternionic mass bound requested there) log n_model ≤ (1/2)Σ_i [K_i:ℚ]n_i² log n_i + 2m² log m + O_p(g²) ≤ (1/2)Σ over blocks k n² log n + O_p(g²), counting B_0^m as a block (k, n) = (1, 2m).
For bad A no block has k = 1 and n ≥ 0.99g, so H1/H2 and weighted-square-concentration (with C = C_p + the O_p constant) give log n_A < 0.495 g² log g for g ≥ g_0.

(ST.0: A(p, g) = Σ_A n_A over isomorphism classes of abelian varieties) The number of bad ppav classes is at most B(p, g)·exp(0.495 g² log g), while A(p, g) ≥ n_{E_0^g} ≥ exp((1/2)g² log g − C_0 g²); the ratio is at most exp(−0.005 g² log g + O_p(g²)).
acceptance: g = 1: every principally polarized abelian variety is an elliptic curve E = E^1 with 1 ≥ 0.99, so no class is bad.
The alternative B_0^m cannot be dropped without new input: principal polarizations on B_0^m have log count 2m² log m + O(m²), the same leading term per dimension as E^g (E644).

nodes.title: Kolmogorov distance between probability measures on ℝ
nodes.statement: For Borel probability measures μ, ν on ℝ with distribution functions F_μ(x) = μ((−∞, x]) and F_ν, the Kolmogorov distance is d_K(μ, ν) = sup_{x ∈ ℝ} |F_μ(x) − F_ν(x)|. It takes values in [0, 1], is symmetric, satisfies the triangle inequality, vanishes exactly when μ = ν, and dominates |μ((−∞, x]) − ν((−∞, x])| for every x.
hypotheses: μ, ν Borel probability measures on ℝ
proofSteps: Define d_K as the supremum over x of |cdf μ x − cdf ν x| (Mathlib ProbabilityTheory.cdf); the family is bounded by 1 (Mathlib ProbabilityTheory.cdf_le_one), so the supremum is a real number and dominates each term (Mathlib le_ciSup).
For probability measures cdf μ x = μ((−∞, x]) (Mathlib ProbabilityTheory.cdf_eq_real); equal distribution functions give equal measures.

sources.excerpt: If Conjecture 5.2 is true, then the discrepancy between the normalized spacing measure µg = µ(Ag/Fp) for Ag/Fp and the GUE normalized spacing measure µGUE is ≥ 0.99.

nodes.title: Normalized eigenangle spacing measure
nodes.statement: Let θ be a finite multiset of N ≥ 1 angles in [0, 2π) (repetitions kept). Sort it as θ_1 ≤ ⋯ ≤ θ_N; its cyclic gaps are θ_{i+1} − θ_i (1 ≤ i < N) and the wrap-around gap θ_1 + 2π − θ_N. The normalized spacing measure is μ(θ) = (1/N) Σ_gaps δ_{(N/2π)·gap}, a probability measure on [0, ∞) of mean 1. For an integral polynomial P, its eigenangles are the arguments in [0, 2π) of its complex roots with multiplicity; for a g-dimensional abelian variety A/𝔽_p the spacing measure of A is μ(θ(P_A)) for its Frobenius polynomial P_A (degree 2g, roots of absolute value √p), and μ_g is the average of these over the uniform measure on the isomorphism classes of g-dimensional ppavs over 𝔽_p.
hypotheses: θ a finite multiset of angles in [0, 2π)
proofSteps: Sort θ (Mathlib Multiset.sort), form the list of consecutive differences with the wrap-around gap, rescale by N/2π and average the point masses (Mathlib MeasureTheory.Measure.dirac).
Eigenangles: map the roots of P in ℂ (Mathlib Polynomial.roots) to Complex.arg reduced into [0, 2π) (Mathlib toIcoMod).
The gaps are nonnegative and sum to 2π (telescoping), so μ(θ) is a probability measure on [0, ∞) with mean 1.
The average μ_g over ppav classes uses ST.0's ppav count and the Frobenius polynomial of the Part II.
acceptance: Four equal angles give gaps 0, 0, 0, 2π, so μ = (3/4)δ_0 + (1/4)δ_4.
The angles {0, π} give μ = δ_1 (the wrap-around gap counts).

sources.locator: arXiv v1, Corollary 5.14 and its proof, p.34
sources.excerpt: If z(E), z(E) are roots of the Frobenius characteristic polynomial of E, then z, z both occur with multiplicity ≥ h in the Frobenius characteristic polynomial of A. But then for α = h/g ≥ 0.99, the normalized spacing measure is αδ0+ weighted sum of point masses

nodes.title: Repeated eigenangles force mass at zero spacing
nodes.statement: Let θ be a multiset of N angles in [0, 2π) containing two distinct values s ≠ t each with multiplicity at least h. Then the normalized spacing measure satisfies μ(θ)({0}) ≥ 2(h − 1)/N. (Correction of the source's αδ_0 with α = h/g, E645.)

s ≠ t each of multiplicity ≥ h
proofSteps: In the sorted list the ≥ h copies of s are consecutive and give ≥ h − 1 zero gaps; likewise for t; these gap positions are distinct.
The wrap-around gap θ_1 + 2π − θ_N is positive for angles in [0, 2π), so it is not counted among them.
Each zero gap contributes mass 1/N at 0.

nodes.title: Kolmogorov distance dominates a difference of left-tail masses
nodes.statement: For Borel probability measures μ, ν on ℝ and x ∈ ℝ: μ((−∞, x]) − ν((−∞, x]) ≤ d_K(μ, ν). In particular, if μ is supported on [0, ∞) and ν((−∞, 0]) = 0 (for instance ν atomless and supported on [0, ∞)), then d_K(μ, ν) ≥ μ({0}).
hypotheses: μ, ν probability measures on ℝ
proofSteps: cdf μ x = μ((−∞, x]) for probability measures (Mathlib ProbabilityTheory.cdf_eq_real), and |cdf μ x − cdf ν x| ≤ d_K(μ, ν) (kolmogorov-distance API).
For μ supported on [0, ∞), μ((−∞, 0]) = μ({0}).
acceptance: μ = δ_0, ν = uniform on [0, 1]: d_K = 1 = μ({0}).
μ = ν: both sides are 0.

nodes.title: Conditionally, ppav spacing statistics over 𝔽_p are far from any atomless law (corrected Corollary 5.14)
nodes.statement: Under the hypotheses of most-ppavs-have-a-large-elliptic-or-real-weil-factor (p as in the corrected Lemma 5.11, H1 and H2), let μ_g be the average over the g-dimensional ppav classes over 𝔽_p of the normalized eigenangle spacing measures of their Frobenius polynomials. Then μ_g({0}) ≥ 0.99 − o(1), and for every probability measure ν on ℝ with ν((−∞, 0]) = 0 — in particular the GUE spacing law, which is absolutely continuous on [0, ∞) — liminf_{g→∞} d_K(μ_g, ν) ≥ 0.99. (Printed: discrepancy ≥ 0.99 for each g in an unspecified metric, under Conjecture 5.2 alone; E644, E645.)
hypotheses: p satisfies the corrected conclusion of Lemma 5.11
H1 and H2
proofSteps: By most-ppavs-have-a-large-elliptic-or-real-weil-factor, a proportion 1 − o(1) of ppav classes have a factor E^h (h ≥ 0.99g) or B_0^m (2m ≥ 0.99g).

(Part II: Frobenius polynomials are multiplicative and isogeny invariant) For E^h the Frobenius polynomial of A is divisible by (x² − a_E x + p)^h, whose two roots are distinct (a_E² ≠ 4p since 4p is not a square); for B_0^m it is divisible by (x² − p)^{2m}, roots ±√p of multiplicity h = 2m. So two distinct eigenangles have multiplicity ≥ h ≥ 0.99g.
zero-gap-mass-from-repeated-angles gives mass ≥ 2(h − 1)/(2g) ≥ 0.99 − 1/g at 0 for each such class; averaging, μ_g({0}) ≥ (1 − o(1))(0.99 − 1/g).
μ_g is supported on [0, ∞) (normalized-eigenangle-spacing-measure API), so kolmogorov-distance-lower-bound-from-an-atom gives d_K(μ_g, ν) ≥ μ_g({0}) − ν((−∞, 0]) = μ_g({0}).
acceptance: For ν = δ_1 (the spacing law of equally spaced angles) the conclusion also holds.
The bound is on liminf in g; no statement is made for fixed g.

nodes.title: Conditionally, ppavs over 𝔽_p violate the enhanced Cohen–Lenstra prediction (corrected Corollary 5.20)
nodes.statement: Let p be an odd prime satisfying the corrected conclusion of Lemma 5.11 and assume H1 and H2 (as in most-ppavs-have-a-large-elliptic-or-real-weil-factor). Let S be the set of primes ℓ ≠ p with ℓ < (p + 1)², and assume that for each ℓ ∈ S the limit CL_{(1,2),ℓ}(0, 0) = lim_{g→∞} Haar_g{F ∈ M_g(ℤ_ℓ) : coker(1 − F) = 0 and coker(1 − F²) = 0} exists (E646). Then, for (A, λ) uniform among the g-dimensional ppav classes over 𝔽_p, Prob(A(𝔽_p)[S^∞] = 0 and A(𝔽_{p²})[S^∞] = 0) → 0 as g → ∞, whereas CL_{(1,2),S}(0, 0) = ∏_{ℓ∈S} CL_{(1,2),ℓ}(0, 0) > 0. Hence the joint law of (A(𝔽_p)[S^∞], A(𝔽_{p²})[S^∞]) does not converge to CL_{(1,2),S}: the enhanced Cohen–Lenstra model does not describe this family. (Printed for every p satisfying Lemma 5.11; false in its proof at p = 2, E647.)
hypotheses: p odd, satisfying the corrected Lemma 5.11
H1 and H2
existence of CL_{(1,2),ℓ}(0,0) for ℓ ∈ S
proofSteps: By most-ppavs-have-a-large-elliptic-or-real-weil-factor, with probability 1 − o(1) A has an isogeny factor E (h ≥ 1 suffices) or B_0.

(Part II, corrected Lemma 5.19, odd p) E(𝔽_p) and E(𝔽_{p²}) are not both p-groups, so some prime ℓ ≠ p divides #E(𝔽_p) or #E(𝔽_{p²}); by the Hasse bound (EllipticCurves Layer 3) ℓ ≤ #E(𝔽_{p²}) ≤ (p + 1)², and (p + 1)² is not prime, so ℓ ∈ S.
#B_0(𝔽_p) = (p − 1)² is even, and 2 ∈ S.
(Part II: point counts are isogeny invariant and multiplicative) #E(𝔽_{p^r}) or #B_0(𝔽_{p^r}) divides #A(𝔽_{p^r}), so A(𝔽_p)[S^∞] or A(𝔽_{p²})[S^∞] is nonzero (Cauchy's theorem).

Positivity: the event depends on F mod ℓ only; the finite-g probabilities are ≥ ∏_{j≥1}(1 − 2^{−j}) for ℓ = 2 and ≥ 2∏_{j≥1}(1 − 3^{−j}) − 1 > 0 for odd ℓ (Example 5.17: ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/zero-cokernel-probability-at-two, ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/zero-cokernel-probability-lower-bound-at-odd-primes, on the finite-level laws of ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/enhanced-cohen-lenstra-finite-level-law), so the assumed limits are positive and so is their finite product.

nodes.title: The quadratic families S_n over F_q(t)
nodes.statement: Let q be an odd prime power, K = F_q(t) and n ≥ 0. Let P_n be the set of squarefree polynomials f ∈ F_q[t] of degree exactly n, and let (F_q^×)² act on P_n by multiplication. The family S_n is the quotient P_n/(F_q^×)², and its element [f] is the quadratic extension L_f = K[y]/(y² − f) of K (a field whenever n is odd, since then f is not a square in K). For odd n, L_f is ramified at the place ∞ of K and its discriminant divisor has degree n + 1; L_f and L_{f'} are K-isomorphic exactly when f' = u²f for a unit u ∈ F_q^×. The ring O_{L_f} is the integral closure of F_q[t] in L_f. The monic representatives P_n^mon ⊂ P_n are recorded as part of the data: for even q the square classes of F_q^× collapse and the parametrisation is not the one used here.
hypotheses: q odd (the Kummer description y² = f needs characteristic ≠ 2)
n ≥ 0; S_n is the EVW family for n odd
squarefree means squarefree in F_q[t]; degree is natDegree
proofSteps: Define P_n and P_n^mon as sets of polynomials, and the setoid f ~ f' ⇔ ∃ u ∈ F_q^×, f' = u² f; S_n is its quotient type.

Define the quadratic polynomial y² − f over the rational function field and L_f as its adjoining field; irreducibility for odd n is the lemma that an odd-degree polynomial is not a square in F_q(t) (compare degrees), making AdjoinRoot a field.

The K-isomorphism criterion: two Kummer extensions K(√f), K(√f') of a field of characteristic ≠ 2 coincide iff f'/f is a square in K; for squarefree f, f' of the same degree this forces f'/f ∈ (F_q^×)² (unique factorisation).
acceptance: S_1 has 2q elements (q monic linear polynomials, two square classes of leading coefficients), not 2(q − 1).
Each class of S_n contains exactly (q − 1)/2 polynomials, so averages over S_n equal averages over P_n.

nodes.title: Size of the odd-degree quadratic family
nodes.statement: Let q be odd. For every odd n ≥ 3, |S_n| = 2(q^n − q^{n−1}); for n = 1, |S_1| = 2q.
hypotheses: q odd
n odd; the case n = 1 is stated separately
proofSteps: Each class of S_n has exactly (q − 1)/2 representatives in P_n (API card_quadraticFamily_fiber: u² f = f forces u = ±1 since f ≠ 0).
P_n = ⊔_{a ∈ F_q^×} a·P_n^mon, so |P_n| = (q − 1)|P_n^mon|.
By ST.4/count-of-squarefree-monic-polynomials-over-a-finite-field, |P_n^mon| = q^n − q^{n−1} for n ≥ 2 and q for n = 1.
Therefore |S_n| = |P_n|/((q − 1)/2) = 2|P_n^mon|.
